                "latexMainText": "\n\\hfill \\\\\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Definition}}\\\\\n\n\\begin{itemize}\n    \\item The configuration space is usually denoted $\\Omega$. As indicated by its name, the set $\\Omega$ contains all the possible configurations of a probabilistic model.\n    \\item Its elements are usually denoted $\\omega$, and we will call them 'elementary configurations'.\n\\end{itemize}\n\n\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\nWarning : the name of the space $\\Omega$ and its elements $\\omega$ vary according to contexts and languages. $\\Omega$ is often called the 'sample space' or 'universe', and the elements $\\omega$ 'samples','outcomes' or 'realizations'.  \\\\\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Examples (1)}}\\\\\n\nProbabilistic models are very useful to analyse dice rolls and card games. What is a relevant configuration space \n\\begin{itemize}\n    \\item to model a dice roll ? %$\\Omega = \\{1,2,3,4,5,6\\}$\n    \\item to model $2$ dice rolls ? %$\\Omega = \\{1,2,3,4,5,6\\} \\times \\{1,2,3,4,5,6\\}$\n    \\item to model $n$ dice rolls ? What is the size of this configuration space? %$\\Omega = \\{1,2,3,4,5,6\\}^n$, which is of size $6^n$.\n\\end{itemize}\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Examples (2)}}\\\\\n\nAssume that $\\mathcal{S}$ is a $52$ card deck and that we are interested in modeling an experiment where a player draws cards from the card game. \nWhat should we chose as configuration space when \n\\begin{itemize}\n    \\item the player draws one card ? %$\\Omega_1 = \\mathcal{S}$\n    \\item the player draws one card, puts it back and draws another card ? %$\\Omega_2 = \\Omega_1 \\times \\Omega_1$\n    \\item the player draws two cards without putting them back ? %$\\Omega_2 $, or $\\Omega_2\\setminus \\{ (\\omega,\\omega),  \\omega \\in \\Omega_1 \\}$\n\\end{itemize}\n\nAssume a player draws $n$ cards without putting them back in the deck. What is the size of the smallest configuration space describing the possible results ? \n\n%$$52\\times (52-1)\\times (52-2)\\times ... \\times (52-n+1)=\\frac{52!}{(52-n)!}$$\n\n\nNote that when using Cartesian products, we have $(a,b)\\neq (b,a)$. The order between the card draws is taken into account. In card games, the order in which cards are drawn is often not important. In that case, when drawing $2$ cards, we have $(a,b)\\sim (b,a)$.\n\n\\vspace{0.1cm}\n\nIf we do not distinguish results up to permutations, what is the size of the configuration space when\n\\begin{itemize}\n    \\item the player draws one card ? %$52$\n\n    \\item the player draws $n$ cards without putting them back  ? \n    %$$\\frac{52!}{(52-n)!n!}=\n    %\\begin{pmatrix}52\\\\ n \\end{pmatrix}$$\n\\end{itemize}\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Examples (3)}}\\\\\n\n\nIn this course we are particularly interested in signal and image processing problems. \n\n\\vspace{0.1cm}\n\nWhat are the relevant configuration spaces when studying \n\n\\begin{itemize}\n    \\item real signals observed on $1000$ points ? %$\\Omega = \\mathbb{R}^{1000}$\n    \\item continuous real signals of duration $1$ second ? %$\\Omega =C([0,1])$\n    \\item $256\\times 256$ color images ? %$\\Omega = \\mathbb{R}^{256\\times 256 \\times 3}$\n\\end{itemize}\n"

When $\\Omega$ is not a finite set, some mathematical problems can appear, and not every subset $A\\subset \\Omega$ is considered to be an event. For instance when $\\Omega = \\mathbb{R}$, events are subsets of $\\mathbb{R}$ which can be constructed 'easily' from intervals. For instance\n$$ A= \\bigcup_{i\\in \\mathbb{N}} \\left[\\frac{i}{2},\\frac{i+1}{2}\\right] $$\nis an event. Its probability is given by the sum of $P\\left([\\frac{i}{2},\\frac{i+1}{2}]\\right)$. \n\nOn the other hand, if we accept the axiom of choice, it is possible to define complicated sets which cannot be expressed as a (countable) union or intersections of intervals. These subsets lead to unconvienient results, and we often which to exclude them. We need then to restrict the set of subset on which we will define the values of probabilities. This is done via the use of $\\sigma$-algebras.\n\n \\\\\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Definition}}\\\\\n\nThe events are the subsets of $\\Omega$ on which we will define probability values. The set of events is called the $\\sigma$-algebra. In order to be consistent with the probability calculus, the $\\sigma$-algebra $\\mathcal{A}$ on $\\Omega$ must satisfy the following axioms:\n\\begin{itemize}\n\\item $\\Omega \\in  \\mathcal{A}$ ($\\rightarrow$ axiom 1 of probabilities)\n\\item $A \\in \\mathcal{A} \\Rightarrow A^{c}\\in \\mathcal{A}$ ($\\rightarrow$ consequence 1 of probabilities)\n\\item if $A_i\\in \\mathcal{A}$ for $i\\in \\mathbb{N}$, then $\\bigcup_{i\\in \\mathbb{N}} A_i \\in \\mathcal{A}$ ($\\rightarrow$ axiom 3 of probabilities)\n\\end{itemize}\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Examples}}\\\\\n\n\\begin{itemize}\n    \\item When $\\Omega$ is finite, the $\\sigma$-algebra is usually $\\mathcal{P}(\\Omega)$: every subset of $\\Omega$ is an event.\n    \\item when $\\Omega= \\mathbb{R}$, the $\\sigma$-algebra is obtained by taking countable unions of intervals and their complements.\n\\end{itemize}\n\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Stochastic process}}\\\\\n\nThough the concept of $\\sigma$-algebra is first used to avoid the problems brought by some subsets of $\\mathbb{R}$ and can be seen as a mere technicallity, it later becomes an important tool to formalize properties of stochastic processes.                 "text": "<div class=\"remark\" id=\"rem:ProbAss\">\n<p><strong>Remark 3</strong> (<strong>Assignment of\r\nprobabilities</strong>). </p>\n<p><br/>\r\nTo model real life situations, we assign probabilities to events that\r\nreflect what we know about the situation. The probabilities on the\r\nconfiguration space\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi mathvariant=\"normal\">\u03a9</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\Omega</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nare usually assigned according to one of the two following\r\nprinciples.</p>\n<ul>\n<li><p><strong>Indistinguishability</strong>.                 "latexMainText": "\n\\hfil \\\\\nTo model real life situations, we assign probabilities to events that reflect what we know about the situation. The probabilities on the configuration space $\\Omega$ are usually assigned according to one of the two following principles.  \n\n\\begin{itemize}\n    \\item \\textbf{Indistinguishability}. Assume that in a certain experiment, the elements of $\\Omega$ are perfectly indistinguishable. The probability of an event $A$ is then given by the number of configuration $k$ in which it occurs ($\\omega \\in A$) divided by the total number of configuration $n$: $\\frac{k}{n}$. It is for instance the case when we draw a card from a card game without seeing what is on the card: they are all indistinguishable.\n    \\item \\textbf{Probabilities as frequencies}. Assume that an experiment that produces output value in $\\Omega$ has been repeated $n$ times. If $k$ of the output values belongs to the event $A$, the probability assigned to $A$ is the number $\\frac{k}{n}$. This can be used to evaluate the probabilities of the outcomes of an asymmetrical die. We will come back to the link between probabilities and frequencies later in the course.\n\\end{itemize}\n\nWe will come back in detail on the assignment of probabilities in the section \"Statistical estimation\".\n\nIndependently from  how they are assigned, probability values should verify several rules.\n"

It must verify the following axioms:\n\\begin{itemize}\n    \\item axiom 1: $P(\\Omega) = 1$\n    \\item axiom 2: $P(A\\subset \\Omega) \\geq 0$\n    \\item axiom 3: if $A\\cap B=\\emptyset$ then $P(A\\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)$ (also true for countable sums)\n\\end{itemize}\n\nDirect consequences:\n\\begin{itemize}\n    \\item consequence 1:$P(A^c) = 1-P(A)$ \n    \\item consequence 2 :$P(\\emptyset) = 0$\n    \\item consequence 3:$P(A\\cup B) = P(A)+P(B)-P(A\\cap B)$\n\\end{itemize}\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Interpretation}}\\\\\n\nThe probability gives a notion of 'size' to events. Given that the size of $\\Omega$ is $1$, the size of events can be interpreted as the proportion they occupy in $\\Omega$. Hence, the $P$ of probability can also be read as the $P$ of \\textbf{proportion}.\\\\\n\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\nAssume that a die is a perfect cube. All faces are indistinguishable from each other, except for the written number. In this case, it is relevant to assign probabilities according to the indistinguishability principle:\n\n$$ P(\\{1\\}) = \\frac{1}{6}, P(\\{2\\}) = \\frac{1}{6},P(\\{3\\}) = \\frac{1}{6},$$ \n$$P(\\{4\\}) = \\frac{1}{6},P(\\{5\\}) = \\frac{1}{6},P(\\{6\\}) = \\frac{1}{6}.$$\n\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\nThe distribution is called uniform. It is now possible to compute the probability of every event, using the axiom 3 (if $A\\cap B=\\emptyset$ then $P(A\\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)$):\n\n$$ P\\left(\\{2,4,6\\}\\right) = P\\left(\\{2\\}\\cup\\{4\\}\\cup \\{6\\}\\right)=P(\\{2\\})+P(\\{4\\})+P(\\{6\\})=\\frac{1}{2}.$$\n\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\nAssume now that our die is a bit damaged. It is no longer perfectly symmetrical. Hence, we can no longer use the principle of indistinguishability. In that case a relevant approach is to roll  the die many time and to assign probabilities according to the frequency of apparition of the numbers.\n\n$$ P(\\{1\\}) = \\frac{k_1}{N}, P(\\{2\\}) = \\frac{k_2}{N},P(\\{3\\}) = \\frac{k_3}{N},$$ \n$$P(\\{4\\}) = \\frac{k_4}{N},P(\\{5\\}) = \\frac{k_5}{N},P(\\{6\\}) = \\frac{k_6}{N}.$$\n\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\nExactly as before, the probability of other events is calculated with the rule 'if $A\\cap B=\\emptyset$ then $P(A\\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)$'.\n\n"

                "latexMainText": "\n\\hfill \\\\\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Introduction}}\\\\\n\nConsider a game where a player rolls a dice and gains a score depending on the face of the dice. The face ($x$) and the gain ($y$) are related by the following equation:\n\n\\[\ny = x^2-10.\n\\]\n\n\\(y\\) and \\(x\\) are variables of the equation. When we build a probabilistic model, we want to know what are the possible values that the variables can take, and in which proportions.\n\n\\medskip\n\nIn this particular setting, everything is determined by the dice's face, and due to symmetry considerations, we assign each face an equal proportion: let\n\n\\[\n\\Omega = \\{1, \\dots, 6\\}, \n\\quad\nP(\\{i\\}) = \\frac{1}{6}.\n\\]\nThe variables \\(x\\) and \\(y\\) take different values depending on the dice's face \\(i \\in \\Omega\\). Hence they can be seen as functions of \\(\\Omega\\):\n\n\\[\nX(i) = i\n\\quad\\text{and}\\quad\nY(i) = X(i)^2 - 10.\n\\]\n\n\\medskip\n\nThe variables \\(x, y \\in \\mathbb{Z}\\) have been replaced by functions \n\n\\[\nX : \\Omega \\to \\mathbb{N}\n\\quad\\text{and}\\quad\nY : \\Omega \\to \\mathbb{Z}.\n\\]\nwith\n\n\\[\nY = X^2 -10.\n\\]\n\\(X\\) and \\(Y\\) are called ``random variables.''\n\nOnce we are dealing with random variables instead of just variables, the answer to the question \"what is the probability to win a certain amount $y$\" is\n\n\\[\nP(\\{ \\omega \\in \\Omega \\text{ such that } Y(\\omega)=y \\}).\n\\]\n\n\n\\textbf{Remark.}\\\\ \nIt is common to read \"the value of the random variable depends on the result of the experiment\". This formulation can be slightly misleading. Indeed, it is then tempting to believe that a random variable is a function which associates an observed value to each new repetition of an experiment. Assume that the dice is rolled $n$ times. Under that point of view, the random variable $X$ modelling the face would be a function $X:\\{ 1,\\ldots,n \\} \\rightarrow \\{1,\\ldots,6\\}$,\n\n$$ i \\mapsto \\textit{ face observed at the i-th roll}. $$\n\nIt is important to remember that this is not the point of view adopted in the theory of probabilities. The random variables $X : \\Omega \\to \\mathbb{N}$ and $Y : \\Omega \\to \\mathbb{N}$ introduced earlier are part of a model describing a single experiment, not a repetition of dice rolls. If we are interested in modeling multiples dices rolls, we need one random variable $X_i$ taking its values in $\\mathbb{N}$ per roll (see below). \n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Definition}}\\\\\n\nA random variable $X$ taking values in a space $E$ is a function $X:\\Omega\\rightarrow E$. In particular, integer random variables are functions $X:\\Omega\\rightarrow \\mathbb{N}$ and real random variables are functions $X:\\Omega\\rightarrow \\mathbb{R}$.\\\\\n\n\\vspace{0.3cm}\n\nRemark: this is a simplified version of the true definition which requires random variables to be 'measurable functions' that is to say : when $A$ is in the $\\sigma$-algebra of $E$, $X^{-1}(A)$ must be in the $\\sigma$-algebra of $\\Omega$.\\\\\n\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Coordinate random variables}}\\\\\n\nAssume that we roll a dice $n$ times. The configuration space that describes all the possible outcomes is $\\Omega = \\{1,2,3,4,5,6\\}^n$. Let $X_i$ be the $i$-th coordinate function on $\\Omega$. For instance,\n\n$$X_1\\left( (3,2,3,...,6) \\right) = 3. $$\nThese random variables 'extract' the result of the $i$-th roll out of the elementary configuration. \n"

                "latexMainText": "\n\\hfill\\\\\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Introduction}}\\\\\n\nLet $\\Omega$ be a configuration space with a probability $P$, and $X$ be a random variable taking values in a set $E$. Recall that $P$ is a function that takes in input an event of $\\Omega$ and associates its probability. The random variable transports the probability $P$ to the set $E$. The probability of a set $A$ in $E$ is determined by the probability of the inverse image of $A$ in $\\Omega$.\\\\\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Definition}}\\\\\n\nThe law of $P_X$ of the random variable $X:\\Omega \\rightarrow E$ is a probability on $E$ defined by\n$$ P_X(A \\subset E) = P\\left(X^{-1}(A)\\right).$$\nIt is called the law of the random variable $X$.\\\\\n\nRemarks: \n\\begin{itemize}\n    \\item instead of $P_X(A)$, we often write $P(X\\in A)$ (the probability that the value of the random variable $X$ falls in $A$).\n    \\item $E$ can be viewed as another configuration space with a probability $P_X$\n\\end{itemize}\n\n\nIn the previous game, the random variable $Gain:\\Omega=\\{1,2,3,4,5,5\\}\\rightarrow \\{-1,1\\}$,\n$$Gain(1)=Gain(3)=Gain(5)=-1 $$\n$$Gain(2)=Gain(4)=Gain(6)=1 $$\ninduces a probability distribution on $\\{-1,1\\}$. We have\n$$P_{Gain}(\\{-1\\}) = P(Gain^{-1}(\\{-1\\}))=P(\\{1\\})+P(\\{3\\})+P(\\{5\\}) $$\n$$P_{Gain}(\\{1\\}) = P(Gain^{-1}(\\{1\\}))=P(\\{2\\})+P(\\{4\\})+P(\\{6\\}).$$\n\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Definition: cumulative distribution}}\\\\\n\nLet $X$ be a real random variable ($E=\\mathbb{R}$). The probability $P_X$ can be represented by its cumulative distribution $F_X:\\mathbb{R}\\rightarrow \\mathbb{R}$, defined by\n\n$$F_X(a) = P_X\\left(]-\\infty,a]\\right).$$\n\n\n\nAll the information on $P_X$ is contained in $F_X$. Since the cumulative distribution is a function $\\mathbb{R}\\rightarrow \\mathbb{R}$, sometimes it is conceptually simpler to manipulate $F_X$ than the probability itself which is a function from the subsets of $\\mathbb{R}$ to $\\mathbb{R}$.\n\n\\begin{itemize}\n    \\item How do we compute $P_X(]a,b])$ from $F_X$? \n    %$$P_X(]a,b]) = F_X(b)-F_X(a)$$\n    \\item What do we know about $\\lim_{x\\rightarrow \\infty} F_X(x)$ ?\n    %$$\\lim_{x\\rightarrow \\infty} F_X(x)=1$$\n    \\item Can we have $x<y$ and $F_X(x)>F_X(y)$? %No!\n    \\item If for $x\\in [0,1]$, $F_X(x)=x$, what is $P_X([2,3])$? %$P_X([2,3])=0$\n\\end{itemize}\n\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Definition: density of a real random variable}}\\\\\n\nLet $X$ be a real random variable. Sometimes, the law of $X$ admits a density. When it exists, the density of $X$ is a function $f_X$ such that\n\n$$ P_X([a,b]) = \\int_a^b f_X(x)dx.$$\n\n\n\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\nRemark: we defined the cumulative distribution and density of a 'random variable' but note that it depends on $X$ only through the probability $P_X$. Hence the density can be defined for a probability $P$ on $\\mathbb{R}$ even if it is not defined as the law of a random variable.\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Exercises}}\\\\\n\n\nFor a real random variable $X$, \n\\begin{itemize}\n    \\item show that $\\int_{-\\infty}^{+\\infty}f_X(x)dx=1$\n    %$$\\int_{-\\infty}^{+\\infty}f_X(x)dx = P_X([-\\infty,+\\infty])=1 $$\n    \\item show that $f_X=(F_X)'$.\n    %$$F_X(x)= P_X\\left(]-\\infty,x]\\right) = \\int_{-\\infty}^{x}f_X(u)du $$\n    %Hence the result.\n\\end{itemize}\n\n"

                "display_order": 17,
                "latexMainText": "\n\\hfill\\\\\n\\hfill\\\\\nMost probability problems of this course start by defining a configuration space $\\Omega$ and a probability $P$ on it. Though, many real life problems involving probabilities make no mention of the space $\\Omega$.\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Example: weather}}\\\\\n\nAssume that we want to study the wind speed in Marseille. We can use the variable $s\\in\\mathbb{R}$ for the value of the wind speed. Since it is a higly variable quantity, we might decide to build a probabilistic model. The variable $s$ is then promoted to a random variable $S:\\Omega\\to \\mathbb{R}$.  \n\nQuestion : what should we take as $\\left(\\Omega,P \\right)$ and what should the function $S$ be ? \n\nNote first that ultimately, we are only interested in the law of $S$. This tells us what will be, in our model, the probability of each value of possible speeds. \n\nWe will now consider different scenarios, each time increasing the complexity of the modeling.\n\nA basic, and a bit artificial, construction, would be : let $\\Omega = \\mathbb R$ and let $S$ be the identity function, $S(x)=x$. Chosing a particular probability $P$ on $\\Omega$ gives imediatly the law of $S$ since $P=P_S$. This makes sens if we already have a candidate distribution, for instance coming from observations: if the wind speed was $s$ km/h in a fraction $p$ of the previous observation, we can set $P(\\{s\\})=p$ (more rigorously we would need a density value since the variable is real).   \n\nAssume that if the temperature $t\\in\\mathbb{R}_+$ and the air pressure $p_r\\in \\mathbb{R}_+$ are know, the wind speed can be deduced by a formula,\n\n\\[\ns = g(t,p_r)\n\\]\n\nIn that case we could be interested in taking $\\Omega = \\mathbb{R}_+ \\times \\mathbb{R}_+$. The temperatur and pressure would become random variables $T(\\omega_1,\\omega_2)=\\omega_1$ and $P_r(\\omega_1,\\omega_2)=\\omega_2$ with\n\n\\[\nS = g(T,P_r).\n\\]\n\nWe would have then to find a probability $P$ on $\\Omega$ which models the couples $(t,p_r)$. The law $P_S$ would then be given by\n\n\\[\nP_S(A) = P(\\lbrace (\\omega_1,\\omega_2)\\in \\Omega,S(\\omega_1,\\omega_2)=g(T(\\omega_1,\\omega_2),P_r(\\omega_1,\\omega_2))= g(\\omega_1,\\omega_2)\\in A \\rbrace).\n\\]\n\nConsider now a more realistic scenario where the previous relation is not deterministic, and $s$ only fluctuates around $g(t,p_r)$. We could consider a new configuration space $\\Omega = \\mathbb{R}_+ \\times \\mathbb{R}_+ \\times \\mathbb{R}$ with $T$ and $P_r$ still corresponding to the first and second coordinnate, with a third random variable $F$ for a third coordinate modeling the fluctuations, and with\n\n\\[\nS = G(T,P_r) + F\n\\]\n\nThis model would require a probability on $\\Omega = \\mathbb{R}_+ \\times \\mathbb{R}_+ \\times \\mathbb{R}$ reflecting the relations between the values of the temperature, pressure and fluctuation. \n\nA further analysis could later break down the fluctuation in different component, leading to a new configuration space $\\Omega$.\n\nHere, in each scenario, we carefully described $\\Omega$ and the different functions. One could argue that all the relevant quantities are functions of the positions and speeds of all the particules of the air. This would suggest to chose $\\Omega = (\\mathbb R^3\\times \\mathbb R^3)^N$ where $N$ is the number of particules. Wind speed, temperature, air pressure or fluctuations are functions of the type $\\Omega \\rightarrow \\mathbb{R}$, hence they are random variables. Doing that would enable us to always use the same configuration space $\\Omega$ regardless of the details of the modelisation.  \n\n\\begin{comment}\nSince we know that the wind speed is related to the temperature $T$, we can attempt to predict the wind speed from the temperature. The wind speed is a vector of $\\mathbb{R}^3$ and the temperature is a positive number, hence our problem can be fully modeled by the configuration space $\\Omega_1 = \\mathbb{R}^3 \\times \\mathbb{R}_+$. From a database of measurements, we can estimate the probability of an elementary configuration by $P_1(\\{(s,t)\\})=\\frac{n_{(s,t)}}{n}$, where $n_{(s,t)}$ is the number of times $(s,t)$ has been measured and $n$ is the total number of measurements. With the law $P_1$, it is possible to calculate the conditional probability (which we will define later) of the wind speed given the temperature. With this conditional probability, it is possible to say what is the most probable value of wind speed for a given temperature.\n\nNow assume that temperature is a poor predictor of wind speed: given a temperature, the probability over wind speed has a high variance. In order to improve our analysis, it is common to incorporate new parameters in our model. We could, for instance consider the atmospheric pressure $Pr$. The new configuration space would then be $\\Omega_2 = \\mathbb{R}^3 \\times \\mathbb{R}_+ \\times \\mathbb{R}_+$, with probability $P_2$. Luckily, given a temperature and a pressure, the probability on the wind speed  has a small variance. \n\nOtherwise, we could incorporate more and more parameters, and consider new configuration spaces. In practice, instead of changing the configuration space each time we want to add a parameter, we treat the parameters as random variables of a larger configuration space. At a given moment, all the meteorological parameters are a function of the positions and speeds of the particles, which could be described by the configuration space $\\Omega =  (\\mathbb{R}^3 \\times \\mathbb{R}^3)^N$, where $N$ is the number of particles. Wind speed, temperature, and air pressure are functions of the type $\\Omega \\rightarrow \\mathbb{R}^d$, hence they are random variables.  \n\\end{comment}\n\nIn practice, evaluating and manipulating a probability $P$ on the positions and velocities of each particles is unrealistic. Though only the joint law of the studied variables matters, in our case the joint law $P_{(T,P_r,F)}$ of the random variable $(T,P_r,F):\\Omega \\rightarrow \\mathbb{R}_+ \\times \\mathbb{R}_+ \\times \\mathbb{R}$. Technically speaking, $\\mathbb{R}_+ \\times \\mathbb{R}_+ \\times \\mathbb{R}$ is no longer referred to as a configuration space, given that additional parameters may be included in our analysis. \n\nFinally, note that the precise form of $\\Omega =  (\\mathbb{R}^3 \\times \\mathbb{R}^3)^N$ is not particularly helpful. It is only necessary to know that the relevant parameters are functions on $\\Omega$. In this context, the term 'universe' to refer to $\\Omega$ is particularly appropriated.\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Moral}}\\\\\n\nIn practice, the general configuration space $\\Omega$ and its probability are often not precisely described, or even mentioned. In these cases, what matters is the joint probability law of the variables of interest. \n\n"

The value of the signal at the $i$-th measurement is also a coordinate random variable and its law is a marginal of $P$.\n\\end{itemize}\n\n"

Given a event $A$ with $P(A>0)$, the idea of conditioning with respect to $A$ is to focus on the configurations $\\omega \\in A$ and forget about the configurations $\\omega \\notin A$. We would like to define a new probability which respects the proportions of the events included in $A$ and gives zero probability to event which do not intersect $A$.\\\\\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Definition}}\\\\\n\nLet $A$ be an event of $\\Omega$, with $P(A)>0$. We define the probability conditional to the event $A$ by\n$$P_A(B) = \\frac{P(B\\cap A)}{P(A)}.$$\n$P_A(B)$ is called the probability of $B$ given $A$, or probability of $B$ knowing $A$, and is usually noted $P(B|A)$.\\\\\n\n \nExercise: check that $P_A$ is a probability on $\\Omega$ \\\\\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Examples: Assume that the marginal $P_F(\\{y\\})$ is non null. We can condition $P$ by the event $E\\times \\{y\\}$, 'the second coordinate is $y$'. This gives a new probability on $E\\times F$, which can be interpreted as a probability on $E$ as follow. \n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Definition}}\\\\\n\nAssume that $P(E\\times \\{y\\})>0$. For $A\\subset E$, we define the conditional probability of $A$ knowing $E\\times \\{y\\}$ as \n\n\\begin{eqnarray*}\nP(A | E\\times\\{y\\} ) &\\leftarrow& P(A\\times \\{y\\} | E\\times \\{y\\} )\\\\\n&=& \\frac{P((A\\times \\{y\\})\\cap (E\\times \\{y\\}))}{P(E\\times \\{y\\})}\\\\\n&=& \\frac{P((A\\cap E)\\times \\{y\\})}{P_F(\\{y\\})}\\\\\n&=& \\frac{P(A\\times \\{y\\})}{P_F(\\{y\\})}.\\\\\n\\end{eqnarray*}\n\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\nAssume now that $P$ has a density $f$ and that its marginal on $F$ has a density $f_F$. This implies that $P(E\\times \\{y\\})=0$, and it is hence not possible to define the conditional probability knowing $E\\times \\{y\\}$. We can however define a conditional density at $x\\in E$ as\n$$ f(x|y) = \\frac{f((x,y))}{f_F(y)}, $$\nprovided that $f_F(y)>0$. Note that the conditional density is not the density of the conditional probability, since it is not defined. Defining the conditional probability knowing the event $E\\times \\{y\\}$ can be done using the notion of conditional expectation, but it is out of the scope of this course. \\\\\n\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Conditional probabilities of a joint law}}\\\\\n\nAssume now $X:\\Omega \\rightarrow E$ and $Y:\\Omega \\rightarrow F$. The joint law $P_{(X,Y)}$, is a probability on $E\\times F$. In this context we use particular notations to condition on some $y\\in F$. When $A\\subset E$, \n\n$$ P_{(X,Y)}(A|E\\times \\{y\\}) \\text{ is written } P(X\\in A |Y=y).$$\n\nUsing shortened notation, we can write\n    \n$$P(X\\in A |Y=y) \\rightarrow P(A|y)= \\frac{P(A,y)}{P(y)}.$$\n\n\\vspace{0.5cm}\n\nAnd when it exists, the conditional density is noted\n$$ f(x|Y=y) = \\frac{f_{(X,Y)}(x,y)}{f_Y(y)}.$$\n\nIn general, when conditioning a joint law by a coordinate value, we can remember the synthetic formula\n    \n$$ \\text{conditional}  = \\frac{\\text{joint}}{ \\text{marginal}}.$$\n    %\\vspace{0.5cm}\n"

                "latexMainText": "\n\\hfill\\\\\n\\hfill\\\\\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Motivation}}\\\\\n\n\nConsider again $2$ dice rolls with a uniform probability distribution $P$. Consider the two events\n\n\\begin{itemize}\n    \\item '$A$': $\\{6\\}\\times \\{1,..,6\\}$, the first roll is $6$. $P(A)=\\frac{1}{6}$\n    \\item '$B$': $\\{1,..,6\\}\\times \\{6\\}$, the second roll is $6$. $P(B)=\\frac{1}{6}$\n\\end{itemize}\n\nRemember that conditional probabilities are given by\n\n$$ P(B|A) = \\frac{P(A\\cap B)}{P(A)} = \\frac{P(\\{(6,6)\\})}{\\{6\\}\\times \\{1,..,6\\}}=\\frac{1}{6} $$\n\nHence $P(B)=P(B|A)$: the probability of getting $6$ on the second roll is the same as the probability of getting $6$ on the second roll knowing that the first roll was a $6$. We say in that case that the event $B$ does not depend on the event $A$. Reversing the conditioning in the formula shows that $A$ is also independent of $B$.\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Definition}}\\\\\n\n\nTwo events $A$ and $B$ are called independent when \n\n$$ P(A\\cap B) =P(A)P(B)$$\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Interpretation}}\\\\\n\nWhen $P(A)>0$: the proportion of $B\\cap A$ in $A$ is the same as the proportion of $B$ in $\\Omega$\n\n$$ \\frac{P(B\\cap A)}{P(A)} = \\frac{P(B)}{P(\\Omega)}=P(B).$$\n\nIn other words, conditioning probabilities to the event $A$ does not change the probability of $B$.\\\\\n\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\nWhen $P(B)>0$, the same can be said about the proportion of $A\\cap B$ in $B$.\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Example}}\\\\\n\nLet $\\Omega$ be the $52$ card deck with uniform distribution $P$. Show that the events 'the card is a diamond' and 'the card is an ace' are independent.\n\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\n\\begin{itemize}\n    \\item $ P(\\{ (ace,diamond) \\}) = \\frac{1}{52} $\n    \\item $ P( \\{ ace \\}\\times \\{hearts, diamonds, clubs, spades \\} ) = \\frac{4}{52} =\\frac{1}{13}$\n    \\item $ P( \\{2,..., ace\\}\\times \\{ diamonds\\} ) = \\frac{13}{52} =\\frac{1}{4}$\n\\end{itemize}\nand\n\n$$\\frac{1}{4} \\times \\frac{1}{13} = \\frac{1}{52},$$\n\nthey are independent.\n"

                "latexMainText": "\n\\hfill\\\\\n\\hfill\\\\\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Motivation}}\\\\\n\nThe notion of independence of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ is based on the notion of independence of events. \\\\\n\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\nConsider two consecutive dice rolls. Call $X$ and $Y$ the 2 coordinates random variables on the configuration space $\\Omega =\\{1,2,3,4,5,6 \\}^2$ endowed with the uniform distribution $P$.\\\\\n\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\nCheck that events $X^{-1}(\\{i\\})\\subset \\Omega$ and $Y^{-1}(\\{j\\})\\subset \\Omega$ are independent for all $i$ and $j$. Rephrased in common language: obtaining an $i$ for the first roll is independent of obtaining a $j$ for the second roll.\\\\\n\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\nMore generally we will require the independence of all events in $\\Omega$ described by a constraint on the values of $X$ and all events described by a constraint on the values of $Y$. In that case, an information on one of them does not affect the other.\n\n\n%Still take $X:\\Omega \\rightarrow E$ and $Y:\\Omega \\rightarrow F$. %Assume that $\\forall y,P_Y(y)>0$, and that $\\forall A \\subset E$,\n\n%$$P(X\\in A |Y=y) $$\n\n%is the same for all values of $y$. Fixing the value of $Y$ does %not influence the conditional probability of $A$ $\\rightarrow$ %knowing $Y$ does not influences $X$. This motivates the notion of %independence of RV.\\\\\n\n%$$P(X\\in A |Y=y) = P(X^{-1}(A) \\cap Y^{-1}({y})) $$\n\n%\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\n%It will become clear that if $Y$ does not influence $X$ then $X$ %does not influences $Y$.\\\\\n\n%\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\n%Consider the dice roll experiment with the uniform probability. %Call $X$ and $Y$ the 2 coordinates random variables on $\\Omega %=\\{1,2,3,4,5,6 \\}$.\n\n%$$P(X=i | Y = 1) = \\frac{1}{6}, P(X=i | Y = 2) = \\frac{1}{6} ...$$\n\n%Hence conditioning by a value on the first experiment always %gives the same probability on the second experiment. We also have %that \n\n%$$P(Y=i | X = 1) = \\frac{1}{6}, P(Y=i | X = 2) = \\frac{1}{6} ...$$\n\n%So knowing something on any of the rolls does not influence %probabilities on the other roll.\\\\\n\n\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Definition}}\\\\\n\nTwo random variables $X:\\Omega \\rightarrow E$ and $Y:\\Omega \\rightarrow F$ are independent when\n\n$$ \\forall A\\subset E,B\\subset F,\\quad X^{-1}(A) \\text{ and } Y^{-1}(B) \\text{ are independent events in } \\Omega.$$\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Remarks}}\\\\\n\n\\begin{itemize}\n    \\item Recall that it means that when $P(Y^{-1}(B))>0$, conditioning the probability $P$ on $\\Omega$ to $Y^{-1}(B)$ does not change the probability of $X^{-1}(A)$. The other direction holds when $P(X^{-1}(A))>0$.\\\\\n    \\item It is clear that independence is a symmetric relation.\\\\\n\\end{itemize}\n"

In the discrete case the joint law $\\bm P$ is given by\n\n$$ \\bm P(\\{(x_1,...,x_n)\\}) = P(\\{x_1\\})P(\\{x_2\\}) .. P(\\{x_n\\}).$$\n\nIf $P$ has a density $f$, the joint density $\\bm f$ is\n\n$$ \\bm f((x_1,...,x_n)) = f(x_1)f(x_2) .. f(x_n).$$\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Example}}\\\\\n\nIn the modelling of the repetition of $n$ dice rolls, we have always used the uniform probability over all possible configurations. From this, we deduced the independence of the different rolls.\\\\\n\n%\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\nThe reasoning usually goes the other way. Let $\\Omega=\\{1,2,3,4,5,6\\}^n$ and the $X_i$ be the coordinate random variables. It is usually reasonable to assume that the $X_i$ are independent, and that their law is uniform on $\\{1,2,3,4,5,6\\}$. They are hence i.i.d. variables. This determines the probability on $\\Omega$:\n\\begin{eqnarray*}\nP(\\{\\omega=(\\omega_1,...,\\omega_n)\\}) &=& P_{(X_1,...,X_n)}(\\{\\omega=(\\omega_1,...,\\omega_n)\\})\\\\\n&=& \\prod P_{X_i}(\\{\\omega_i \\}) = \\frac{1}{6^n}.\\\\\n\\end{eqnarray*}\n\nHence $P$ is uniform.\n"

                "latexMainText": "\n\\hfill\\\\\n\\hfill\\\\\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Idea}}\\\\\n\nLet $\\Omega=\\{1,2\\}$ with $P(\\{1\\})=\\frac{1}{10}$ and $P(\\{2\\})=\\frac{9}{10}$. Let $X$ be a real random variable, $X:\\Omega \\rightarrow \\mathbb{R}$. For each elementary configuration $\\omega$, $X$ takes the value $X(\\omega)$. The 'expectation' of $X$ is the 'average' value of the $X(\\omega)$ with respect to the probabilities of the $\\{\\omega\\}$. In our example:\n\n$$\\mathbb{E}(X) = X(1).P(\\{1\\}) + X(2).P(\\{2\\}) = X(1)\\times \\frac{1}{10} + X(2)\\times \\frac{9}{10}.$$\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Definition}}\\\\\n\nIf $\\Omega=\\mathbb{Z}$, the average of a random variable $X:\\Omega \\rightarrow \\mathbb{R}$ becomes:\n\n$$ \\mathbb{E}(X) = \\sum_{i\\in\\Omega} X(i)\\times P(\\{i\\}).$$\n\nNow consider the case $\\Omega=\\mathbb{R}$, with a probability $P$ of density $f$. The formula for the expectation becomes (when the integral exists)\n\n$$ \\mathbb{E}(X) = \\int_{-\\infty}^{+\\infty} X(\\omega) f(\\omega)d\\omega.$$\n\n\nThere is a definition of the expectation which does not depend on the nature of $\\Omega$ and $P$ using Lebesgue integral (as opposed to Riemann integrals). Lebesgue integration is beyond the scope of this course but it is useful to be familiar with its notations. The expectation (average / mean) of $X$ becomes\n\n$$\\mathbb{E}(X) = \\int_{\\Omega} X(\\omega)dP(\\omega),\\text{ or simply}  \\int_{\\Omega} XdP$$\n\nWhen $\\Omega$ is discrete, the Lebesgue integral becomes a sum over $\\Omega$, while when $P$ has a density, $dP$ can be replaced by $f(\\omega)d\\omega$. \\\\\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{$\\mathbb{E}(X)$ from the law $P_X$}}\\\\\n\n\nIn the discrete case, the previous definition is based on the sum of the $X(\\omega)$ over all the configurations $\\omega \\in \\Omega$, weighted by the probabilities $P(\\{\\omega\\})$. The same result can be obtained by summing all the possible values $x\\in E$ that $X(\\omega)$ can take, weighted by their probabilities $P_X(\\{x\\})$. \\\\\n\nThis approach leads to the following important equalities\n\n\\begin{itemize}\n    \\item If $E=\\mathbb{Z}$, we have that\n    \n    $$\\mathbb{E}(X) = \\sum_{i\\in \\mathbb{Z}} i.P_X(\\{i\\}).$$\n    \n    %Exercise: show this formula when $\\Omega = \\mathbb{Z}$.\n    \\item If $E=\\mathbb{R}$ and if the law $P_X$ has a density $f_X$, we have\n    \n    $$\\mathbb{E}(X)= \\int_{-\\infty}^{+\\infty} xf_X(x)dx $$\n    \n    %Exercise: show this formula when $\\Omega = \\mathbb{R}$, $f$ is the density of $P$ and $X$ is a diffeomorphism .\n\\end{itemize}\n\nExercise: Prove the result when $X:\\mathbb{Z}\\rightarrow \\mathbb{Z}$.\n\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Expectation of $\\varphi(X)$}}\\\\\n\n\nLet $X:\\Omega \\rightarrow \\mathbb{Z}$ and $\\varphi:\\mathbb{Z}\\rightarrow  \\mathbb{Z}$. \n\n\\begin{eqnarray}\n\\mathbb{E}(\\varphi\\circ X) &=& \\sum_y y P_{\\varphi\\circ X}(\\{y\\})\\\\\n\\end{eqnarray}\n\nWe will reformulate the term $P_{\\varphi\\circ X}(\\{y\\})$.\n\n\\begin{eqnarray}\nP_{\\varphi\\circ X}(\\{y\\})&=& P(\\{ \\omega\\in \\Omega, \\varphi(X(\\omega))=y \\})  \\\\\n                         &=& P( X^{-1}(\\varphi^{-1}(\\{y\\})))\\\\\n                         &=& P_X(\\varphi^{-1}(\\{y\\}))\n\\end{eqnarray}\n\n\nHence\n\n\\begin{eqnarray}\n\\mathbb{E}(\\varphi\\circ X) &=& \\sum_y y P_{\\varphi\\circ X}(\\{y\\})\\\\\n                            &=& \\sum_y y P_X(\\varphi^{-1}(\\{y\\})).\n\\end{eqnarray}\n\nBut we have seem previously that \n\n$$ \\sum_y y P_X(\\varphi^{-1}(\\{y\\})) = \\sum_x \\varphi(x)P_X(\\{x\\}) $$ \nwhere the role previously played by $X$ is now played by $\\varphi$.\n\nWe finally obtain the important following formula \n\n$$ \\mathbb{E}(\\varphi\\circ X)  = \\sum_x \\varphi(x)P_X(\\{x\\}). $$ \n\nWhen $X$ takes its values in $\\mathbb{R}$ rather that in $\\mathbb{Z}$, the formula becomes\n\n$$ \\mathbb{E}(\\varphi\\circ X)  = \\int \\varphi(x)f_X(x)\\mathrm{d}x, $$ \n\nprovided that $P_X$ has a density function $f_X$. For simplicity we assumed that $\\varphi$ takes its values in $\\mathbb{Z}$ but the result is still true when $\\varphi$ is real valued.\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Linearity}}\\\\\n\nThe set of random variables $X:\\Omega \\rightarrow \\mathbb{R}$ is a vector space ($(X+Y)(\\omega)=X(\\omega)+Y(\\omega)$). The set of random variables such that $\\mathbb{E}(X)=\\int_{\\Omega} XdP$ exists is again a vector space.\nSince integrals are linear, the expectation $\\mathbb{E}:L^1(\\Omega)\\rightarrow \\mathbb{R}$ \n\n$$X \\mapsto \\mathbb{E}(X)=\\int_{\\Omega} XdP$$\n\nis a linear application valued in $\\mathbb{R}$ (i.e. a linear form). In other words, we have the fundamentals properties:\n\n$$\\mathbb{E}(\\alpha X) = \\alpha \\mathbb{E}(X) \\quad \\text{ and } \\quad  \\mathbb{E}(X+Y) = \\mathbb{E}(X) + \\mathbb{E}(Y).$$\n\n"

The deviation from the mean is given by the Euclidean norm of the centered variable $X_{c} = X-\\mathbb{E}(X)$. When it exists, the variance is defined by,\n\n$$v(X)= \\mathbb{E}\\left((X-\\mathbb{E}(X))^2\\right)=cov(X,X)=\\|X_c\\|^2,$$\n\nand the standard deviation by\n\n$$\\sigma(X)=\\sqrt{v(X)} =\\|X_c\\|.$$\n\n\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Alternative formula}}\\\\\n\nWe have the important equality\n$$v(X)=\\mathbb{E}(X^2)-\\mathbb{E}(X)^2.$$\n\nProof:\n\\begin{eqnarray*}\nv(X)&=&\\mathbb{E}\\left((X-\\mathbb{E}(X))^2\\right)\\\\\n&=&\\mathbb{E}\\left(X^2-2\\mathbb{E}(X)X+\\mathbb{E}(X)^2)\\right)\\\\\n&=&\\mathbb{E}(X^2)-2\\mathbb{E}(\\mathbb{E}(X)X)+\\mathbb{E}(\\mathbb{E}(X)^2)\\\\\n&=&\\mathbb{E}(X^2)-2\\mathbb{E}(X)\\mathbb{E}(X)+\\mathbb{E}(\\mathbb{E}(X)^2)\\\\\n&=&\\mathbb{E}(X^2)-\\mathbb{E}(X)^2 \\\\\n\\end{eqnarray*}\n"

Alternatively we can write,\n\n\\begin{eqnarray*}\nv(X+Y) &=& \\mathbb{E}( (X+Y - \\mathbb{E}(X+Y))^2) \\\\\n&=& \\mathbb{E}( (X+Y - \\mathbb{E}(X)+\\mathbb{E}Y))^2) \\\\\n&=& \\mathbb{E}( (X-\\mathbb{E}(X))^2+(Y- \\mathbb{E}(Y))^2 + 2((X-\\mathbb{E}(X))(Y- \\mathbb{E}(Y))) \\\\\n&=&v(X)+v(Y)+2\\mathbb{E}(XY-X\\mathbb{E}(Y)-\\mathbb{E}(X)Y+\\mathbb{E}(X)\\mathbb{E}(Y))\\\\\n&=&v(X)+v(Y)+2(\\mathbb{E}(X)\\mathbb{E}(Y)-\\mathbb{E}(X)\\mathbb{E}(Y)-\\mathbb{E}(X)\\mathbb{E}(Y)+\\mathbb{E}(X)\\mathbb{E}(Y))\n\\end{eqnarray*}\n\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Important consequence}}\\\\\n\n\nHence, when $X_1,...,X_n$ are independent variables with identical distributions,\n$$v\\left(\\frac{1}{n}\\sum_i X_i\\right)=\\frac{1}{n^2}v\\left(\\sum_i X_i\\right)  =  \\frac{1}{n^2}\\sum_i v(X_i)=\\frac{1}{n}v(X_1)\\xrightarrow[n\\rightarrow \\infty]{} 0$$ \n\nThis is a very important result: summing independent and identically distributed (i.i.d) variables reduces the variance in $\\frac{1}{n}$ and the standard deviation in $\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{n}}$.\n"

xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mi>\u2119</mi><mo form=\"prefix\" stretchy=\"false\">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>\u2265</mo><mi>a</mi><mo form=\"postfix\"                 "display_order": 46,
                "latexMainText": "\n\nLet $X$ be a random variable taking its values in positive numbers, $X:\\Omega \\rightarrow \\mathbb{R}_{\\geq 0}$, and let $a>0$.\n\n\\begin{itemize}\n    \\item[$1)$] \\textbf{Markov's inequality:}  \n\n    $$P(X\\ge a)\\le \\frac{\\mathbb{E}(X)}{a}.$$\n    \\item[$2)$] \\textbf{Chebychev's inequality:} \n\n    $$P(|X-\\mathbb{E}(X)|\\ge a)\\le \\frac{v(X)}{a^2}.$$\n\\end{itemize}\n\nChebychev's inequality implicitely assumes that $v(X)$ can be properly defined, which is not always the case for an arbitrary function $X:\\Omega \\rightarrow \\mathbb{R}_{\\geq 0}$. \n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Proofs}}\\\\\n\n\n\\textbf{Step 1. Decomposition of the random variable $X$:}\\\\\nWe start by expressing $X$ as the sum of two parts using indicator functions:\n$$\nX = X\\cdot \\mathbf{1}_{\\{X<a\\}} + X\\cdot \\mathbf{1}_{\\{X\\ge a\\}}.\n$$\nHere, $\\mathbf{1}_{\\{X<a\\}}:\\Omega\\rightarrow \\{0,1\\}$ is the indicator function that takes the value $1$ when $X(\\omega)<a$ and $0$ otherwise, and similarly $\\mathbf{1}_{\\{X\\ge a\\}}$ equals $1$ when $X\\ge a$ and $0$ elsewhere. This decomposition splits $\\Omega$ into two disjoint regions: one where the value of $X$ is less than $a$, and another where it is at least $a$.\\\\[0.2cm]\n\n\\textbf{Step 2. Taking the expectation:}\\\\\nSince the expectation is a linear operator, we have\n$$\n\\mathbb{E}(X) = \\mathbb{E}(X\\cdot \\mathbf{1}_{\\{X<a\\}}) + \\mathbb{E}(X\\cdot \\mathbf{1}_{\\{X\\ge a\\}}).\n$$\n\n\n\\textbf{Step 3. Bounding the second term:}\\\\\nNotice that the function $X\\cdot \\mathbf{1}_{\\{X\\ge a\\}}$ is always greater that $a\\cdot \\mathbf{1}_{\\{X\\ge a\\}}$:\n$$\nX\\cdot \\mathbf{1}_{\\{X\\ge a\\}} \\ge a\\cdot \\mathbf{1}_{\\{X\\ge a\\}}.\n$$\n \nHence taking expectations on both sides gives\n$$\n\\mathbb{E}(X\\cdot \\mathbf{1}_{\\{X\\ge a\\}}) \\ge a\\,\\mathbb{E}(\\mathbf{1}_{\\{X\\ge a\\}}).\n$$\nNow note that the expectation of an indicator function is just the probability of the corresponding event,\n$$\n\\mathbb{E}(\\mathbf{1}_{\\{X\\ge a\\}}) = \\sum_{\\omega,X(\\omega)\\ge a}1.P(\\{ \\omega \\}) = P(X\\ge a).\n$$\nThus,\n$$\n\\mathbb{E}(X\\cdot \\mathbf{1}_{\\{X\\ge a\\}}) \\ge a\\,P(X\\ge a).\n$$\n\n\\textbf{Step 4. Concluding Markov's inequality:}\\\\\nSince $\\mathbb{E}(X) = \\mathbb{E}(X\\cdot \\mathbf{1}_{\\{X<a\\}}) + \\mathbb{E}(X\\cdot \\mathbf{1}_{\\{X\\ge a\\}})$ and the first term is superior or equal to $0$, it follows that\n$$\n\\mathbb{E}(X) \\ge \\mathbb{E}(X\\cdot \\mathbf{1}_{\\{X\\ge a\\}}) \\ge a\\,P(X\\ge a).\n$$\nRearranging the inequality, we obtain\n$$\nP(X\\ge a)\\le \\frac{\\mathbb{E}(X)}{a}.\n$$\n\n\\vspace{0.5cm}\n\n\n\\textbf{Proof of Chebychev's inequality:}\\\\\nApply Markov's inequality to the random variable $Y=(X-\\mathbb{E}(X))^2$. It is possible since $Y\\geq 0$. Specifically, for any $a>0$, we have\n$$\nP\\Big((X-\\mathbb{E}(X))^2\\ge a^2\\Big)\\le \\frac{\\mathbb{E}\\big((X-\\mathbb{E}(X))^2\\big)}{a^2}=\\frac{v(X)}{a^2}.\n$$\nSince the event $\\{\\omega\\in \\Omega,(X(\\omega)-\\mathbb{E}(X))^2\\ge a^2\\}=\\{\\omega\\in \\Omega,|X(\\omega)-\\mathbb{E}(X)|\\ge a\\}$, this inequality can be rewritten as\n$$\nP(|X-\\mathbb{E}(X)|\\ge a)\\le \\frac{v(X)}{a^2}.\n$$\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Important consequence}}\\\\\n\nChebychev's inequality is a fundamental tool in probability theory as it quantifies the dispersion of a random variable around its mean. It shows that regardless of the distribution, the probability of deviating significantly from the mean is controlled by the variance. This is a key step in the proof of the law of large numbers.\n"

                "latexMainText": "\n\n\nLet $\\Sigma$ be a $n\\times n$ symmetric matrix with positive eigenvalues. The Gaussian density on $\\mathbb{R}^n$ parametrised by $\\mu \\in \\mathbb{R}^n$ and $\\Sigma$ is given by\n\n$$\nf_{\\mu,\\Sigma}(x) = \\frac{1}{(2\\pi)^{n/2} (\\det\\Sigma)^(1/2)}e^{-\\frac{1}{2}(x-\\mu)^T\\Sigma^{-1} (x-\\mu)},\n$$\nwhere $x=\\begin{pmatrix} x_1 \\\\.\\\\x_n \\end{pmatrix}$\n\nIf the law of a random variable $X$ has the density $f_{\\mu,\\Sigma}$, it is not difficult to prove that $\\mathbb{E}(X)=\\mu$. A more difficult calculation, which we detail below gives:\n\n$$cov(X)=\\Sigma.$$ \n\n\\hfill\\\\\n\\hfill\\\\\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{A detailed descprition of the 2D case}}\\\\\n\n\n\\textbf{Prerequisite:}\n\nLet \\(Z\\) be a random vector $Z \\;=\\; \\begin{pmatrix} Z_1 \\\\[6pt] Z_2 \\end{pmatrix} \\;\\in\\; \\mathbb{R}^2$ with density\n\n\\[\nf_Z(p) = \\frac{1}{2\\pi} \\exp\\left(-\\frac{1}{2}\\,\\bigl(p_1^2 + p_2^2\\bigr)\\right).\n\\]\nwhere \\(p = \\begin{pmatrix} p_1 \\\\ p_2 \\end{pmatrix} \\in \\mathbb{R}^2.\\)\n\nLevel lines of \\(f_Z\\) are circles.\n\n%!!!!!!!!! image !!!!!!!!!!!!!\n\nThe law is called *isotropic* because it looks the same in every direction.\n\nThe covariance matrix of \\(Z\\) is given by\n\\[\n\\mathrm{cov}(Z) \n\\;=\\; \n\\begin{pmatrix}\n\\mathrm{var}(Z_1) & \\mathrm{cov}(Z_1, Z_2)\\\\[6pt]\n\\mathrm{cov}(Z_2, Z_1) & \\mathrm{var}(Z_2)\n\\end{pmatrix}\n\\;=\\;\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n1 & 0\\\\[6pt]\n0 & 1\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n\\]\n\nIndeed, \\(\\mathrm{var}(Z_1) = \\mathrm{var}(Z_2) = 1\\) and since we have seen that\n\n\\[\nf_Z(p) \\;=\\; f_{Z_1}(p_1)\\,f_{Z_2}(p_2),\n\\]\nit follows that \\(Z_1\\) and \\(Z_2\\) are independent and therefore\n\\(\\mathrm{cov}(Z_1, Z_2) = 0.\\)\n\n\n\\textbf{General case:}\n\nLet $\\Sigma$ be a $2 \\times 2$ symmetric matrix with positive eigenvalues,\n\\[\n\\Sigma = R D R^{-1} = R \\begin{pmatrix} \\sigma_1^2 & 0 \\\\ 0 & \\sigma_2^2 \\end{pmatrix} R^{-1}\n\\]\n\nSince $R$ is an orthogonal matrix, $RR^T = I$ and $R^T = R^{-1}$, \n\n\\[\n\\Sigma = R D R^T\n\\]\n\nLet $X: \\Omega \\to \\mathbb{R}^2$ be a random vector, whose density is\n\n\\[\n\\forall p = \\begin{pmatrix} p_1 \\\\ p_2 \\end{pmatrix}, \\quad f_X(p) = \\frac{1}{2\\pi \\det(\\Sigma)^{1/2}} e^{-\\frac{1}{2} (p^T \\Sigma^{-1} p)}.\n\\]\n\nIt can be proved that the density actually has an integral equal to 1:\n\n\\[\n\\iint f_X \\left( \\begin{pmatrix} p_1 \\\\ p_2 \\end{pmatrix} \\right) dp_1 dp_2 = 1.\n\\]\n\nWe can rewrite the determinant as\n\\begin{align*}\n\\det(\\Sigma) &= \\det \\left( R \\begin{pmatrix} \\sigma_1^2 & 0 \\\\ 0 & \\sigma_2^2 \\end{pmatrix} R^T \\right)\\\\\n&= \\det \\left( R R^T \\begin{pmatrix} \\sigma_1^2 & 0 \\\\ 0 & \\sigma_2^2 \\end{pmatrix} \\right)\\\\\n&= \\det(R R^T) \\det \\left( \\begin{pmatrix} \\sigma_1^2 & 0 \\\\ 0 & \\sigma_2^2 \\end{pmatrix} \\right)\\\\\n&= 1 \\cdot \\sigma_1^2 \\sigma_2^2.\n\\end{align*}\nHence\n\n\\[\nf_X(p) = \\frac{1}{2\\pi \\sigma_1 \\sigma_2} e^{-\\frac{1}{2} p^T \\Sigma^{-1} p}\n\\]\nLet $Y$ be a random vector such that $Y = R^{-1} X$, or equivalently $X = RY$. For any $A \\subset \\mathbb{R}^2$,\n\n\\begin{align*}\nP_X(A) &= P\\left( \\{\\omega, X(\\omega) \\in A\\} \\right) \\\\\n&= P\\left( \\{\\omega, RY(\\omega) \\in A\\} \\right) \\\\\n&= P\\left( \\{\\omega, Y(\\omega) \\in R^{-1}(A)\\} \\right) \\\\\n&= P_Y\\left( R^{-1}(A) \\right).\n\\end{align*}\n\n%\\begin{figure}\n%\\includegraphics[width=0.5\\textwidth]{XY}\n%\\end{figure}\n\nHence,\n\n\\[\nP_X(A) = \\int_A f_X(p) \\, dp_1 dp_2 = \\int_{R^{-1}(A)} f_X(R p) J_R(p) \\, dp_1 dp_2\n\\]\n\n\\[\n= P_Y(R^{-1} A) = \\int_{R^{-1}(A)} f_Y(p) \\, dp_1 dp_2\n\\]\n\nSince it is true $\\forall A \\subset \\mathbb{R}^2$, it can be proved that $\\forall p$, $f_X(Rp) J = f_Y(p)$. Since $J_R(p) = \\left| \\det \\left( \\mathrm{d} R_p\\right) \\right| = \\left| \\det(R) \\right| = 1 $\n(accept this if you are not familiar with differentials and change of variable in multiple integrals), we can write\n\n\\begin{align*}\nf_Y(p) &=& \\frac{1}{2\\pi \\sigma_1 \\sigma_2} e^{-\\frac{1}{2} (R p)^T \\Sigma^{-1} R p}\\\\\n&=& \\frac{1}{2\\pi \\sigma_1 \\sigma_2} e^{-\\frac{1}{2} p^T R^T \\Sigma^{-1} R p}\n\n\\end{align*}\n\nRecall that $\\Sigma^{-1} = R D^{-1} R^T$. Hence,\n\n\\begin{align*}\nf_Y(p) &= \\frac{1}{2\\pi \\sigma_1 \\sigma_2} e^{-\\frac{1}{2} p^T R^T R D^{-1} R^T R p} \\\\\n&= \\frac{1}{2\\pi \\sigma_1 \\sigma_2} e^{-\\frac{1}{2} p^T D^{-1} p}\n\\end{align*}\n\nLet $Z$ be a random vector such that $Y = \\sqrt{D}Z =  \\begin{pmatrix} \\sigma_1 & 0 \\\\ 0 & \\sigma_2 \\end{pmatrix} Z$. By applying the same reasoning as previously, we obtain\n\n\\[\nf_Y \\left( \\sqrt{D} p \\right) J = f_Z(p).\n\\]\n\nThough the term $J$ is now equal to $\\sigma_1 \\sigma_2$. Hence,\n\n\\begin{align*}\nf_Z(p) &= \\frac{1}{2\\pi} e^{-\\frac{1}{2} (p_1^2 + p_2^2)}.\n\\end{align*}\n\n$Z$ is an isotropic (``same in all directions'') Gaussian random vector of variance 1.\n\n$X$ is obtained by applying squeezing and stretching to the coordinate axes, followed by a rotation:\n\n\\[\nX = R \\sqrt{D} Z.\n\\]\n\nAfter the rescaling of the axes, we obtain an ellipse whose axes are the coordinate axes. \nThe orthogonal matrix $R$ (in 2D and 3D, orthogonal $\\sim$ rotations) sends the canonical basis to a new orthogonal basis, \nwhich will be the axes of the new ellipse. \nSince $R$ is the matrix of eigenvectors of $\\Sigma$, the axes of the new ellipse are the eigenvectors of $\\Sigma$.\n\nThe covariance matrix of $X$ can be obtained from the covariance of $Z$:\n\n\\begin{align*}\n\\text{cov}(X) &= \\mathbb{E} (X X^T) \\\\\n&= \\mathbb{E} \\left( R \\sqrt{D} Z \n                \\left( R \\sqrt{D} Z \\right)^T \\right) \\\\\n&= \\mathbb{E} \\left( R \\sqrt{D} \n                  Z Z^T \n                  \\sqrt{D} R^T \\right) \\\\\n&= R \\sqrt{D} \n   \\mathbb{E} (Z Z^T) \n   \\sqrt{D} R^T \\\\\n&= R \\sqrt{D} \n   \\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 1 \\end{pmatrix} \n   \\sqrt{D} R^T \\\\\n&= R D R^T \\\\\n&= \\Sigma.\n\\end{align*}\n\n\nHence for an arbitrary bivariate Gaussian density:\n\n\\[\n\\frac{1}{2\\pi \\det(\\Sigma)^{1/2}} e^{-\\frac{1}{2} p^T \\Sigma^{-1} p},\n\\]\n\n$\\Sigma$ is the covariance matrix of the distribution, and the diagonalization \n\\[\n\\Sigma = R D R^T\n\\]\ngives us the orientation and shape of the ellipses describing the level lines.\n\n\n"

                "latexMainText": "\n\n\nThe (weak) law of large numbers shows that the empirical mean concentrates around the true mean as we increase the number of random variables. The Central Limit Theorem (CLT) is a stronger result which describes more precisely how the empirical mean is distributed around the true mean. We will not prove the theorem.\\\\\n\n\\medskip\n\nAssume that $X_1,X_2,\\ldots$ are i.i.d.\\ random variables with \n\n\\[\n\\mathbb{E}(X_i)=\\mu \\quad \\text{and} \\quad v(X_i)=\\sigma^2.\n\\]\nWe have seen already that \n\n\\[\n\\mathbb{E}(\\bar{X}_n)=\\mu, \\quad v(\\bar{X}_n)=\\frac{\\sigma^2}{n},\n\\]\nwhere $\\bar{X}_{n}$ is the empirical mean. The WLLN tells us that the probability of $\\bar{X}_{n}$ being \"far\" from $\\mu$ goes to zeros. In some sens, the law of $\\bar{X}_{n}$ converges to a Dirac in $\\mu$. In order to characterize more precisely how this convergence happens, we \"zoom in\" around $\\mu$. To do so, we shift the random variable to move the mean to $0$, and we multiply it by a scaling factor in order to make it of variance $1$:    \n\n\\[\nZ_n=\\frac{\\sqrt{n}\\,(\\bar{X}_n-\\mu)}{\\sigma}.\n\\]\nIt is easy to check that $\\mathbb{E}(Z_n)=0$ and that $v(Z_n)=1$. The CLT states that as $n\\to\\infty$, the distribution of $Z_n$ approaches a Gaussian distribution of mean $0$ and variance $1$. In other words, for any interval $[a,b]$,\n\n\\[\n\\lim_{n\\to\\infty}P_{Z_n}\\Bigg( [a,b] \\Bigg)\n=\\int_{a}^{b} \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2\\pi}} e^{-\\frac{t^2}{2}}dt.\n\\]\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Gaussian noise}}\\\\\n\nThe physical processes generating noises can often be modeled by a sum of independent tiny contributions. The CLT is a way to explain why noise values often follow a Gaussian distribution. \n\n"

                "summary": "<div class=\"discussion\" id=\"disc:What makes an estimator good or bad?\">\n<p><strong>Discussion 1</strong> (<strong>What makes an estimator good\r\nor bad?</strong>). </p>\n</div>",
                "hasSummary": false,
                "hasTitle": true,
                "title": "<strong>What makes an estimator good\r\nor bad?</strong>",
                "display_order": 57,
                "latexMainText": "\nThis question is non-trivial.\n\nAssume that the repetition of an experiment produced the observations \\( (x_1, \\dots, x_n)\\in S^n \\). We want to build a probabilistic model of the experiment. Further assume that we restrict the considered set of probability distributions on $S$ to the parametric statistical model $\\mathcal M$. To chose the probabilisty distribution modelling the experiment, we will use an estimator $T$ which will output a distribution on $S$ belonging to $\\mathcal M$. \n\n\nRemark. We can model the experiment with a probability distribution, but in most (if not all) situations, the probability distribution remains a model, and is not a \u201cdefining feature\u201d of the experiment. So, given observations \\( (x_1, \\dots, x_n) \\), is there a single \u201ccorrect\u201d distribution in \\( \\mathcal{M} \\)? No. \n\nConsider a statistical model made of two distributions \\( \\mathcal{M} = \\{ P_1, P_2 \\} \\). \n\nAn estimator \\( T \\) is \"good for \\( P_1 \\)\" if\n\n\\[\nP_1\\left( \\text{observations } (x_1, \\dots, x_n) \\text{ for which } T(x_1, \\dots, x_n) = P_1 \\right) \\text{ is high}\n\\]\n\\[\n\\Leftrightarrow P_1\\left( \\text{observations } (x_1, \\dots, x_n) \\text{ for which } T(x_1, \\dots, x_n) = P_2 \\right) \\text{ is small}.\n\\]\n\nIn other words, ``under the eyes of the distribution \\( P_1 \\)'', the value of \\( T \\) is usually \\( P_1 \\). We could choose a constant estimator \\( T(x_1, \\dots, x_n) = P_1 \\), \\( \\forall x_1, \\dots, x_n \\). The estimator would be perfect from the point of view of \\( P_1 \\), but would be very bad from the point of view of \\( P_2 \\): in that case,\n\n\\[\nP_2\\left( \\left\\{ (x_1, \\dots, x_n), \\, T(x_1, \\dots, x_n) = P_2 \\right\\} \\right) = 0.\n\\]\n\nA ``good'' estimator is an estimator that achieves a good compromise between\n\n\\[\nP_1\\left( \\left\\{ (x_1, \\dots, x_n) \\mid T(x_1, \\dots, x_n) = P_1 \\right\\} \\right)\n\\quad \\text{and} \\quad\nP_2\\left( \\left\\{ (x_1, \\dots, x_n) \\mid T(x_1, \\dots, x_n) = P_2 \\right\\} \\right)\n\\]\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Example}}\\\\\n\nLet \\( p_1 = 0.1 \\) and \\( p_2 = 0.9 \\). We denote by \\( P_1 \\) and \\( P_2 \\) the corresponding Bernoulli distributions. We define:\n\\[\nT(x_1, \\dots, x_n) =\n\\begin{cases}\nP_1 & \\text{if } \\frac{1}{n} \\sum x_i \\leq 0.5 \\\\\nP_2 & \\text{otherwise}\n\\end{cases}\n\\]\nHere, we consider the set of sequences of length $n$ made of 0 and 1,\n\n\\[\n\\left\\{\n\\begin{array}{l}\n0 \\quad - \\quad - \\quad - \\quad - \\quad 0 \\\\\n1 \\quad \\;0 \\quad - \\quad - \\quad - \\quad 0\\\\\n....................................\\\\\n\\end{array}\n\\right\\}\n\\text{A}\n\\qquad\nT = \\mathbb{P}_1 \\text{ on A and } \\mathbb{P}_1(A) \\text{ is large}\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\left\\{\n\\begin{array}{l}\n....................................\\\\\n1 \\quad - \\quad - \\quad - \\quad \\;1 \\quad 0 \\\\\n1 \\quad - \\quad - \\quad - \\quad - \\quad 1\n\\end{array}\n\\right\\}\n\\text{B}\n\\qquad\nT = \\mathbb{P}_2 \\text{ on B and } \\mathbb{P}_2(B) \\text{ is large}\n\\]\n\n\\bigskip\n\n\\noindent\nSo $T$ is a good estimator. Compute the values of $P_1(A)$ and $P_2(B)$ as an exercise.\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{\"Link with real life\"}}\\\\\n\nAssume that an experiment produced observations and that we know that either $P_1$ or $P_2$ is a good model. If $P_1$ is a good model, then the observation $(x_1, \\dots, x_n)$ has good chances to be in $A$, in which case $T(x_1, \\dots, x_n) = P_1$. So the function $T$ enables to recover the good probability model. Same would hold if $P_2$ was the good model.\n\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Exercise}}\\\\\n\nAn estimator \\( T \\) should make a compromise between \\( P_1(T = P_1) \\) and \\( P_2(T = P_2) \\).                 "latexMainText": "\n\n\nThe more the law of $\\hat{\\theta}_n$ is concentrated around the true parameter $\\theta_{\\text{true}}$, the better. When $\\Theta\\subset \\mathbb{R}$, define 3 important quantities:\n\n\\begin{itemize}\n  \\item \\textbf{Mean Square Error (MSE)}:\n  \\[\n  \\mathbb{E}_{\\theta_{\\text{true}}} \\left( \\| \\hat{\\theta} - \\theta_{\\text{true}} \\|^2 \\right) \n  \\]\n\n  \\item \\textbf{The bias}:\n  \\[\n  \\mathbb{E}_{\\theta_{\\text{true}}}(\\hat{\\theta}) - \\theta_{\\text{true}}\n  \\]\n\n  \\item \\textbf{The variance}:\n  \\[\n  \\mathbb{E}_{\\theta_{\\text{true}}} \\left( \\left\\| \\hat{\\theta} - \\mathbb{E}_{\\theta_{\\text{true}}}(\\hat{\\theta}) \\right\\|^2 \\right) = \\left\\| \\hat{\\theta} - \\mathbb{E}_{\\theta_{\\text{true}}}(\\hat{\\theta}) \\right\\|^2\n  \\]\n\\end{itemize}\n\nThe MSE quantifies how far $\\hat{\\theta}$ is from $\\theta_{\\text{true}}$ on average. The MSE can be decomposed using the bias-variance decomposition.\n\n\\[\n\\mathbb{E}_{\\theta_{\\text{true}}} \\left( \\hat{\\theta} - \\mathbb{E}_{\\theta_{\\text{true}}}(\\hat{\\theta}) \\right) = 0\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\mathbb{E}_{\\theta_{\\text{true}}} \\left( \\left( \\mathbb{E}_{\\theta_{\\text{true}}}(\\hat{\\theta}) - \\theta_{\\text{true}} \\right) \\cdot \\left( \\hat{\\theta} - \\mathbb{E}_{\\theta_{\\text{true}}}(\\hat{\\theta}) \\right) \\right) = 0 \n\\\n\\]\nRemember that $\\langle u, v \\rangle = 0 \\Rightarrow \\|u + v\\|^2 = \\|u\\|^2 + \\|v\\|^2$. Hence\n\n\\[\n\\begin{aligned}\n\\mathbb{E}_{\\theta_{\\mathrm{true}}}\\!\\Bigl(\n  \\bigl(\n    \\underbrace{ \\hat{\\theta}-\\mathbb{E}_{\\theta_{\\mathrm{true}}}(\\hat{\\theta})\n      + (\\mathbb{E}_{\\theta_{\\mathrm{true}}}(\\hat{\\theta})-\\theta_{\\mathrm{true}}) }_{\\displaystyle \\hat{\\theta}-\\theta_{\\mathrm{true}}}\n  \\bigr)^{2}\n\\Bigr)\n&=\n\\left( \\mathbb{E}_{\\theta_{\\mathrm{true}}}(\\hat{\\theta}) - \\theta_{\\mathrm{true}} \\right)^2\n+ \\mathbb{E}_{\\theta_{\\mathrm{true}}}\\!\\left( \\left( \\hat{\\theta} - \\mathbb{E}_{\\theta_{\\mathrm{true}}}(\\hat{\\theta}) \\right)^2 \\right).\n\\end{aligned}\n\\]\n\n\n\n\n\\vspace{0.3cm}\n\nOr,\n\\[\n\\text{MSE} = \\text{bias}^2 + \\text{variance}\n\\]\n\n\nThough the most important thing is to have a small MSE, we often like to have bias $= 0$. This means that $\\hat{\\theta}$ is ``evenly distributed'' around $\\theta_{\\text{true}}$. \nIn that case, $\\text{MSE} = \\text{variance}$.\n\n"

                "display_order": 67,
                "latexMainText": "\nConsider a statistical model $\\mathcal{M}$ parametrized by $\\theta$. How difficult is it to build a \u201cgood\u201d estimator? \\\\\n\nGeneral idea: if the probability distributions in $\\mathcal{M}$ are very different from each other, they are easy to distinguish. If the distribution are almost identical, it will be difficult to build a good estimator. If we quantify how different the probability distributions are in $\\mathcal{M}$, we can also hope to quantify how good can an estimator can be. To do so, we will first start by describing a way to quantify variations between probability distributions. This will later lead us to the Cramer-Rao bound (CRB), which informs us on how good an estimator can be. Though the CRB is a fundamental brick of the theory of statistical estimation, there exists many other ways of linking distances between probability distirbutions and quality of estimators, which we will not address in this course.  \\\\\n\n\\medskip\n\nAssume that there are $P, Q \\in \\mathcal{M}$ which are very similar. \nIt will be very difficult for the estimator to identify them properly.\nThe Cram\u00e9r\u2013Rao bound is an upper bound on the quality of an estimator, \nbased on how close to each other the probability distributions of $\\mathcal{M}$ are. \nFor each $\\theta$, the bound looks at how similar $P$ and $P_{\\theta + \\Delta}$ are. \\\\\n\nBefore giving the bound, analyse first how to quantify the magnitude of a variation around a distribution. Consider the set $S = \\{1, \\dots, n\\}$ and a probability $P$ on $S$. Note $p_i := P(\\{i\\})$.\nConsider $Q$ another distribution and note $\\Delta = Q - P$, $\\Delta_i = q_i - p_i$.\\\\\n\nThe larger $\\Delta$ is, the more different $Q$ is from $P$. Assume that $\\Delta_i \\simeq 0.1$. Is this a big change for $p_i$? Remember that $p_i$ is a proportion. \nTo measure the change in a proportion, it\u2019s often useful to look at the \\emph{relative change}\n\\[\n\\frac{\\Delta_i}{p_i} = \\frac{q_i}{p_i} - 1.\n\\]\nGoing from $p_i = 0.1$ to $0.2$ is then considered a much bigger change than from $0.8$ to $0.9$. How large is the function $i \\mapsto \\frac{\\Delta_i}{p_i}$? Remember the $L^2$ norm of functions:\n\\[\n\\|f\\|^2 = \\int f(x)^2 \\, dx \\quad \\text{or} \\quad \\sum_i f(i)^2\n\\]\nWe sum the values of $f^2$. Since we are measuring a deviation from $P$, we might want to weight the importance of each $i$ by its importance under $P$. \nWe get then:\n\\[\n\\left\\| i \\mapsto \\frac{\\Delta_i}{p_i} \\right\\|_P^2 \n= \\sum_i \\left( \\frac{\\Delta_i}{p_i} \\right)^2 p_i\n\\]\nwhich is actually \n\\[\n\\mathbb{E}_P \\left( \\left( \\frac{\\Delta}{p} \\right)^2 \\right),\n\\]\nwhere $\\frac{\\Delta}{p}$ refers to the function $i \\mapsto \\frac{\\Delta_i}{p_i}$, interpreted as a random variable ($\\Omega = S$, with the probability $P$). Note that \n\\[\n\\sum_i \\frac{\\Delta_i}{p_i} p_i = \\sum_i \\Delta_i = \\sum_i q_i - p_i = 0.\n\\]\nThis can be rewritten as \n\\[\n\\mathbb{E}_P \\left( \\frac{\\Delta}{p} \\right) = 0.\n\\]\n\nHence \n\\[\n\\left\\| i \\mapsto \\frac{\\Delta_i}{p_i} \\right\\|_P^2 = \\operatorname{Var}_P \\left( \\frac{\\Delta}{p} \\right).\n\\]\n\nIf this number is large, the change $P \\to P + \\Delta$ is important.\n\n\\textbf{Remark:} There are possibly different ways of evaluating the magnitude of variations of a probability. \nThis natural, but particular, way of evaluating the magnitudes of variations is the one that appears in the Cram\u00e9r\u2013Rao bound (CRB).\n\n"

                "display_order": 68,
                "latexMainText": "\n\nLet $\\mathcal{M}=\\{P_{\\theta},\\theta\\in \\Theta\\}$ be a parametric statistical model of probability distributions on a set $S$, with $\\Theta \\subset \\mathbb{R}$. Note $\\ell$ the likelihood function: $\\ell(\\theta; x) = P_\\theta(\\{x\\})$ when $S$ is discret,  \nor $\\ell(\\theta; x) = f_\\theta(x)$ when $S$ is continuous and when $P_\\theta$ has a density.\\\\\n\n\\medskip\n\nInstead of looking at variations between $2$ fixed distirbution in $\\mathcal{M}$ as done in the previous discussion \\ref{disc:Variations between probability distributions}, we will look at infinitesimal variations around the parameter $\\theta$. Hence, instead of the term $\\frac{\\Delta}{p}$ of the previous discussion, let us introduce the \"score function\"\n\n$$V(\\theta;x)= \\frac{\\frac{\\partial \\ell}{\\partial \\theta}(\\theta; x) }{\\ell(\\theta; x)}, $$\n\nwhere\n\n\\[\n\\frac{\\partial \\ell}{\\partial \\theta}(\\theta; x) := \\lim_{\\Delta \\theta \\to 0} \\frac{\\ell(\\theta + \\Delta \\theta; x) - \\ell(\\theta; x)}{\\Delta \\theta}\n\\]\n\nAt fixed $\\theta$, is the function $x\\mapsto V(\\theta;x)$ large or small? If it is small, \n$P_\\theta$ resembles $P_{\\theta + \\Delta \\theta}$ and it will be hard for an estimator to tell them apart. On the contrary, if it is large, we have chances to build an estimator which can identify $\\theta$ \nwith a relatively good precision. To evaluate the \"size\" of this function, define as previously \n\n\\begin{align*}\n\\left\\| x\\mapsto V(\\theta;x) \\right\\|_{\\theta}^2&=& \\sum_{x\\in S} V(\\theta;x)^2 l(\\theta;x) \\quad \\text{(discret case)}\\\\\n&=&\\int_S V(\\theta;x)^2 l(\\theta;x)\\mathrm{d}x \\quad \\text{(continuous case)}\\\\\n\\end{align*}\n\nLet $X$ be any random variable taking its values in $S$ with law $P_{\\theta}$. We have (why?)\n\n$$\n\\left\\| x\\mapsto V(\\theta;x) \\right\\|_{\\theta}^2 = \\mathbb{E}\\left( V(\\theta;X)^2 \\right)\n$$\n\nAgain, following the previous discussion we can show that the expectation of the score function is null which. Hence the norm squared of $V(\\theta;X)$ is just its variance. We have in the discret case\n\\[\n\\mathbb{E}(V(\\theta; X)) \n= \\sum_x \\frac{\\frac{\\partial \\ell}{\\partial \\theta} (\\theta ; x)}{\\ell(\\theta ; x)} \\ell (\\theta;x) \n= \\sum_x \\frac{\\partial \\ell}{\\partial \\theta}(\\theta;x) \n\\]\n\\[\n= \\sum_x \\lim_{h \\to 0} \\frac{1}{h} \\left( P_{\\theta + h}(x) - P_\\theta(x) \\right) \n= \\lim_{h \\to 0} \\frac{1}{h} \\left( \\sum_x P_{\\theta + h}(x) - \\sum_x P_\\theta(x) \\right) =\n\\]\n\\[\n=\\lim_{h \\to 0} \\frac{1}{h} \\left( 1 - 1 \\right) = 0\n\\]\nThe calculation works in the continous case as well provided that we can exchange the derivation and the integral. Hence\n\\[\n\\mathbb{E} \\left( V(\\theta; X)^2 \\right) = \\operatorname{Var}(V(\\theta; X))\n\\]\n\n\nNote that $\\frac{\\partial}{\\partial \\theta} \\ln \\ell \n= \\frac{\\frac{\\partial}{\\partial \\theta} \\ell}{\\ell}$. Hence we also have\n\n$$\\mathbb{E}\\left( V(\\theta;X)^2 \\right) = \\mathbb{E}\\left( \\left( \\frac{\\partial \\ln \\ell}{\\partial \\theta}(\\theta;X) \\right)^2 \\right)$$\n\nThis term is called the Fisher information and is noted $\\mathcal{I}(\\theta) $. The first line should be known by heart:\n\n\\begin{align*}\n\\mathcal{I}(\\theta) &=& \\mathbb{E} \\left( \\left( \\frac{\\partial \\ln \\ell}{\\partial \\theta} (\\theta ; X) \\right)^2 \\right)\\\\\n&=& \\operatorname{Var}(V(\\theta; x))\\\\\n&=& \\mathbb{E} \\left( V(\\theta; x)^2 \\right)\\\\\n&=& \\left\\| x\\mapsto V(\\theta;x) \\right\\|_{\\theta}^2.\\\\\n\\end{align*}\n\nAssume that $\\mathcal{I}(\\theta_{true})$ is close to $0$: changing $\\theta$ around $\\theta_{true}$ almost does not change $P_{\\theta}$. In other word, approximately knowing the true distribution gives almost no information on the actual value of the parameter $\\theta$. Hence the name Fisher \"information\".\n\nSimilarly, as we will see in the CRB, the bigger $\\mathcal{I}(\\theta)$, the easier it is to identify the distribution $P_{\\theta}$. It as natural to believe that the more data we have the easier it is to estimate a distribution. In the independent scenario assumption, this is materialized by the following calculation. \n\n \\[\n  \\ell(\\theta; x_1, x_2) = \\ell(\\theta; x_1) \\ell(\\theta; x_2)\n\\rightarrow \n  \\ln \\ell(\\theta; x_1, x_2) = \\ln \\ell(\\theta; x_1) + \\ln \\ell(\\theta; x_2)\n\\]\nHence\n  \\[\n  \\mathbb{E} \\left( \\left( \\frac{\\partial}{\\partial \\theta} \\ln \\ell(\\theta; X_1, X_2) \\right)^2 \\right)\n  = \\operatorname{Var} \\left( \\frac{\\partial}{\\partial \\theta} \\ln \\ell(\\theta; X_1) \n  + \\frac{\\partial}{\\partial \\theta} \\ln \\ell(\\theta; X_2) \\right),\n  \\]\n\nand if $X_1$ and $X_2$ are independent,\n\n\n\\begin{align*}\n\\mathbb{E} \\left( \\left( \\frac{\\partial}{\\partial \\theta} \\ln \\ell(\\theta; X_1, X_2) \\right)^2 \\right) &=& \\operatorname{Var} \\left( \\frac{\\partial}{\\partial \\theta} \\ln \\ell(\\theta; X_1) \\right) \n  + \\operatorname{Var} \\left( \\frac{\\partial}{\\partial \\theta} \\ln \\ell(\\theta; X_2) \\right)\\\\\n&=& 2 \\cdot \\operatorname{Var} \\left( \\frac{\\partial}{\\partial \\theta} \\ln \\ell(\\theta; X_1) \\right).\n\\end{align*}\n\nFor $n$ observations, it gives\n  \\[\n  \\mathcal{I}_n(\\theta) = n \\cdot \\mathcal{I}(\\theta),\n  \\]\nthe value of the information grows proportionnally to the number of observations.\n"

Note that such an estimator is biased:\r\n<math display=\"block\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo form=\"prefix\" stretchy=\"false\">(</mo><msub><mi>\u03b8</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>e</mi></mrow></msub><mo form=\"postfix\" stretchy=\"false\">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>\ud835\udd3c</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>e</mi></mrow></msub><mo form=\"prefix\" stretchy=\"false\">(</mo><mover><mi>\u03b8</mi><mo accent=\"true\">\u0302</mo></mover><mo form=\"postfix\" stretchy=\"false\">)</mo><mo>\u2212</mo><msub><mi>\u03b8</mi><mtext mathvariant=\"normal\">true</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>\u03b8</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>\u2212</mo><msub><mi>\u03b8</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>e</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mspace width=\"1.0em\"></mspace><msup><mi>b</mi><mo>\u2032</mo></msup><mo form=\"prefix\" stretchy=\"false\">(</mo><msub><mi>\u03b8</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>e</mi></mrow></msub><mo form=\"postfix\" stretchy=\"false\">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>\u2212</mi><mn>1</mn><mi>.</mi></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">b(\\theta_{true})=\\mathbb{E}_{true}(\\hat \\theta) - \\theta_{\\text{true}}=\\theta_0-\\theta_{true}, \\quad b'(\\theta_{true})=-1.</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nApplying the correct formula for biased estimators only tells that the\r\nvariance is positive.                 "summary": "<div class=\"theorem\" id=\"th:The Cramer-Rao bound\">\n<p><strong>Theorem 9</strong> (<strong>The Cramer-Rao bound</strong>).\r\n</p>\n</div>",
                "hasSummary": false,
                "hasTitle": true,
                "title": "<strong>The Cramer-Rao bound</strong>",
                "display_order": 69,
                "latexMainText": "\nFix a parameter $\\theta_{\\text{true}}$. This sets a probability distribution $P_{\\theta_{true}}$, or simply $P_{true}$, on $S$. Under the independence assumption, this distribution gives a distribution on $S^n$. Recall that an estimator $\\hat \\theta$ is a function $S^n\\rightarrow \\Theta$. The more the law of $\\hat \\theta$ is concentrated around $\\theta_{\\text{true}}$ the better. When $\\Theta \\subset \\mathbb{R}$, this can be quantified by the mean squared error. If the estimator $\\hat{\\theta}$ is assumed unbiased, the MSE is simply the variance.\\\\\n\n\\medskip\n\nFor any unbiased estimator $\\hat{\\theta}$, the \\textbf{Cram\u00e9r\u2013Rao bound} is\n\\[\n\\operatorname{Var}_{\\text{true}}(\\hat{\\theta}) \\geq \n\\frac{1}{\\mathcal{I}(\\theta_{true})}.\n\\]\n\nThis is the relation announced in the begining of discussion \\ref{disc:Variations between probability distributions}.\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Remarks}}\\\\\n\n\\begin{itemize}\n  \\item The bound depends on $\\theta_{\\text{true}}$, some parameters might be easier to estimate than others.\n  \n  \\item The bound only looks at the neighborhood of $P_\\theta$. Even if neighboring distributions are significantly different from $P_\\theta$, \n  there might be a $\\theta'$ far from $\\theta$ with $P_{\\theta'} \\simeq P_\\theta$. \n  If $\\theta_{\\text{true}} = \\theta$ or $\\theta'$, $\\operatorname{Var}(\\hat{\\theta})$ will be large even though it is not reflected in the bound. This shows that there are cases for which there are no estimators which achieve the minimal variance given by the bound.\n  \\item When the estimator $\\hat{\\theta}$ has a bias $b(\\theta_{true}) = \\mathbb{E}_{true}(\\hat{\\theta}) - \\theta_{true}$, the bound becomes\n  \\[\n  \\operatorname{Var}_{\\text{true}}(\\hat{\\theta}) \n  \\geq \\frac{(1 + b'(\\theta_{\\text{true}}))^2}\n         {\\mathcal{I}(\\theta_{\\text{true}})}\n  \\]\n  \\item Consider a constant estimator $\\hat \\theta = \\theta_0 \\in \\Theta$. When $\\theta_{\\text{true}}=\\theta_0$, the estimator always gives the correct value, which mean that its variance is $0$, apparently contradicting the CRB. Note that such an estimator is biased:\n  $$b(\\theta_{true})=\\mathbb{E}_{true}(\\hat \\theta) - \\theta_{\\text{true}}=\\theta_0-\\theta_{true}, \\quad b'(\\theta_{true})=-1.$$ \n  Applying the correct formula for biased estimators only tells that the variance is positive. So, the CRB still holds, though not it is not very usefull.\n\n\\end{itemize}\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Proof of the CRB (clean this!!)}}\\\\\n\n\nAssume that $X$ follows $P_{\\theta_{\\text{true}}}$. In the discrete case, we have\n\\[\n\\mathbb{E}(V(\\theta_{\\text{true}}, X) \\hat{\\theta}(X)) \n= \\sum_{i \\in S} V(\\theta_{\\text{true}} ; i) \\hat{\\theta}(i) P_X(i)\n\\]\n\\[\n= \\sum_{i \\in S} \\frac{\\partial \\ell}{\\partial \\theta}(\\theta_{\\text{true}}, i) \n\\cdot \\frac{1}{\\ell(\\theta_{\\text{true}}, i)} \\hat{\\theta}(i) P_X(i)\n\\]\n\\[\n= \\sum_{i \\in S} \\frac{\\partial}{\\partial \\theta} \\ell(\\theta_{\\text{true}}, i) \n\\cdot \\hat{\\theta}(i) \\cdot \\underbrace{ \\frac{P_X(i)}{\\ell(\\theta_{\\text{true}}, i)} \n }_{\\text{because } P_X(i) = \\ell(\\theta_{\\text{true}}, i)}\n\\]\n\n\\[\n= \\sum_{i \\in S} \\frac{\\partial}{\\partial \\theta} P_{\\theta}(i)\\big|_{\\theta = \\theta_{\\text{true}}} \\cdot \\hat{\\theta}(i)\n\\]\n\n\\[\n= \\frac{\\partial}{\\partial \\theta} \\left( \\sum_{i \\in S} P_\\theta(i) \\cdot \\hat{\\theta}(i) \\right) \\Big|_{\\theta = \\theta_{\\text{true}}}\n= \\frac{\\partial}{\\partial \\theta} \\left( \\mathbb{E}_\\theta(\\hat{\\theta}) \\right) \\Big|_{\\theta = \\theta_{\\text{true}}}\n= \\frac{\\partial}{\\partial \\theta} (\\theta) \\Big|_{\\theta = \\theta_{\\text{true}}} = 1 \n\\quad \\text{(unbiased hypothesis)}\n\\]\n\nFurthermore,\n\\[\n\\mathbb{E}(V(\\theta_{\\text{true}}, X) \\hat{\\theta}(X)) = \n\\mathbb{E}\\left( V(\\theta_{\\text{true}}, X)(\\hat{\\theta}(X) - \\theta_{\\text{true}}) \\right)\n\\quad \\text{(because } \\mathbb{E}(V) = 0 \\text{)}\n\\]\n\nThe Cauchy\u2013Schwarz inequality:\n\\[\n1=\\mathbb{E}\\left( V(\\theta_{\\text{true}}, X)(\\hat{\\theta}(X) - \\theta_{\\text{true}}) \\right) \\leq \\operatorname{Var}(V(\\theta_{\\text{true}}, X)) \\cdot \\operatorname{Var}(\\hat{\\theta}(X))\n\\]\n\\[\n\\Rightarrow \\quad \n\\operatorname{Var}(\\hat{\\theta}(X)) \\geq \\frac{1}{\\operatorname{Var}(V(\\theta_{\\text{true}}, X))}\n\\]\n\n\n"

0) = 1 - p, \\quad \\ell(p; 1) = p\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\frac{\\partial}{\\partial p} \\ln \\ell(p; 0) = \\frac{-1}{1 - p}, \\quad \n\\frac{\\partial}{\\partial p} \\ln \\ell(p; 1) = \\frac{1}{p}\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\mathbb{E} \\left( \\left( \\frac{\\partial}{\\partial p} \\ln \\ell(p_{\\text{true}}, X) \\right)^2 \\right)\n= \\left( \\frac{-1}{1 - p_{\\text{true}}} \\right)^2 \\cdot \\mathbb{P}(X = 0)\n+ \\left( \\frac{1}{p_{\\text{true}}} \\right)^2 \\cdot \\mathbb{P}(X = 1)\n\\]\n\n\\[\n= \\frac{1}{(1 - p_{\\text{true}})^2} (1 - p_{\\text{true}}) + \\frac{1}{p_{\\text{true}}^2} p_{\\text{true}}\n= \\frac{1}{(1 - p_{\\text{true}}) p_{\\text{true}}}\n\\]\n\nSo for an unbiased estimator $\\hat{p}$ of $p$ based on $n$ observations:\n\\[\n\\operatorname{Var}_{p_{\\text{true}}}(\\hat{p}) \n\\geq \\frac{1/n}{\\frac{1}{(1 - p_{\\text{true}}) p_{\\text{true}}}} \n= \\frac{1}{n} \\cdot (1 - p_{\\text{true}}) p_{\\text{true}}\n\\]\n\nConsider the estimator\n\\[\n\\hat{p}(x_1, \\dots, x_n) = \\frac{1}{n} \\sum_{i=1}^n x_i.\n\\]\n\nLet $X_i$ be i.i.d. $\\sim \\text{Bern}(p_{\\text{true}})$,\n\n\\[\n\\mathbb{E}_{p_{\\text{true}}}(\\hat{p}) = \\mathbb{E} \\left( \\hat{p}(X_1, \\dots, X_n) \\right)\n= \\frac{1}{n} \\sum_{i=1}^n \\mathbb{E}(X_i) = p_{\\text{true}} \\quad \\Rightarrow \\quad \\hat{p} \\text{ is unbiased}\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\operatorname{Var}_{p_{\\text{true}}}(\\hat{p}) = \\operatorname{Var} \\left( \\hat{p}(X_1, \\dots, X_n) \\right)\n= \\operatorname{Var} \\left( \\frac{1}{n} \\sum X_i \\right) \n= \\frac{1}{n^2} \\sum \\operatorname{Var}(X_i)\n= \\frac{1}{n} p_{\\text{true}} (1 - p_{\\text{true}})\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\hat{p} \\text{ attains the CRB, we cannot find an estimator with a better variance.}\n\\]\n\n\n"

                "latexMainText": "\n\nLet $\\theta_{true}$ be the true parameter and\n$\\mathcal I(\\theta)$ the Fisher information for a single observation.\nUnder some usual regularity assumptions on the probability distributions, we can show (we will not prove it) that the average squared error of the MLE shrinks like\n\\[\n           \\operatorname{MSE}\\!\\bigl(\\hat\\theta_{\\text{MLE}}\\bigr)\n           \\;=\\;\\frac{1}{n\\,\\mathcal I(\\theta_{true})}\\;+\\;o\\!\\Bigl(\\tfrac1n\\Bigr).\n\\]\n\nThis means that for large $n$, the $\\operatorname{MSE}$ can be approximated by $\\frac{1}{n\\,\\mathcal I(\\theta_{true})}$. Remember that the $\\operatorname{MSE}$ is larger than the variance, and that the variance is larger or equal to $\\frac{1}{n\\,\\mathcal I(\\theta_{true})}$ (CRB). Hence the MLE is practically as accurate as theory allows when the sample size $n$ is large. We says that the estimator is \"asymptotically efficient\".\\\\\n\n\\medskip\n\nRemark: the MLE is not always unbiased, but for large $n$ the bias becomes smaller and smaller, which makes the above argument valid. \n\n"
