                "latexMainText": "\nWe have seen previously that the MLE is given by\n\\[\n\\hat{\\theta}_{\\text{MLE}}(x) = \\arg\\max_{\\theta} P_{\\theta}(x)\n\\]\nConsider the simple example $\\mathcal{M} = \\{\\mathbb{P}_1, \\mathbb{P}_2\\}$, $\\theta \\in \\{1, 2\\}$.\n\\[\n\\hat{\\theta}_{\\text{MLE}}(x) = \\arg\\max_i P_i(x)\n\\]\nAssume that $l(1; x) = 0.2$, for some observed data $x$, and that\n$l(2; x) = 0.9$. In the absence of any other information,\n$\\mathbb{P}_2$ looks like a better model than $\\mathbb{P}_1$.\n\nIn some cases however, we might have prior information on the models\n$\\mathbb{P}_1$ and $\\mathbb{P}_2$. Medical tests are a common example of that situation.\nThe possible values of a test are $\\{\\text{positive}, \\text{negative}\\}$.\nIf the patient is ill, the test has certain probability values,\n$P_{\\text{ill}}(\\text{positive})$ and $P_{\\text{ill}}(\\text{negative})$. Assume that $P_{\\text{ill}}(\\text{positive}) = 0.999$ and\n$P_{\\text{ill}}(\\text{negative}) = 0.001$.\nIf the patient is healthy, assume that\n$P_{\\text{healthy}}(\\text{positive}) = 0.002$ and\n$P_{\\text{healthy}}(\\text{negative}) = 0.998$.\n\n\\[\n\\begin{array}{c|cc}\n & \\text{healthy} & \\text{ill} \\\\\n\\hline\n\\text{positive} & 0.002 & 0.999 \\\\\n\\text{negative} & 0.998 & 0.001 \\\\\n\\end{array}\n\\]\nThe data $x$ is in $\\{\\text{positive}, \\text{negative}\\}$, and the statistical model \n$\\mathcal{M} = \\{P_\\theta\\}$ with $\\theta \\in \\{\\text{healthy}, \\text{ill}\\}$.\nAssume that the test value $x$ is ``positive''. The MLE estimator of $\\theta$ gives\n\\[\n\\hat{\\theta}_{\\text{MLE}}(\\text{positive}) = \\arg\\max_i P_i(\\text{positive}) = \\text{ill}\n\\]\nBut assume that we know that approximately 1 person in 1000 has the disease.\nThis gives us a ``prior probability'' on parameters $\\theta \\in \\{\\text{healthy}, \\text{ill}\\}$:\n\\[\nP_{\\text{prior}}(\\text{ill}) = 10^{-3}, \\quad P_{\\text{prior}}(\\text{healthy}) = 1 - 10^{-3}\n\\]\n$P_{\\text{ill}}$ and $P_{\\text{healthy}}$ were originally defined as two separate probabilities on observations. The prior enables to construct a probability on the Cartesian product\n\\[\n\\{\\text{healthy}, \\text{ill}\\} \\times \\{\\text{positive}, \\text{negative}\\},\n\\]\nby interpreting $P_{\\text{ill}}$ and $P_{\\text{healthy}}$ as conditional probabilities:\n\\[\nP_{\\text{healthy}}(\\text{positive}) \\rightarrow P(\\text{positive} \\mid \\text{healthy})\n\\]\n\\[\nP(\\text{healthy}, \\text{positive}) = P(\\text{positive} \\mid \\text{healthy}) \\cdot P_{\\text{prior}}(\\text{healthy}).\n\\]\nWe can then reverse the conditioning and look at probabilities conditioned by the observation:\n\\[\nP(\\text{ill} \\mid \\text{positive}) = \\frac{P(\\text{ill}, \\text{positive})}{P(\\text{positive})}\n\\]\n\\[\n= \\frac{P(\\text{positive} \\mid \\text{ill}) \\cdot P_{\\text{prior}}(\\text{ill})}\n       {P(\\text{positive} \\mid \\text{ill}) \\cdot P_{\\text{prior}}(\\text{ill}) + \n        P(\\text{positive} \\mid \\text{healthy}) \\cdot P_{\\text{prior}}(\\text{healthy})}\n\\]\n\\[\n= \\frac{0.999 \\times 10^{-3}}{0.999 \\times 10^{-3} + 0.002 \\times (1 - 10^{-3})}\n\\]\n\\[\n\\approx \\frac{1}{3}\n\\]\nThe probability of being ill is actually only $\\frac{1}{3}$. This is due to \nthe relatively high number of false positives \n$P(\\text{positive} \\mid \\text{healthy}) P_{\\text{prior}}(\\text{healthy})$. Hence, the prior probability can significantly change our interpretation \nof an observed data. The analogue of the MLE estimation in presence \nof a prior probability is called the maximum a posteriori (MAP):\n\\[\n\\hat{\\theta}_{\\text{MAP}}(x) = \\arg\\max_{\\theta} P(\\theta \\mid x)\n\\]\nSince $P_\\theta$ is now interpreted as a conditional probability, the MLE can \nbe rewritten as\n\\[\n\\hat{\\theta}_{\\text{MLE}}(x) = \\arg\\max_{\\theta} P(x \\mid \\theta)\n\\]\nwhich highlights the symmetry between the two estimators.\n\n\nIn the previous example, the MAP estimator for one test always \noutputs ``healthy''. However, a positive test still informs us that \nthe probability of being ill is $\\frac{1}{3}$. If the disease is dangerous, \nwe probably don\u2019t want to discard this information.\n\n"

The loss function is \nsometimes called a cost function and noted $C(\\theta_1, \\theta_2)$, which \navoids ambiguities with the log-likelihood $L$.                 "latexMainText": "\n\nIn the entire course, the $\\log$ function refers to $\\log_2(x)=\\frac{ln(x)}{ln(2)}$. Since $x \\log \\frac{1}{x} \\to 0$ as $x \\to 0$, we always consider that $0\\log(0)=0$.\\\\ \n\nFor discrete probability distributions, define the following quantities\n\n\n\\begin{itemize}\n  \\item Shannon entropy\n  \\[\n    H(P) = \\sum_i p_i \\log \\frac{1}{p_i} = - \\sum_i p_i \\log p_i.\n  \\]\n\n  \\item Cross-entropy\n  \\[\n    H(P,Q) = \\sum_i p_i \\log \\frac{1}{q_i}\n           = - \\sum_i p_i \\log q_i.\n  \\]\n\n  \\item Kullback-Leibler divergence\n  \\[\n    D_{\\mathrm{KL}}(P,Q) = \\sum_i p_i \\log\\!\\left(\\frac{p_i}{q_i}\\right)\n    = H(P,Q) - H(P).\n  \\]\n\\end{itemize}\n\nIf $X$ is a random variable, its entropy is defined as the entropy of its law:\n\n  \\[\n    H(X) = H(P_X),\n  \\]\n\nwhere $P_X$ denotes the distribution of $X$. Same for cross-entropies and $D_{\\mathrm{KL}}$.\\\\\n\nFor distributions on $\\mathbb{R}$ with densities define the analogous quantities,\n\n\\begin{itemize}\n  \\item Differential (Shannon) entropy\n  \\[\n    H(f) = \\int f(x)\\,\\log\\!\\left(\\frac{1}{f(x)}\\right)\\,dx.\n  \\]\n\n  \\item Differential cross-entropy\n  \\[\n    H(f,g) = \\int f(x)\\,\\log\\!\\left(\\frac{1}{g(x)}\\right)\\,dx\n           = - \\int f(x)\\,\\log g(x)\\,dx.\n  \\]\n\n  \\item Kullback-Leibler divergence\n  \\[\n    D_{\\mathrm{KL}}(f,g) = \\int f(x)\\,\\log\\!\\left(\\frac{f(x)}{g(x)}\\right)\\,dx\n    = H(f,g) - H(f).\n  \\]\n\n\\end{itemize}\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Discrete vs continuous}}\\\\\n\n\n\\medskip\n\\noindent$\\triangle$ \\textbf{Discrete versus continuous entropy.}\nThe value of the differential entropy cannot be simply obtained as a limit of the\ndiscrete entropy. Let $P_{\\Delta}$ be a discrete probability approximating the\ndensity $f$,\n\n\\[\n  p_\\Delta(i) = f(x_i)\\,\\Delta.\n\\]\nThe entropy of $P_{\\Delta}$ is given by\n\n\\[\n  H(P_\\Delta) = \\sum_i p_\\Delta(i)\\log\\frac{1}{p_\\Delta(i)}\n    = \\sum_i f(x_i)\\,\\Delta \\left(\\log\\frac{1}{f(x_i)} + \\log\\frac{1}{\\Delta}\\right)\n\\]\n\\[\n    = \\sum_i f(x_i)\\log\\frac{1}{f(x_i)}\\,\\Delta\n      + \\log\\frac{1}{\\Delta}\\sum_i f(x_i)\\,\\Delta.\n\\]\n\nIf we replace $\\Delta$ by $2^{-n}$, we get\n\n\\[\n  H(P_{2^{-n}}) = H(f) + o(1) + n\\bigl(1+o(1)\\bigr) = n + o(1) \\not\\to H(f).\n\\]\n\n\\medskip\n\\noindent$\\triangle$ \\textbf{Discrete versus continuous cross-entropy.}\nDefine similarly $Q_{\\Delta}$ as a discrete approximation of the density $g$,\n$q_\\Delta(i) = g(x_i)\\,\\Delta$. The discrete cross-entropy is\n\n\\begin{align*}\n  H(P_\\Delta,Q_\\Delta)\n    &= \\sum_i p_\\Delta(i)\\log\\frac{1}{q_\\Delta(i)}\n      = \\sum_i f(x_i)\\Delta \\log\\frac{1}{g(x_i)\\Delta} \\\\\n    &= \\sum_i f(x_i)\\Delta\\left(\\log\\frac{1}{g(x_i)} + \\log\\frac{1}{\\Delta}\\right) \\\\\n    &= \\sum_i f(x_i)\\log\\frac{1}{g(x_i)}\\,\\Delta\n       + \\log\\frac{1}{\\Delta}\\sum_i f(x_i)\\,\\Delta \\\\\n    &= H(f,g) + \\log\\frac{1}{\\Delta} + o(1),\n\\end{align*}\nso again, $H(P_\\Delta,Q_\\Delta)$ diverges as $\\Delta\\to0$.\n\n\n\\medskip\n\\medskip\n\\noindent$\\triangle$ \\textbf{Discrete versus continuous $D_{\\mathrm{KL}}$.}\n\\noindent On the other hand, the discrete KL divergence does tend to the continuous version. With $p_\\Delta(i)=f(x_i)\\Delta$ and\n$q_\\Delta(i)=g(x_i)\\Delta$ we get\n\n\\begin{align*}\nD_{\\mathrm{KL}}(P_\\Delta,Q_\\Delta)\n  &= \\sum_i f(x_i)\\,\\Delta \\;\n     \\log\\!\\left(\\frac{f(x_i)\\,\\Delta}{g(x_i)\\,\\Delta}\\right)\\\\[0.5em]\n  &= \\sum_i f(x_i)\\,\\Delta \\;\n     \\log\\!\\left(\\frac{f(x_i)}{g(x_i)}\\right) \\qquad\n     \\\\[0.5em]\n  &\\xrightarrow[\\Delta\\to 0]{}\\;\n     \\int f(x)\\,\\log\\!\\left(\\frac{f(x)}{g(x)}\\right)\\,dx\n     \\;=\\; D_{\\mathrm{KL}}(f,g).\n\\end{align*}\n\n\n"

                "latexMainText": "\n\nConsider a finit set $\\mathcal X$ and a family of probability distributions $P_{\\theta}$ over $\\mathcal X$, parametrized by $\\theta$. Denote $p_{\\theta}$ the probability mass function,\n\n\\[ p_{\\theta}(x)=P{\\theta}(\\{x\\}). \\]\n\nConsider $n$ observation $x_1,\\dots,x_n\\in \\mathcal X$. The log-likelihood is\n\n\\begin{eqnarray*}\n\\ell (\\theta;x_1,\\dots,x_n) &=& \\sum_{i=1}^{n} \\log(p_{\\theta}(x_i)\\\\\n&=& \\sum_{x\\in \\mathcal X}h(x)\\log(p_{\\theta}(x_i)),\n\\end{eqnarray*}\n\nwhere $h(x)$ is the number of times that $x$ appears in the sequence $x_1,\\dots,x_n$. The function $\\bar h = \\frac{1}{n}h$ is a normalized histogram representing the \"empirical probability\". We have that \n\n\\[ \n\\ell (\\theta,x_1,\\dots,x_n) =-n H(\\bar h, p_{\\theta})\n\\]\n\nSo maximizing $\\ell (\\theta,x_1,\\dots,x_n)$ is the same as minimizing the cross entropy between the empirical probability and the model. Sometimes, it is also formulated using the Kullback Leibler divergence. Indeed, since $H(\\bar h)$ does not depend on $\\theta$, we can also maximize\n\n\\[\n\\ell (\\theta,x_1,\\dots,x_n) + nH(\\bar h) = -n(H(\\bar h,p_{\\theta})-H(\\bar h)) = -nD_{\\mathrm{KL}}(\\bar h,p_{\\theta}),\n\\]\n\nand the maximization of the likelihood becomes a minimization of the Kullback Leibler divergence between the empirical data and the model.\n\n"

                "summary": "<div class=\"theorem\" id=\"th:Some properties of entropy\">\n<p><strong>Theorem 12</strong> (<strong>Some properties of\r\nentropy</strong>). </p>\n<ul>\n<li><p>Adding zeros or permuting the components does not change the\r\nentropy</p></li>\n<li><p>When\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi>X</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">X</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nand\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi>Y</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">Y</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nare indp.,\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo form=\"prefix\" stretchy=\"true\">(</mo><mo form=\"prefix\" stretchy=\"false\">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo form=\"postfix\" stretchy=\"false\">)</mo><mo form=\"postfix\" stretchy=\"true\">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>H</mi><mo form=\"prefix\" stretchy=\"false\">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo form=\"postfix\" stretchy=\"false\">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>H</mi><mo form=\"prefix\" stretchy=\"false\">(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo form=\"postfix\" stretchy=\"false\">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">H\\left( (X,Y) \\right) = H(X) + H(Y)</annotation></semantics></math>.</p></li>\n<li><p><math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi>H</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">H</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nis stricly concave, maximal for the uniform distribution, and minimal\r\nfor Dirac probability distributions.</p></li>\n</ul>\n</div>",
                "hasSummary": true,
                "hasTitle": true,
                "title": "<strong>Some properties of\r\nentropy</strong>",
                "display_order": 79,
                "latexMainText": "\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Statement}}\\\\\n\n\\begin{itemize}\n    \\item i) Adding zeros or permuting the components does not change the entropy. Let \n\n  \\[\n    P = (p_1,\\dots,p_n), \\qquad \n    P' = (p_1,\\dots,p_n,0), \\qquad \n    P_\\pi = (p_{\\pi(1)},\\dots,p_{\\pi(n)}),\n  \\]\n\n  where $\\pi$ is a permutation of $\\{1,\\dots,n\\}$. Then\n\n  \\begin{align*}\n    H(P) \n       = H(P') \n       = H(P_\\pi).\n  \\end{align*}\n\n    \\item ii) If $X$ and $Y$ are independent, then\n\n  \\[\n    H\\left( (X,Y) \\right) = H(X) + H(Y).\n  \\]\n  \n    $\\triangle$ Do not confuse the entropy of the joint random variable $(X,Y)$\n  with the notion of cross-entropy:\n\n  \\[\n    H((X,Y)) \\;\\neq\\; H(X, Y).\n  \\]\n\n    \\item iii) The entropy is a strictly concave function\n\n    $$ H(\\lambda P + (1-\\lambda)Q) \\geq \\lambda H(P) +(1-\\lambda)H(Q) $$\n\n    \\item iv) The uniform distribution is the unique maximum of the entropy function. Let $U$ be the uniform distribution over $n$ elements,\n\n    \\[\n    U = \\left(\\frac{1}{n},\\dots,\\frac{1}{n}\\right).\n    \\]\n\n    Then $ H(U) = H(P,U) $ and $H(U)-H(P)=D_{\\mathrm{KL}}\\geq 0$.\n\n    \\item v) For the Dirac mass $P = \\delta_k$ (i.e. $p_k = 1$, $p_i = 0$ for $i\\neq k$),\n\n  \\[\n    H(\\delta_k) = 0\n  \\]\n\\end{itemize}\n\nFrom iv) and v), we see that the entropy function $H$ measures how concentrated ($P = \\delta_k$), or spread ($U$), a distribution is.\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Proofs}}\\\\\n\n\\begin{itemize}\n    \\item i) \n      \\begin{align*}\n    H(P)\n      &= \\sum_{i=1}^n p_i \\log\\frac{1}{p_i}\n         + 0\\log\\frac{1}{0}\n       = H(P') \\qquad\\text{(by convention $0\\log \\tfrac{1}{0}=0$)} \\\\\n      &= \\sum_{i=1}^n p_{\\pi(i)} \\log\\frac{1}{p_{\\pi(i)}} \n       = H(P_\\pi).\n  \\end{align*}\n\n    \\item ii) If $X$ and $Y$ are independent, then\n\n  \\[\n    H\\left( (X,Y) \\right) = H(X) + H(Y).\n  \\]\n\n  Indeed, if $P_X$ and $P_Y$ denote the laws of $X$ and $Y$, independence gives\n\n  \\[\n    P(X=x,Y=y) = P_X(x) P_Y(y).\n  \\]\n\n  Then\n\n  \\begin{align*}\n    H((X,Y))\n      &= - \\sum_{x,y} P(X=x,Y=y)\n           \\log P(X=x,Y=y) \\\\\n      &= - \\sum_{x,y} P_X(x)P_Y(y)\n           \\log\\bigl(P_X(x)P_Y(y)\\bigr) \\\\\n      &= - \\sum_{x,y} P_X(x)P_Y(y)\n           \\bigl[\\log P_X(x) + \\log P_Y(y)\\bigr] \\\\\n      &= - \\sum_{x,y} P_X(x)P_Y(y)\\log P_X(x)\n         \\;-\\; \\sum_{x,y} P_X(x)P_Y(y)\\log P_Y(y).\n  \\end{align*}\n\n  Now use $\\sum_y P_Y(y) = 1$ and $\\sum_x P_X(x) = 1$:\n\n  \\begin{align*}\n    - \\sum_{x,y} P_X(x)P_Y(y)\\log P_X(x)\n      &= - \\sum_x P_X(x)\\log P_X(x)\\left(\\sum_y P_Y(y)\\right)\n       = H(X),\\\\\n    - \\sum_{x,y} P_X(x)P_Y(y)\\log P_Y(y)\n      &= - \\sum_y P_Y(y)\\log P_Y(y)\\left(\\sum_x P_X(x)\\right)\n       = H(Y).\n  \\end{align*}\n\n  Hence $H((X,Y)) = H(X)+H(Y)$.\n\n    \\item iii) Prove first that function $f\\colon(0,\\infty)\\to\\mathbb{R}$ defined by $f(x)=x\\log x$ is strictly convex.\n\n    \\begin{proof}\n    We compute the derivatives:\n    \\[\n    f'(x) = \\log x + 1, \\qquad\n    f''(x) = \\frac{1}{x}, \\quad x>0.\n    \\]\n    Since $f''(x) = 1/x \\ge 0$ for all $x>0$, the second derivative is nonnegative\n    on its domain. Hence $f$ is convex on $(0,\\infty)$.\n    \\end{proof}\n\n    Since $H$ is obtained by summing $f$ at different points, we get,\n\n\n    \\begin{align*}\n    H(\\lambda P + (1-\\lambda)Q)\n    &= -\\sum_{i=1}^n \\left(\\lambda p_i + (1-\\lambda)q_i\\right)\n        \\log \\left(\\lambda p_i + (1-\\lambda)q_i\\right) \\\\\n    &= -\\sum_{i=1}^n f\\bigl(\\lambda p_i + (1-\\lambda)q_i\\bigr) \\\\\n    &\\ge -\\sum_{i=1}^n \\left[\\lambda f(p_i) + (1-\\lambda)f(q_i)\\right]\n        \\qquad\\text{(by convexity of $f$)} \\\\\n    &= -\\lambda \\sum_{i=1}^n f(p_i)\n        - (1-\\lambda)\\sum_{i=1}^n f(q_i) \\\\\n    &= \\lambda H(P) + (1-\\lambda) H(Q).\n    \\end{align*}\n\n\n\n    \\item iv) Let $U$ be the uniform distribution over $n$ elements,\n\n    \\[\n    U = \\left(\\frac{1}{n},\\dots,\\frac{1}{n}\\right).\n    \\]\n\n    Then \n\n    \\begin{align*}\n    H(U) - H(P)\n      &= \\sum_{i=1}^n \\frac{1}{n}\\,\\log\\frac{1}{\\tfrac{1}{n}}\n         - H(P) \\\\\n      &= \\sum_{i=1}^n p_i\\,\\log\\frac{1}{\\tfrac{1}{n}}\n         - H(P)\\\\\n      &= H(P,U) - H(P)\n       = D_{\\mathrm{KL}}(P \\,\\|\\, U) \\;\\ge\\; 0.\n   \\end{align*}\n\n   The equality holds only if $P=U$ so $U$ is the unique maximizer of the entropy. The unicity can also be deduced from the strict concavity. \n\n    \\item v) \n\n      \\[\n    H(\\delta_k)\n      = -\\sum_{i=1}^n p_i \\log p_i\n      = -\\bigl(0\\log 0 + \\cdots + 1\\log 1 + \\cdots + 0\\log 0\\bigr)\n      = 0.\n  \\]\n\n\\end{itemize}\n\n"

                "latexMainText": "\n\n\\begin{itemize}\n  \\item $\\mathcal{A}$ is a set of symbols: an \\emph{alphabet}. Typically $\\mathcal{A} = \\{0, 1\\}$.\n  \n  \\item $\\mathcal{A}^*$ is the set of words (finite sequences of symbols).\n  \n  \\item A code is a function $c: S \\to \\mathcal{A}^*$, where $S$ is the source alphabet (a finite set of source symbols).\n  \n  \\item \\textbf{Non-singular:} The code $c$ said non-singular when it is injective. That is, \n\n  \\[\n    c(s_1)=c(s_2) \\implies s_1=s_2.\n  \\]\n  \n  \\item \\textbf{Prefix:} A prefix of a word $w$ is a word $x$ such that $w = xy$ where $y$ is a word (concatenation). If the length $\\ell(y) \\neq 0$, then $x$ is a ``proper'' prefix.\n  \n  \\item \\textbf{Prefix Code:} A code $c$ is a ``Prefix code'' (or instantaneous code) if no codeword is a prefix of another. Formally:\n\n  \\[\n    \\forall s_i, s_j \\in S \\text{ with } i \\neq j, \\quad c(s_i) \\text{ is not a prefix of } c(s_j).\n  \\]\n\\end{itemize}\n\n\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Extension of a code}}\\\\\n\n\n\\noindent\nThe code $c$ is extended to a function on sequences $c: S^* \\to \\mathcal{A}^*$ by concatenation:\n\n\\[\n  c(s_{i_1} s_{i_2} \\dots s_{i_k}) = c(s_{i_1})c(s_{i_2}) \\dots c(s_{i_k}).\n\\]\nA code is said to be \\textbf{uniquely decodable} if this extended function is injective.\n\n\\begin{itemize}\n  \\item \\textbf{Proposition:} Any prefix code is uniquely decodable.\n\\end{itemize}\n\n\\begin{proof}\nLet $c$ be a prefix code. Suppose we have two sequences of source symbols that produce the same encoded string:\n\n\\[\n  c(s_{i_1}) \\dots c(s_{i_k}) = c(s_{j_1}) \\dots c(s_{j_\\ell}).\n\\]\n\nLet $W$ be this encoded string. By definition, $W$ starts with the codeword $c(s_{i_1})$ and also starts with the codeword $c(s_{j_1})$. This implies that $c(s_{i_1})$ is a prefix of $c(s_{j_1})$ or $c(s_{j_1})$ is a prefix of $c(s_{i_1})$.\n\nSince $c$ is a prefix code, no codeword can be a proper prefix of another. Therefore, we must have equality:\n\n\\[\n  c(s_{i_1}) = c(s_{j_1}).\n\\]\n\nSince a prefix code is necessarily non-singular (a distinct codeword cannot be a prefix of another, so they cannot be equal unless the source symbols are equal), this implies:\n\n\\[\n  s_{i_1} = s_{j_1}.\n\\]\n\nWe can now remove this codeword from the left of the string and repeat the argument for the remaining suffixes. By induction, the entire sequence of source symbols must be identical. Thus, the extension is injective.\n\\end{proof}\n\n"

                "display_order": 81,
                "latexMainText": "\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Statement}}\\\\\n\n\\begin{enumerate}\n  \\item Let $S = \\{s_1, \\dots, s_n\\}$ be the source alphabet and let $c: S \\to \\{0,1\\}^*$ be a prefix code.\n  Let $\\ell_i = \\mathrm{length}(c(s_i))$ denote the length of the codeword associated with symbol $s_i$.\n\n  Then:\n  \\[\n    \\sum_{i=1}^n 2^{-\\ell_i} \\le 1.\n  \\]\n\n  \\item \\textbf{Converse:} Given a set of integers $\\{\\ell_1, \\dots, \\ell_n\\}$ satisfying\n  \\[\n    \\sum_{i=1}^n 2^{-\\ell_i} \\le 1,\n  \\]\n  there exists a prefix code $c: S \\to \\{0,1\\}^*$ with lengths $\\mathrm{length}(c(s_i)) = \\ell_i$ for all $i=1,\\dots,n$.\n\\end{enumerate}\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Proofs}}\\\\\n\n\n\\begin{proof}[\\textbf{Proof of 1)}]\nLet $L = \\max_i \\ell_i$. Consider a full binary tree of depth $L$.\n\\begin{itemize}\n    \\item The total number of leaf nodes at depth $L$ is $2^L$.\n    \\item For each symbol $s_i$, the codeword $c(s_i)$ has length $\\ell_i$. If we map this codeword to a node in the tree, the number of its descendants (leaves) at depth $L$ is $2^{L-\\ell_i}$.\n    \\item Since $c$ is a prefix code, no codeword is a prefix of another. This implies that no codeword node is an ancestor of another. Consequently, the sets of descendants at depth $L$ corresponding to each $c(s_i)$ are disjoint:\n    \\[\n    \\{\\text{descendants of } c(s_i)\\} \\cap \\{\\text{descendants of } c(s_j)\\} = \\emptyset \\quad \\text{for } i \\neq j.\n    \\]\n\\end{itemize}\nThe sum of the number of disjoint descendants cannot exceed the total number of leaves at depth $L$:\n\\[\n\\sum_{i=1}^n 2^{L-\\ell_i} \\le 2^L.\n\\]\nDividing both sides by $2^L$:\n\\[\n\\sum_{i=1}^n 2^{-\\ell_i} \\le 1.\n\\]\n\\end{proof}\n\n\\begin{proof}[\\textbf{Proof of 2) Converse}]\nAssume without loss of generality that the lengths are ordered: $\\ell_1 \\le \\ell_2 \\le \\dots \\le \\ell_n$.\nWe construct the code iteratively on a binary tree.\n\n\\begin{itemize}\n    \\item \\textbf{Step 1:} Choose any node at depth $\\ell_1$ for $c(s_1)$.\n    \n    \\item \\textbf{Step 2:} We want to choose a node at depth $\\ell_2$. The number of total nodes at depth $\\ell_2$ is $2^{\\ell_2}$.\n    The codeword $c(s_1)$ (of length $\\ell_1 \\le \\ell_2$) ``consumes'' or forbids all its descendants at level $\\ell_2$. The number of such forbidden descendants is $2^{\\ell_2 - \\ell_1}$.\n    \n    The number of available nodes at level $\\ell_2$ is:\n    \\[\n    2^{\\ell_2} - 2^{\\ell_2 - \\ell_1} = 2^{\\ell_2} (1 - 2^{-\\ell_1}).\n    \\]\n    Since $\\sum 2^{-\\ell_i} \\le 1$, we know $2^{-\\ell_1} < 1$, so strictly positive nodes are available. We pick one for $c(s_2)$.\n\n    \\item \\textbf{Step 3:} At level $\\ell_3$, the total nodes are $2^{\\ell_3}$.\n    The forbidden nodes are the descendants of $c(s_1)$ (count: $2^{\\ell_3-\\ell_1}$) and $c(s_2)$ (count: $2^{\\ell_3-\\ell_2}$).\n    The number of free nodes is:\n    \\[\n    2^{\\ell_3} - 2^{\\ell_3 - \\ell_1} - 2^{\\ell_3 - \\ell_2} = 2^{\\ell_3} \\left( 1 - 2^{-\\ell_1} - 2^{-\\ell_2} \\right).\n    \\]\n    From the hypothesis $\\sum 2^{-\\ell_i} \\le 1$, the term in the parenthesis is positive, so we can choose $c(s_3)$.\n\n    \\item \\textbf{Step $k$:} Generalizing, at step $k$, the number of available nodes at level $\\ell_k$ is:\n    \\[\n    2^{\\ell_k} - \\sum_{j=1}^{k-1} 2^{\\ell_k - \\ell_j} = 2^{\\ell_k} \\left( 1 - \\sum_{j=1}^{k-1} 2^{-\\ell_j} \\right).\n    \\]\n    Since $\\sum_{i=1}^m 2^{-\\ell_i} \\le 1$, the partial sum $\\sum_{j=1}^{k-1} 2^{-\\ell_j}$ is strictly less than 1 (assuming $k \\le m$ and valid lengths). Thus, there is at least one free node available to assign to $c(s_k)$.\n\\end{itemize}\nBy induction, we can construct the entire prefix code.\n\\end{proof}\n\n\n\n\n\n"

                "latexMainText": "\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Statement}}\\\\\n\n\\begin{itemize}\n  \\item Let $S = \\{s_1, \\dots, s_m\\}$ be a source with a probability distribution $P(s_i) = p_i$.\n  \\item Let $c: S \\to \\{0,1\\}^*$ be a code.\n  \\item The expected length of the code is defined as:\n\n  \\[\n    L(c) = \\mathbb{E}[\\ell(c)] = \\sum_{i=1}^m p_i \\ell_i,\n  \\]\n\n  where as usual $\\ell_i = \\ell(c(s_i))$.\n\\end{itemize}\n\n\\noindent \\textbf{Theorem.} Let $L^*$ be the minimum expected length of a prefix code for the distribution $P$. Then:\n\n\\[\n  H(P) \\le L^* \\le H(P) + 1.\n\\]\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Proof}}\\\\\n\n\\noindent \\textbf{1. Lower Bound: $L(c) \\ge H(P)$}\n\n\\begin{proof}\nLet $c$ be any prefix code. By the Kraft inequality, we know that $\\sum_{i=1}^n 2^{-\\ell_i} \\le 1$.\n\nLet us build a distribution $Q$ based on the code lengths. Start with $q_i = 2^{-\\ell_i}$.\nSince $\\sum q_i$ might be strictly less than 1 (if the tree is not full), we introduce a \"slack\" probability mass to make it sum to 1.\nLet\n\n\\[\n  q_{n+1} = 1 - \\sum_{i=1}^n q_i, \\quad \\text{and let } p_{n+1} = 0.\n\\]\n\nNow, we have two probability distributions $P' = (p_1, \\dots, p_n, 0)$ and $Q' = (q_1, \\dots, q_n, q_{n+1})$ on $\\{1, \\dots, n+1\\}$.\n\nWe compute the expected length:\n\n\\begin{align*}\n  L(c) &= \\sum_{i=1}^n p_i \\ell_i \\\\\n       &= \\sum_{i=1}^n p_i \\log \\frac{1}{2^{-\\ell_i}} \\\\\n       &= \\sum_{i=1}^n p_i \\log \\frac{1}{q_i}.\n\\end{align*}\n\nSince $p_{n+1} = 0$, we have $p_{n+1} \\log \\frac{1}{q_{n+1}} = 0$ (by convention). Thus, we can extend the sum to $n+1$:\n\n\\[\n  L(c) = \\sum_{i=1}^{n+1} p_i \\log \\frac{1}{q_i} = H(P', Q').\n\\]\n\nFrom the properties of Cross-Entropy (Gibbs' inequality), we know that $H(P', Q') \\ge H(P')$.\nSince adding a zero probability event does not change the entropy ($H(P') = H(P)$), we obtain:\n\n\\[\n  L(c) \\ge H(P).\n\\]\n\\end{proof}\n\n\\bigskip\n\n\\noindent \\textbf{2. Upper Bound: $L^* \\le H(P) + 1$}\n\n\\begin{proof}\nWe construct a specific code (often called the Shannon code) to show that a code satisfying the bound exists.\n\nFor each symbol $s_i$, let us choose the integer length:\n\n\\[\n  \\ell_i = \\left\\lceil \\log \\frac{1}{p_i} \\right\\rceil.\n\\]\n\nFirst, we must check if a prefix code with these lengths exists. We check the Kraft inequality:\n\n\\[\n  \\sum_{i=1}^n 2^{-\\ell_i} \n  = \\sum_{i=1}^n 2^{-\\lceil \\log \\frac{1}{p_i} \\rceil} \n  \\le \\sum_{i=1}^n 2^{-\\log \\frac{1}{p_i}} \n  = \\sum_{i=1}^n p_i \n  = 1.\n\\]\n\nSince the sum is $\\le 1$, by the converse of the Kraft--McMillan theorem, a prefix code with these lengths exists.\n\nNow, we compute the expected length of this code. Using the property $x \\le \\lceil x \\rceil < x + 1$:\n\n\\begin{align*}\n  L(c) &= \\sum_{i=1}^n p_i \\ell_i \\\\\n       &= \\sum_{i=1}^n p_i \\left\\lceil \\log \\frac{1}{p_i} \\right\\rceil \\\\\n       &< \\sum_{i=1}^n p_i \\left( \\log \\frac{1}{p_i} + 1 \\right) \\\\\n       &= \\underbrace{\\sum_{i=1}^n p_i \\log \\frac{1}{p_i}}_{H(P)} + \\underbrace{\\sum_{i=1}^n p_i}_{1}.\n\\end{align*}\n\nThus,\n\n\\[\n  L(c) < H(P) + 1.\n\\]\n\nSince the optimal code $L^*$ is necessarily shorter than or equal to this specific code, $L^* \\le H(P) + 1$.\n\\end{proof}\n\n\n"

In an optimal code, every element is coded by a string (sequence) of length $N = \\log_2 2^N$.\n  \n  \\item When trying to describe an element, $N$ bits of information are needed.\n\n  \\item If we are given the first $n$ bits describing an element, only $N-n$ bits are then needed to identify the element.\n  \\item Hence, the \\textbf{information gain} is $n$.\n  \\item Here, the probability of the event described (fixing the first $n$ bits) is:\n  \\[\n    p = \\frac{2^{N-n}}{2^N} = 2^{-n}.\n  \\]\n  We say that the information associated with the event is $n=\\log \\frac{1}{p}$.\n\n  \\item In general, we define the \\textbf{information content} of an event $E$ as\n  \\[\n    I(E) = \\log\\left(\\frac{1}{P(E)}\\right) = -\\log P(E).\n  \\]\n  \n\\end{itemize}\n\n"

                "latexMainText": "\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Construction}}\\\\\n\n\\begin{itemize}\n  \\item $S$ is a finite set (source alphabet) with a probability distribution $P$.\n  \n  \\item A \\textbf{Huffman code} $c$ is constructed recursively (Bottom-Up construction):\n  \n  \\begin{enumerate}\n    \\item \\textbf{Base Case:} If $|S|=2$, assign $0$ to one symbol and $1$ to the other.\n    \n    \\item \\textbf{Recursive Step:}\n    \\begin{itemize}\n        \\item Identify the two symbols $s_i, s_j$ with the lowest probabilities $p_i, p_j$.\n        \\item Merge them into a new ``meta-symbol'' $s_{ij}$ with probability $p_{ij} = p_i + p_j$.\n        \\item Define a reduced source $S' = (S \\setminus \\{s_i, s_j\\}) \\cup \\{s_{ij}\\}$.\n        \\item Construct a Huffman code $c'$ for $S'$.\n    \\end{itemize}\n    \n    \\item \\textbf{Code Construction (Back-propagation):}\n    Once the code $c'$ for the reduced set is known, the codes for the original symbols are:\n    \\[\n      c(s_i) = c'(s_{ij}) \\cdot 0 \\quad \\text{(append 0 to the parent's code)}\n    \\]\n    \\[\n      c(s_j) = c'(s_{ij}) \\cdot 1 \\quad \\text{(append 1 to the parent's code)}\n    \\]\n    \\emph{(where $\\cdot$ denotes concatenation).}\n  \\end{enumerate}\n\\end{itemize}\n\n\n\\noindent\\textbf{Theorem (Optimality):}\n\nIf $L_{\\text{Huff}}$ denotes the expected length of a Huffman code and $L(C)$ is the expected length of any other prefix code for the same distribution, then:\n\n\\[\n  L_{\\text{Huff}} \\le L(C).\n\\]\n\nWe will not prove this result. Because Huffman codes are optimal, they satisfy the tight bounds of Shannon's Source Coding Theorem:\n\\[\n  H(P) \\le L_{\\text{Huff}} < H(P) + 1.\n\\]\nThis confirms that Huffman coding is an \\emph{entropic code}: it compresses data to within 1 bit of the theoretical limit per symbol.\n\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Example}}\\\\\n\n\\textbf{Source Probabilities and Reduction Steps:}\n\n\\begin{center}\n\\begin{tabular}{lccccc}\n\\textbf{Sym} & \\textbf{P} & \\textbf{Step 1} & \\textbf{Step 2} & \\textbf{Step 3} & \\textbf{Step 4} \\\\\n\\hline\n$a$ & 0.01 & $\\left. \\begin{matrix} 0.01 \\\\ 0.06 \\end{matrix} \\right\\"

                "latexMainText": "\n\\begin{itemize}\n  \\item Let $X_1, \\dots, X_n$ be $n$ i.i.d. random variables taking their values in a finite set $S = \\{s_1, \\dots, s_k\\}$, with probabilities:\n  \n  \\[\n    P(X_j = s_i) = p_i.\n  \\]\n\n  \\item At fixed $\\omega\\in \\Omega$, let $h(\\omega)$ be the \\textbf{histogram} of the values $X_j(\\omega)$. \n  Formally, $h$ is a random variable mapping the universe $\\Omega$ to the set of functions from $S$ to $\\mathbb{R}$:\n  \n  \\[\n     h: \\Omega \\to \\{ f: S \\to \\mathbb{R} \\}\n  \\]\n  \n  It is defined by:\n  \n  \\[\n     h(\\omega)(s_i) = \\text{Number of } X_j \\text{ such that } X_j(\\omega) = s_i.\n  \\]\n\n  \\item \\textbf{Vector Definition:}\n  $h$ can also be defined algebraically. Identify each symbol $s_i$ with the canonical basis vector $e_i \\in \\mathbb{R}^k$:\n  \n  \\[\n    e_i = (0, \\dots, 0, \\underbrace{1}_{\\text{index } i}, 0, \\dots, 0).\n  \\]\n  \n  If we identify the random variable $X_j$ with the vector corresponding to its value, then the histogram is simply the sum:\n  \n  \\[\n    h = \\sum_{j=1}^n X_j.\n  \\]\n  \n  Here, $h(\\omega) \\in \\mathbb{R}^k$, and the $i$-th component, denoted $h(\\omega)_i$, counts the number of occurrences of symbol $s_i$ in the sequence.\n\\end{itemize}\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Definition}}\\\\\n\nThe law of $h$ is called a \\textbf{multinomial distribution}. It is a probability distribution over histograms.\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Computation of the law}}\\\\\n\nWe will now describe the law of $h$, as a function of the probabilities $p_i$ of each symbols $s_i$.\\\\\n\n\n\\begin{itemize}\n  \\item Since the variables are i.i.d., the probability of a specific sequence $(s_{i_1}, \\dots, s_{i_m})$ is:\n\n  \\[\n    P(X_1=s_{i_1}, \\dots, X_n=s_{i_n}) \n    = \\prod_{j=1}^n p_{i_j} \n    = \\prod_{i=1}^k p_i^{h_i}.\n  \\]\n  \n  \\textit{(We simply re-grouped symbols, with $p_i$ appearing $h_i$ times).}\n\\end{itemize}\n\nWe now want to compute how many configurations (sequences) $c = (s_{i_1}, \\dots, s_{i_n})$ lead to the same histogram $h = (h_1, \\dots, h_k)$.\n\n\\begin{itemize}\n\n  \\item Consider a specific ``canonical'' configuration $c$ where the symbols are sorted:\n  \n  \\[\n    c = \\Big( \\underbrace{s_1, \\dots, s_1}_{h_1}, \\underbrace{s_2, \\dots, s_2}_{h_2}, \\dots, \\underbrace{s_k, \\dots, s_k}_{h_k} \\Big).\n  \\]\n\n  \\item Let $\\pi: \\{1, \\dots, n\\} \\to \\{1, \\dots, n\\}$ be a permutation. Let $\\pi c$ denote the permuted sequence such that:\n  \n  \\[\n    (\\pi c)_i = c_{\\pi(i)}.\n  \\]\n  \n  All the permuted sequences $\\pi c$ share the same histogram $h$. There are $n!$ possible permutations, but some of them might lead to the same sequence $\\pi c = \\pi' c$, hence there might be less than $n!$ sequence having $h$ as histogram. \n\n  \\item \\textbf{Determining Redundancy:} Given a certain $\\pi$, how many $\\pi'$ satisfy $\\pi c = \\pi' c$?\n  \n  Consider a permutation $\\pi_1$ that affects \\textbf{only} the first $h_1$ indices (positions of $s_1$). Since the values at these positions are identical ($s_1$), applying this permutation does not change the sequence:\n\n   \\[\n    \\pi_1c = c \n  \\]\n\n  hence for all permutation $\\pi$,\n\n  \\[\n    (\\pi \\circ \\pi_1)c = \\pi c \\quad (\\text{even though } \\pi \\circ \\pi_1 \\neq \\pi).\n  \\]\n  \n  There are $h_1!$ ways of choosing such a permutation $\\pi_1$.\n  \n  The same logic applies to $\\pi_2$ (acting on the block of $s_2$), up to $\\pi_k$.\n\n  \\item For each of the $n!$ total permutations $\\pi$, there are $h_1! \\dots h_k!$ permutations that result in the exact same sequence configuration.\n  \n  \\item Hence, the number of distinct configurations leading to the histogram $h$ is the \\textbf{Multinomial Coefficient}:\n  \n  \\[\n    \\begin{pmatrix}\n        n\\\\ h_1,\\dots,h_k\n    \\end{pmatrix} = \\frac{n!}{h_1! h_2! \\dots h_k!} = \\frac{n!}{\\prod_{i=1}^k h_i!}.\n  \\]\n\\end{itemize}\n\n\\textbf{What is the law of $h$?}\\\\\n  \n  Combining the probability of a single sequence with the number of sequences that result in the same histogram, we obtain the probability mass function of the multinomial distribution:\n  \n  \\[\n    P(h = (h_1, \\dots, h_k)) = \\frac{n!}{h_1! \\dots h_k!} p_1^{h_1} \\dots p_k^{h_k}.\n  \\]\n\n"

                "latexMainText": "\n\nWe evaluate the log-probability of observing a histogram $h$ as the sample size $n \\to \\infty$. As done in an earlier remark, observe first that the probability of observing a sequence can be expressed as a cross-entropy.\n\n\\begin{itemize}\n\n  \\item Take the logarithm of $ P(X_1=s_{i_1}, \\dots, X_n=s_{i_n})$:\n  \n  \\begin{align*}\n    \\log P(X_1=s_{i_1}, \\dots, X_n=s_{i_n}) &= \\log \\prod p_i^{h_i}\\\\\n    &=\\sum_{i=1}^k h_i \\log p_i\\\\\n    &= n\\sum_{i=1}^k \\frac{h_i}{n} \\log p_i.\n  \\end{align*}\n\n\n  \\item Note that if we define $\\bar{h}$ as the \\textbf{normalized histogram} (or empirical distribution):\n  \n  \\[\n    \\bar{h} = \\frac{1}{n} (h_1, \\dots, h_k),\n  \\]\n  \n  then the log-probability of a sequence is minus $n$ times the negative cross-entropy between the empirical distribution and the true distribution:\n  \n  \\[\n    \\log P(s_{i_1}, \\dots, s_{i_n}) = - nH(\\bar{h}, P).\n  \\]\n\\end{itemize}\n\nThe Log-probability of the histogram is then given by\n\n  \\begin{align*}\n      \\log P(h = (h_1, \\dots, h_k)) &=  \\log \\left(\\frac{n!}{h_1! \\dots h_k!}\\right) - nH(\\bar h,P)\\\\\n  \\end{align*}\n\nWe will derive an approximation of the first term as $n$ grows.\n\n\\begin{itemize}\n\n  \\item \\textbf{Stirling's formula:}\n  \n  \\[\n    \\log n! = n \\log n - n + O(\\log n)\n  \\]\n\n  \\item \\textbf{Normalized log of the multinomial coefficient:}\n  apply the Stirling formula when $n\\to \\infty$.\n  \n  \\begin{align*}\n    \\frac{1}{n} \\log \\begin{pmatrix}\n        n\\\\ h_1,\\dots,h_k\n    \\end{pmatrix} &= \\underbrace{\\log n - 1 + o(1)}_{\\frac{1}{n}\\log n!} \n    - \\sum_{i=1}^k \\left[ \\frac{h_i}{n}\\log h_i - \\frac{h_i}{n} + \\underbrace{\\frac{1}{n}O(\\log h_i)}_{o(1)} \\right] \n     \\\\\n    &= \\log n - 1 - \\sum_{i=1}^k \\frac{h_i}{n}\\log h_i + \\underbrace{\\sum_{i=1}^k \\frac{h_i}{n}}_{1}  + o(1) \\\\\n    &= \\sum_{i=1}^k \\frac{h_i}{n} \\log n - \\sum_{i=1}^k \\frac{h_i}{n}\\log h_i  + o(1) \\\\\n    &= \\sum_{i=1}^k \\frac{h_i}{n} \\log \\left( \\frac{n}{h_i} \\right)  + o(1)\\\\\n    &= H(\\bar{h}) +o(1)\n  \\end{align*}\n\n\\end{itemize}\n\n\nHence we obtain the \\textbf{normalized log-probability of $h$}: \n\n\n  \\begin{align*}\n      \\frac{1}{n} \\log P(h) & = H(\\bar{h}) - H(\\bar{h}, P) + o(1)\\\\\n      &= -D_{\\mathrm{KL}}(\\bar{h} \\,\\|\\, P) + o(1)\n  \\end{align*}\n\n\\textbf{Interpretation:} $D_{\\mathrm{KL}}(\\bar{h}, P)$ quantifies how likely (or unlikely) it is to observe the empirical distribution $\\bar{h}$ if the samples are truly generated by $P$. The probability decays exponentially with rate $n D_{\\mathrm{KL}}$.\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Remember}}\\\\\n\n\\begin{itemize}\n    \\item Probability of a sequence:\n\n    \\[\n      \\frac{1}{n} \\log \\left( p_1^{h_1} \\dots p_k^{h_k} \\right) = - H(\\bar{h}, P)\n    \\]\n\n    \\item Combinatorial term :\n\n    \\[\n      \\frac{1}{n} \\log \\left( \\frac{n!}{h_1! \\dots h_k!} \\right) =  H(\\bar{h}) + o(1)\n    \\]\n\n    (Or equivalently, the log of the number of configurations is $\\approx n H(\\bar{h})$).\n    \\item Probability of the histogram:\n\n    \\[\n      \\frac{1}{n} \\log \\left(P(h) \\right) = -D_{\\mathrm{KL}}(\\bar{h} \\,\\|\\, P) + o(1)\n    \\]    \n\\end{itemize}\n\n\n"

                "latexMainText": "\nWe saw that entropy is a measure of uniformity. Uniformity can be\ninterpreted as a measure of disorder. $P = \\delta$ represents the highest\nlevel of order. When $P$ is uniform, every element occupies the same\nproportion, which is interpreted as ``maximal disorder''. Many phenomena have a tendency to increase uniformity ($\\sim$ disorder) as time evolves. It is particularly true in physics. Consider a phenomenon to which we associate a probability\n$P_0$ at time $0$. As time evolves, the probability evolves to $P_1,P_2,\\dots$. If the\nphenomenon increases uniformity, the distribution $P_t$ might stabilize\nclose to a point of maximal uniformity. If the phenomenon preserves some\nconstraints $C$, the uniformity is maximized under these constraints. We have then good reason to expect that (when it exists)\n\n\\[\n  P_{\\infty} = \\operatorname{argmax}_{P \\in C} H(P).\n\\]\n\n\n\n"

Let $X_t$ be a random variable taking\nvalues in $\\mathbb{Z}$, modeling the position of the person at time $t$.  \nDenote by $P_t$ its law.\n\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{law of \\(X_{t+1}\\) knowing the event \\(X_t = i\\)}}\\\\\n\n\\[\n\\mathbb P(X_{t+1} = j \\mid X_t = i) =\n\\begin{cases}\n\\dfrac12, & \\text{if } j \\in \\{i-1,i+1\\},\\\\[4pt]\n0, & \\text{otherwise.}\n\\end{cases}\n\\]\n\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{\\(\\mathbb E(X_t) = \\mathbb E(X_{t+1})\\)}}\\\\\n\n\n\\begin{align*}\n\\mathbb E(X_{t+1})\n  &= \\sum_{j=-\\infty}^{+\\infty} j\\,P_{t+1}(j) \\\\\n  &= \\sum_{j} j \\left( \\sum_i P_t(i)\\,\n       P(X_{t+1}=j \\mid X_t=i) \\right) \\\\\n  &= \\sum_{j} j \\left( \\tfrac12 P_t(j-1) + \\tfrac12 P_t(j+1) \\right) \\\\\n  &= \\tfrac12 \\sum_{j=-\\infty}^{+\\infty} (j+1) P_t(j)\n     + \\tfrac12 \\sum_{j=-\\infty}^{+\\infty} (j-1) P_t(j) \\\\\n  &= \\sum_{j} j\\,P_t(j)\n   = \\mathbb E(X_t).\n\\end{align*}\n\nHence the process satisfies the constraint\n\n\\[\n  \\sum_i i\\,P_{t_1}(i) = \\sum_i i\\,P_{t_2}(i).\n\\]\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{\\(H(X_t) < H(X_{t+1})\\)}}\\\\\n\n\nAn assumption is missing: the steps are taken independently.  \nThe variables \\(Y_t = X_{t+1} - X_t\\) are all independent, and independent of \\(X_0\\).\n\nSince\n\n\\[\n  X_t = \\sum_{i=0}^{t-1} Y_i + X_0,\n\\]\n\n\\(Y_t\\) is independent of \\(X_t\\).\n\n\\[\n  X_{t+1} = X_t + Y_t \\quad \\text{hence} \\quad\n  H(X_{t+1}) = H(X_t) + H(Y_t).\n\\]\n\nSince the discrete entropy is always positive or null,\n\n\\[\n  H(X_{t+1}) \\ge H(X_t).\n\\]\n\nHence the process increases entropy.                 "latexMainText": "\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Example 1: law at time $t$ of a random process}}\\\\\n\nWe have a stochastic process over positions in $\\mathbb Z$  (a collection of $X_i$). At fixed realisation $\\omega\\in \\Omega$, we obtain a trajectory $X_0(\\omega),X_1(\\omega),\\dots$. $P_t$ is the probability distribution on positions at time $t$. We showed that its entropy increases.\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Example 2: evolving histogram for a fixed realisation of a random process}}\\\\\n\nConsider all possible attributions of energy levels $\\{1,\\dots,N\\}\\rightarrow \\{0,\\dots,10\\} $  (particules$\\rightarrow$enery levels), and call this set $S$ and its elements \"microstates\". \n\nLet $x_t$ denote the microstate at time $t$. Since the value of $x_{t+1}$ is not a deterministic function of $x_t$, we can consider the random variables $X_{t}$ modeling the uncertainty about the microstate at time $t$. \n  \n As in exemple 1, at each step $t$, we could ask \"what is the law $P_t$ of $X_t$\" or equivalently \"what is the probability of finding a certain association between particles and energy levels\", and look at how its entropy evolves. \n \n This is not what we are doing. For a microstate, we compute the histogram of the energy levels $h$. For a fixed realisation $\\omega\\in\\Omega$, we get a trajectory in the set of microstate $X_0(\\omega),X_1(\\omega),\\dots$, and a trajectory of histograms $h_0=h(X_0(\\omega)),h_1=h(X_1(\\omega)),\\dots$. We are asking how does the entropy of $h_t$ evolves, and we observe that it increases on all the realisations that we tried. \n\n The main difference with example 1 is that we are not tracking the entropy of a model distribution $P_t$, we are tracking the entropy of an empirical distribution along a trajectory.\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Example 3: evolving histogram of a deterministic process}}\\\\\n\nThe last exemple has similarities in nature with exemple 2. The microstate will now refer to the positions and speeds of the collection of balls. This time the micorstate $x_{t+1}$ at time $t+1$ is completely determined by the macrostate at time $t$. Note that even in that case, the uncertainty about the initialization ligitimates the modeling of microstates with random variables $X_t$.\n\n A histogram $h_t$ is computed at each step, and we consider its evolution along a trajectory. We observed that the phenomenon repeats itself on all the tried realisation (= initial conditions).\n \n \n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Moral}}\\\\\n\nEventhough the 3 examples fall under the umbrella of the maximum entropy principle, it is important to note that they are of a relatively different nature. This partly explains why we proved that the entropy increases in the first example but we only considered simulation for example 2 and 3. \n\n"

                "summary": "<div class=\"definition\" id=\"def:Exponential families\">\n<p><strong>Definition 39</strong> (<strong>Exponential\r\nfamilies</strong>). </p>\n<p><math display=\"block\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>\u03b8</mi></msub><mo form=\"prefix\" stretchy=\"false\">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo form=\"postfix\" stretchy=\"false\">)</mo><mspace width=\"0.278em\"></mspace><mo>=</mo><mspace width=\"0.278em\"></mspace><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mo form=\"prefix\" stretchy=\"false\">(</mo><mi>\u03b8</mi><mo form=\"postfix\" stretchy=\"false\">)</mo></mrow></mfrac><mspace width=\"0.167em\"></mspace><mi>h</mi><mo form=\"prefix\" stretchy=\"false\">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo form=\"postfix\" stretchy=\"false\">)</mo><mspace width=\"0.167em\"></mspace><mrow><mi mathvariant=\"normal\">exp</mi><mo>\u2061</mo></mrow><mrow><mo form=\"prefix\" stretchy=\"true\">(</mo><mi>\u03b8</mi><mspace width=\"0.167em\"></mspace><mi>T</mi><mo form=\"prefix\" stretchy=\"false\">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo form=\"postfix\" stretchy=\"false\">)</mo><mo form=\"postfix\" stretchy=\"true\">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mspace width=\"2.0em\"></mspace><mi>x</mi><mo>\u2208</mo><mi>\ud835\udcb3</mi><mi>.</mi></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">p_\\theta(x)\r\n  \\;=\\;\r\n  \\frac{1}{Z(\\theta)}\\,h(x)\\,\\exp\\left(\\theta\\,T(x)\\right),\r\n  \\qquad x \\in \\mathcal X.</annotation></semantics></math></p>\n</div>",

                "title": "<strong>Exponential\r\nfamilies</strong>",
                "display_order": 95,
                "latexMainText": "\nConsider first $\\mathcal X$ to be a finite set.\n\n\\begin{itemize}\n    \\item Let\n    $\n      T : \\mathcal X \\to \\mathbb{R}\n    $\n    be a given function, called the \\emph{sufficient statistic}, for reasons explained later. \n    \\item Fix another function\n    $\n      h : \\mathcal X \\to \\mathbb{R}_{>0},\n    $\n    called the \\emph{carrier term} (or \\emph{base term}).\n    \\item For each parameter $\\theta \\in \\mathbb{R}$, define the \\emph{partition function}\n\n    \\[\n      Z(\\theta)\n      \\;=\\;\n      \\sum_{x \\in \\mathcal X} h(x)\\,\\exp\\left(\\theta\\,T(x)\\right).\n    \\]\n\\end{itemize}\n\nThe corresponding family of probability mass functions $(p_\\theta)_{\\theta \\in \\mathbb{R}}$ on $\\mathcal X$ is defined by\n\n\\[\n  p_\\theta(x)\n  \\;=\\;\n  \\frac{1}{Z(\\theta)}\\,h(x)\\,\\exp\\left(\\theta\\,T(x)\\right),\n  \\qquad x \\in \\mathcal X.\n\\]\n\nIt induces probability distribution $P_\\theta$ on subsets of $\\mathcal X$ by\n\n\\[\n  P_\\theta(A) = \\sum_{x \\in A} p_\\theta(x), \\qquad A \\subset \\mathcal X.\n\\]\n\nThis is a (one-parameter) exponential family in \\emph{canonical form}, with natural parameter $\\theta$, sufficient statistic $T$, carrier term $h$, and log-partition function\n\n\\[\n  \\psi(\\theta) = \\log Z(\\theta).\n\\]\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Vector case}}\\\\\n\n\nMore generally, we can take a vector-valued sufficient statistic\n\n\\[\n  T : \\mathcal X \\to \\mathbb{R}^n,\n  \\qquad\n  T(x) = \\left(T_1(x),\\dots,T_n(x)\\right),\n\\]\n\nand a parameter $\\theta \\in \\mathbb{R}^n$. We use the usual scalar product\n\n\\[\n  \\langle \\theta, T(x) \\rangle = \\sum_{j=1}^n \\theta_j\\,T_j(x).\n\\]\n\nGiven a carrier term $h : \\mathcal X \\to [0,+\\infty[$, we define the partition function\n\n\\[\n  Z(\\theta)\n  \\;=\\;\n  \\sum_{x \\in \\mathcal X} h(x)\\,\\exp\\left(\\langle \\theta, T(x)\\rangle\\right),\n  \\qquad \\theta \\in \\mathbb{R}^n,\n\\]\n\nand the probability mass function\n\n\\[\n  p_\\theta(x)\n  \\;=\\;\n  \\frac{1}{Z(\\theta)}\\,h(x)\\,\\exp\\left(\\langle \\theta, T(x)\\rangle\\right),\n  \\qquad x \\in \\mathcal X.\n\\]\n\nThis defines an $n$-dimensional exponential family.\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Continuous case}}\\\\\n\n\nWe now consider a continuous setting, where $\\mathcal X$ is a subset of Euclidean space\nand probabilities are described by densities.\n\nLet $\\mathcal X \\subset \\mathbb{R}^d$ and let\n\n\\[\n  T : \\mathcal X \\to \\mathbb{R}^n\n\\]\n\nbe a function, again called the (vector-valued) sufficient statistic.  \nFor $x \\in \\mathcal X$ we write\n\n\\[\n  T(x) = \\left(T_1(x),\\dots,T_n(x)\\right),\n\\]\n\nand for $\\theta \\in \\mathbb{R}^n$ we denote the Euclidean inner product\n\n\\[\n  \\langle \\theta, T(x) \\rangle\n  \\;=\\;\n  \\sum_{j=1}^n \\theta_j\\,T_j(x).\n\\]\n\nWe also fix a function\n\n\\[\n  h : \\mathcal X \\to [0,+\\infty[\n\\]\n\ncalled the \\emph{carrier term} (or \\emph{base term}). For each $\\theta \\in \\mathbb{R}^n$ such that\n\n\\[\n  Z(\\theta)\n  \\;:=\\;\n  \\int_{\\mathcal X} h(x)\\,\\exp\\left(\\langle \\theta, T(x) \\rangle\\right)\\,dx\n  < +\\infty,\n\\]\n\nwe define a probability density on $\\mathcal X$ by\n\n\\[\n  p_\\theta(x)\n  \\;=\\;\n  \\frac{1}{Z(\\theta)}\\,h(x)\\,\\exp\\left(\\langle \\theta, T(x) \\rangle\\right),\n  \\qquad x \\in \\mathcal X.\n\\]\n\nThe set\n\n\\[\n  \\Theta\n  \\;=\\;\n  \\left\\{ \\theta \\in \\mathbb{R}^n \\,:\\, Z(\\theta) < +\\infty \\right\\}\n\\]\n\nis called the \\emph{natural parameter space} of the family. In general,\n$\\Theta$ is only a subset of $\\mathbb{R}^n$.\n\nFor $\\theta \\in \\Theta$, we obtain the probability distribution $P_\\theta$ on\n$\\mathcal X$ by\n\n\\[\n  P_\\theta(A)\n  \\;=\\;\n  \\int_A p_\\theta(x)\\,dx,\n  \\qquad A \\subset \\mathcal X.\n\\]\n\nAs in the discrete case, this defines an $n$-parameter exponential family in\ncanonical form, with natural parameter $\\theta \\in \\Theta$.\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Example: exponential distributions}}\\\\\n\n\nWe now show that the usual exponential distribution is an example of an\nexponential family.\n\nLet $\\mathcal X = \\mathbb{R}_+ = [0,+\\infty[$.  \nFor $\\lambda > 0$, define the density\n\n\\[\n  f_\\lambda(x) = \\lambda e^{-\\lambda x}, \\qquad x \\in \\mathcal X.\n\\]\n\nWe want to recognize this family in the general form\n\n\\[\n  p_\\theta(x)\n  =\n  \\frac{1}{Z(\\theta)}h(x) \\exp\\left(\\langle \\theta, T(x)\\rangle\\right),\n  \\qquad x \\in \\mathcal X.\n\\]\n\nIf we take\n\n\\[\n  h(x) = 1, \\quad T(x)=x,\n\\]\nand set $\\theta = -\\lambda$, it is clear that \n\n\\[\n  p_{\\theta}(x)=f_{\\lambda}(x).\n\\]\n\n\nThe partition function is\n\n\\[\n  Z(\\theta)\n  =\n  \\int_{\\mathcal X} \\exp\\left(\\theta T(x)\\right)\\,dx\n  =\n  \\int_{0}^{+\\infty} e^{\\theta x}\\,dx.\n\\]\n\n\\begin{itemize}\n  \\item If $\\theta < 0$, then\n  \\[\n    Z(\\theta)\n    = \\int_{0}^{+\\infty} e^{\\theta x}\\,dx\n    = \\left[\\tfrac{1}{\\theta} e^{\\theta x}\\right]_{0}^{+\\infty}\n    = -\\frac{1}{\\theta} < +\\infty.\n  \\]\n  \\item If $\\theta \\ge 0$, the integral diverges to $+\\infty$.\n\\end{itemize}\n\nHence the natural parameter space is\n\n\\[\n  \\Theta = \\{\\theta \\in \\mathbb{R} : Z(\\theta) < +\\infty\\}\n  =\\; ]-\\infty, 0[\\;.\n\\]\n\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Example: Gaussian distributions}}\\\\\n\nWe now show that the family of all Gaussian distributions on $\\mathbb{R}$ is an\nexample of an exponential family.\n\nLet $\\mathcal X = \\mathbb{R}$.  \nFor $\\mu \\in \\mathbb{R}$ and $\\sigma^2 > 0$, define the density\n\n\\[\n  f_{\\mu,\\sigma^2}(x)\n  =\n  \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2\\pi}\\,\\sigma}\n  \\exp\\!\\left( -\\frac{(x-\\mu)^2}{2\\sigma^2} \\right),\n  \\qquad x \\in \\mathbb{R}.\n\\]\n\nWe want to recognize this family in the general form\n\n\\[\n  p_\\theta(x)\n  =\n  \\frac{1}{Z(\\theta)}h(x) \\exp\\left(\\langle \\theta, T(x)\\rangle\\right),\n  \\qquad x \\in \\mathcal X.\n\\]\n\n\nStarting from the Gaussian density,\n\n\\[\n  f_{\\mu,\\sigma^2}(x)\n  =\n  \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2\\pi}\\,\\sigma}\n  \\exp\\!\\left( -\\frac{(x-\\mu)^2}{2\\sigma^2} \\right),\n\\]\n\nwe expand the exponent:\n\n\\[\n  -\\frac{(x-\\mu)^2}{2\\sigma^2}\n  =\n  \\frac{\\mu}{\\sigma^2}x - \\frac{1}{2\\sigma^2}x^2 - \\frac{\\mu^2}{2\\sigma^2}.\n\\]\n\nHence\n\n\\[\n  f_{\\mu,\\sigma^2}(x)\n  =\n  \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2\\pi}\\,\\sigma}\\exp\\!\\left( - \\frac{\\mu^2}{2\\sigma^2} \\right)\n  \\exp\\!\\left( \\frac{\\mu}{\\sigma^2}x - \\frac{1}{2\\sigma^2}x^2 \\right),\n\\]\n\nWe choose\n\n\\[\n  h(x) = 1, \\qquad\n  T(x) = (x,x^2), \\qquad\n  \\theta = (\\theta_1,\\theta_2).\n\\]\n\nIf we set\n\n\\[\n  \\theta_1 = \\frac{\\mu}{\\sigma^2},\n  \\qquad\n  \\theta_2 = -\\frac{1}{2\\sigma^2},\n\\]\n\nwe get that\n\n\\[\n\\exp\\!\\left( \\frac{\\mu}{\\sigma^2}x - \\frac{1}{2\\sigma^2}x^2 \\right)\n= \\exp\\!\\left( \\langle \\theta,T(x)\\rangle \\right).\n\\]\n\nInverting these relations gives\n\n\\[\n  \\mu = -\\frac{\\theta_1}{2\\theta_2},\n  \\qquad\n  \\sigma^2 = -\\frac{1}{2\\theta_2}.\n\\]\n\nUsing the expressions of $\\mu$ and $\\sigma^2$ in terms of $\\theta$, we obtain\n\n\\[\n  \\frac{\\mu^2}{2\\sigma^2}\n  =\n  -\\frac{\\theta_1^2}{4\\theta_2},\n  \\qquad\n  \\sqrt{2\\pi}\\,\\sigma\n  =\n  \\sqrt{\\frac{\\pi}{-\\theta_2}}.\n\\]\nHence\n\n\\[\n  f_{\\mu,\\sigma^2}(x)\n  =\n  \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{\\frac{\\pi}{-\\theta_2}}}\n  \\exp\\!\\left(\n    \\frac{\\theta_1^2}{4\\theta_2}\n  \\right)\\exp\\!\\left( \\langle \\theta,T(x)\\rangle \\right).\n\\]\n\nWe can therefore write\n\n\\[\n  f_{\\mu,\\sigma^2}(x)\n  =\n  \\frac{1}{Z(\\theta)} \\exp\\!\\left(\\theta_1 x + \\theta_2 x^2\\right)=p_{\\theta}(x),\n\\]\n\nwith\n\n\\[\n  Z(\\theta)\n  =\n  \\sqrt{\\frac{\\pi}{-\\theta_2}}\\,\n  \\exp\\!\\left(-\\frac{\\theta_1^2}{4\\theta_2}\\right).\n\\]\n\nSince $\\sigma^2 = -\\frac{1}{2\\theta_2} > 0$ if and only if $\\theta_2 < 0$, the\nnatural parameter space is\n\n\\[\n  \\Theta = \\{(\\theta_1,\\theta_2) \\in \\mathbb{R}^2 : \\theta_2 < 0\\}.\n\\]\nThe log-partition function is\n\n\\[\n  \\psi(\\theta) = \\log Z(\\theta)\n  = -\\frac{\\theta_1^2}{4\\theta_2}\n    + \\tfrac{1}{2}\\log\\!\\left(\\frac{\\pi}{-\\theta_2}\\right),\n  \\qquad \\theta \\in \\Theta.\n\\]\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Example: Bernoulli distributions}}\\\\\n\nLet $\\mathcal X = \\{0,1\\}$.  \nFor $p \\in ]0,1[$, define the probability mass function\n\n\\[\n  f_p(k) = p^k (1-p)^{1-k}, \\qquad k \\in \\mathcal X.\n\\]\n\nWe want to recognize this family in the general form\n\n\\[\n  p_\\theta(k)\n  =\n  \\frac{1}{Z(\\theta)}\\,h(k)\\,\\exp\\left(\\theta\\,T(k)\\right),\n  \\qquad k \\in \\mathcal X.\n\\]\n\n\nStarting from the Bernoulli pmf,\n\n\\[\n  f_p(k) = p^k (1-p)^{1-k},\n\\]\n\nwe factor out $(1-p)$ and rewrite\n\n\\[\n  f_p(k)\n  =\n  (1-p)\\left(\\frac{p}{1-p}\\right)^k.\n\\]\n\nWe choose\n\n\\[\n  h(k) = 1,\n  \\qquad\n  T(k) = k,\n\\]\n\nand set\n\n\\[\n  \\theta = \\log\\!\\left(\\frac{p}{1-p}\\right).\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\n  e^{\\theta T(k)} = e^{\\theta k}\n  = \\left(\\frac{p}{1-p}\\right)^k,\n\\]\n\nso we can write\n\n\\[\n  f_p(k)\n  =\n  (1-p)\\,e^{\\theta T(k)}.\n\\]\n\nTo express $(1-p)$ in terms of $\\theta$ only, note that\n\n\\[\n  p = \\frac{e^\\theta}{1+e^\\theta},\n  \\qquad\n  1-p = \\frac{1}{1+e^\\theta},\n\\]\nhence\n\n\\[\n  f_p(k)\n  =\n  (1+e^\\theta)^{-1} e^{\\theta T(k)} = p_\\theta(k),\n\\]\nwith\n\n\\[\n  \\frac{1}{Z(\\theta)} = (1+e^\\theta)^{-1},\n  \\qquad\\text{so}\\qquad\n  Z(\\theta) = 1+e^\\theta.\n\\]\n\nSince $Z(\\theta) < +\\infty$ for all $\\theta \\in \\mathbb{R}$, the natural parameter\nspace is\n\n\\[\n  \\Theta = \\mathbb{R}.\n\\]\n\nThe log-partition function is\n\n\\[\n  \\psi(\\theta) = \\log Z(\\theta) = \\log(1+e^\\theta), \\qquad \\theta \\in \\mathbb{R}.\n\\]\n\nThus Bernoulli distributions form a one-parameter exponential family with\n\n\\[\n  T(k) = k, \\qquad h(k) = 1, \\qquad \\Theta = \\mathbb{R}.\n\\]\n\nThe probability $p$ is obtained from the natural parameter $\\theta$  with the logistic function,\n\n\\[\n  p = \\frac{e^{\\theta}}{1+e^{\\theta}}.\n\\]\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Example: Binomial distributions}}\\\\\n\nFix an integer $n \\geq 1$ and let $\\mathcal X = \\{0,1,\\dots,n\\}$.  \nFor $p \\in ]0,1[$, define the probability mass function\n\n\\[\n  f_p(k)\n  =\n  \\begin{pmatrix} n \\\\ k \\end{pmatrix}\n  p^k (1-p)^{n-k},\n  \\qquad k \\in \\mathcal X.\n\\]\n\nWe want to recognize this family in the general form\n\n\\[\n  p_\\theta(k)\n  =\n  \\frac{1}{Z(\\theta)}\\,h(k)\\,\\exp\\left(\\theta\\,T(k)\\right),\n  \\qquad k \\in \\mathcal X.\n\\]\n\nWe chose again \n\n\\[\n  \\theta = \\log\\!\\left(\\frac{p}{1-p}\\right) \\text{ and } T(k)=k,\n\\]\n\nbut set a different carrier term $h(k)$,\n\n\\[\n  h(k) = \\begin{pmatrix} n \\\\ k \\end{pmatrix},\n  \\qquad\n  T(k) = k,\n\\]\n\nWe can check that\n\n\\[\n  f_p(k)\n  =\n  (1+e^\\theta)^{-n} \\, h(k)\\,e^{\\theta T(k)}=p_{\\theta}(k).\n\\]\n\nWe have then \n\n\\[\n  Z(\\theta) = (1+e^\\theta)^n.\n\\]\n\nSince $Z(\\theta) < +\\infty$ for all $\\theta \\in \\mathbb{R}$, the natural\nparameter space is\n\n\\[\n  \\Theta = \\mathbb{R}.\n\\]\n\nThe log-partition function is\n\n\\[\n  \\psi(\\theta) = \\log Z(\\theta) = n \\log(1+e^\\theta), \\qquad \\theta \\in \\mathbb{R}.\n\\]\n\n"

]-\\infty,0[.</annotation></semantics></math></p>\n<p>Hence</p>\n<p><math display=\"block\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mi>\u03c8</mi><mo form=\"prefix\" First,</p>\n<p><math display=\"block\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>\ud835\udd3c</mi><mi>\u03b8</mi></msub><mo form=\"prefix\"                 "latexMainText": "\n\nWe consider a discrete setting where $\\mathcal X$ is finite and probabilities are\ndescribed by probability mass functions. The computations below use sums, but\nthey are exactly the same in the continuous case if we replace sums by\nintegrals and probability mass functions by densities.\n\n\\medskip\n\nLet $T : \\mathcal X \\to \\mathbb{R}^n$ and let $h : \\mathcal X \\to [0,+\\infty[$ be a\ncarrier term. For $\\theta \\in \\mathbb{R}^n$ we define\n\n\\[\n  p_\\theta(x)\n  =\n  \\frac{1}{Z(\\theta)}\\,h(x)\\,\\exp\\left(\\langle \\theta, T(x) \\rangle\\right),\n  \\qquad x \\in \\mathcal X,\n\\]\n\nwith partition function\n\n\\[\n  Z(\\theta)\n  =\n  \\sum_{x \\in \\mathcal X} h(x)\\,\\exp\\left(\\langle \\theta, T(x) \\rangle\\right),\n  \\qquad\n  \\psi(\\theta) = \\log Z(\\theta).\n\\]\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Scalar case}}\\\\\n\nAssume first that $T : \\mathcal X\\to \\mathbb{R}$ is scalar-valued and\n$\\theta \\in \\mathbb{R}$. Then\n\n\\[\n  Z(\\theta) = \\sum_{x \\in \\mathcal X} h(x)\\,\\exp\\left(\\theta\\,T(x)\\right).\n\\]\n\nWe differentiate $Z(\\theta)$ with respect to $\\theta$:\n\n\\[\n  Z'(\\theta)\n  =\n  \\sum_{x \\in \\mathcal X} T(x)\\,h(x)\\,\\exp\\left(\\theta\\,T(x)\\right).\n\\]\n\nHence\n\n\\[\n  \\psi'(\\theta)\n  =\n  \\frac{Z'(\\theta)}{Z(\\theta)}\n  =\n  \\frac{\\sum_{x \\in \\mathcal X} T(x)\\,h(x)\\,\\exp\\left(\\theta\\,T(x)\\right)}\n       {\\sum_{x \\in \\mathcal X} h(x)\\,\\exp\\left(\\theta\\,T(x)\\right)}.\n\\]\n\n\nso the previous fraction is simply,\n\n\\[\n  \\psi'(\\theta)\n  =\n  \\sum_{x \\in \\mathcal X} T(x)\\,p_\\theta(x).\n\\]\n\nThus,\n\n\\[\n  \\mathbb{E}_\\theta[T] = \\psi'(\\theta).\n\\]\n\n\nEquivalently, when $X:\\Omega \\to \\mathcal X$ is any random variable whose law is $P_{\\theta}$,\n\n\\[\n  \\mathbb{E}_\\theta[T(X)] = \\psi'(\\theta).\n\\]\n\nIn the rest of the section, when nothing is specified, $X$ is always assumed to have distribution $P_{\\theta}$.\\\\\n\nFor the variance, differentiate once more:\n\n\\[\n  \\psi''(\\theta)\n  =\n  \\frac{Z''(\\theta) Z(\\theta) - (Z'(\\theta))^2}{Z(\\theta)^2},\n\\]\n\nwith\n\n\\[\n  Z''(\\theta)\n  =\n  \\sum_{x \\in \\mathcal X} T(x)^2\\,h(x)\\,\\exp\\left(\\theta\\,T(x)\\right).\n\\]\n\nWe have\n\n\\[\n  \\frac{Z''(\\theta)}{Z(\\theta)}\n  =\n  \\sum_{x \\in \\mathcal X} T(x)^2\\,p_\\theta(x),\n  \\qquad\n  \\left(\\frac{Z'(\\theta)}{Z(\\theta)}\\right)^2\n  =\n  \\left(\\sum_{x \\in \\mathcal X} T(x)\\,p_\\theta(x)\\right)^2.\n\\]\n\nTherefore\n\n\\[\n  \\psi''(\\theta)\n  =\n  \\sum_{x \\in \\mathcal X} T(x)^2\\,p_\\theta(x)\n  - \\left(\\sum_{x \\in \\mathcal X} T(x)\\,p_\\theta(x)\\right)^2\n  =\n  \\mathrm{Var}_\\theta\\left(T(X)\\right),\n\\]\n\nand we conclude that\n\n\\[\n  \\mathrm{Var}_\\theta\\left(T(X)\\right) = \\psi''(\\theta).\n\\]\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Vector case}}\\\\\n\nWhen $T : \\mathcal X\\to \\mathbb{R}^n$ and $\\theta \\in \\mathbb{R}^n$, the same\ncomputations with partial derivatives show that\n\n\\[\n  \\mathbb{E}_\\theta[T(X)] = \\nabla \\psi(\\theta),\n  \\qquad\n  \\mathrm{Cov}_\\theta(T(X)) = \\nabla^2 \\psi(\\theta),\n\\]\n\nwhere $\\nabla \\psi$ is the gradient of $\\psi$ and $\\nabla^2 \\psi$ its Hessian.\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Example: exponential distributions}}\\\\\n\nConsider the exponential distribution in canonical form introduced earlier:\n\n\\[\n  \\mathcal X= \\mathbb{R}_+ = [0,+\\infty[,\n  \\qquad\n  T(x) = x,\n  \\qquad\n  h(x) = 1.\n\\]\n\nWe have\n\n\\[\n  p_\\theta(x)\n  =\n  \\frac{1}{Z(\\theta)} \\exp(\\theta x),\n  \\qquad x \\in [0,+\\infty[,\n\\]\n\nwith natural parameter space\n\n\\[\n  \\Theta = ]-\\infty,0[\n\\]\n\nand partition function\n\n\\[\n  Z(\\theta) = \\int_0^{+\\infty} e^{\\theta x}\\,dx = -\\frac{1}{\\theta},\n  \\qquad \\theta \\in ]-\\infty,0[.\n\\]\n\nHence\n\n\\[\n  \\psi(\\theta) = \\log Z(\\theta) = \\log\\left(-\\frac{1}{\\theta}\\right)\n  = -\\log(-\\theta).\n\\]\n\nWe can now apply the general formulas. First,\n\n\\[\n  \\mathbb{E}_\\theta[X] = \\mathbb{E}_\\theta[T(X)] = \\psi'(\\theta).\n\\]\n\nSince\n\n\\[\n  \\psi'(\\theta)\n  = \\frac{d}{d\\theta}\\left(-\\log(-\\theta)\\right)\n  = -\\frac{1}{\\theta},\n\\]\n\nwe obtain\n\n\\[\n  \\mathbb{E}_\\theta[X] = -\\frac{1}{\\theta}.\n\\]\n\nFor the variance,\n\n\\[\n  \\mathrm{Var}_\\theta(X) = \\mathrm{Var}_\\theta(T(X)) = \\psi''(\\theta).\n\\]\n\nDifferentiating once more,\n\n\\[\n  \\psi''(\\theta)\n  = \\frac{d}{d\\theta}\\left(-\\frac{1}{\\theta}\\right)\n  = \\frac{1}{\\theta^2},\n\\]\n\nso\n\n\\[\n  \\mathrm{Var}_\\theta(X) = \\frac{1}{\\theta^2}.\n\\]\n\nIn terms of the usual parameter $\\lambda>0$, we had $\\theta = -\\lambda$. Thus\n\n\\[\n  \\mathbb{E}_\\lambda[X] = \\frac{1}{\\lambda},\n  \\qquad\n  \\mathrm{Var}_\\lambda(X) = \\frac{1}{\\lambda^2},\n\\]\n\nwhich are the standard formulas for the exponential distribution.\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Example: Gaussian distributions}}\\\\\n\nWe now consider the Gaussian example. Recall that\n\n\\[\n  \\mathcal X= \\mathbb{R},\n  \\qquad\n  T(x) = (x,x^2),\n  \\qquad\n  h(x) = 1,\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n  p_\\theta(x)\n  =\n  \\frac{1}{Z(\\theta)} \\exp\\left(\\theta_1 x + \\theta_2 x^2\\right),\n  \\qquad x \\in \\mathbb{R},\n\\]\n\nwith natural parameter\n\n\\[\n  \\theta = (\\theta_1,\\theta_2),\n  \\qquad\n  \\Theta = \\{(\\theta_1,\\theta_2)\\in\\mathbb{R}^2 : \\theta_2 < 0\\}.\n\\]\n\nFrom the identification with $\\mathcal N(\\mu,\\sigma^2)$ we obtained\n\n\\[\n  \\mu = -\\frac{\\theta_1}{2\\theta_2},\n  \\qquad\n  \\sigma^2 = -\\frac{1}{2\\theta_2},\n\\]\n\nand the partition function\n\n\\[\n  Z(\\theta)\n  =\n  \\sqrt{\\frac{\\pi}{-\\theta_2}}\\,\n  \\exp\\!\\left(-\\frac{\\theta_1^2}{4\\theta_2}\\right),\n\\]\n\nso that\n\n\\[\n  \\psi(\\theta)\n  = \\log Z(\\theta)\n  = -\\frac{\\theta_1^2}{4\\theta_2}\n    + \\frac{1}{2}\\log\\!\\left(\\frac{\\pi}{-\\theta_2}\\right),\n  \\qquad \\theta \\in \\Theta.\n\\]\n\nFrom the general vector formulas we know that\n\n\\[\n  \\mathbb{E}_\\theta[T(X)] = \\nabla \\psi(\\theta)\n  =\n  \\left(\n    \\frac{\\partial \\psi}{\\partial \\theta_1}(\\theta),\n    \\frac{\\partial \\psi}{\\partial \\theta_2}(\\theta)\n  \\right)\n  =\n  \\left(\\mathbb{E}_\\theta[X],\\,\\mathbb{E}_\\theta[X^2]\\right).\n\\]\n\nWe compute:\n\n\\[\n  \\frac{\\partial \\psi}{\\partial \\theta_1}\n  = -\\frac{\\theta_1}{2\\theta_2},\n  \\qquad\n  \\frac{\\partial \\psi}{\\partial \\theta_2}\n  = \\frac{\\theta_1^2}{4\\theta_2^2} - \\frac{1}{2\\theta_2}.\n\\]\n\nHence\n\n\\[\n  \\mathbb{E}_\\theta[X] = -\\frac{\\theta_1}{2\\theta_2},\n  \\qquad\n  \\mathbb{E}_\\theta[X^2] = \\frac{\\theta_1^2}{4\\theta_2^2} - \\frac{1}{2\\theta_2}.\n\\]\n\nThe variance of $X$ is\n\n\\[\n  \\mathrm{Var}_\\theta(X)\n  =\n  \\mathbb{E}_\\theta[X^2] - \\left(\\mathbb{E}_\\theta[X]\\right)^2\n  =\n  \\left(\\frac{\\theta_1^2}{4\\theta_2^2} - \\frac{1}{2\\theta_2}\\right)\n  - \\left(-\\frac{\\theta_1}{2\\theta_2}\\right)^2\n  =\n  -\\frac{1}{2\\theta_2}.\n\\]\n\nUsing the relations\n\n\\[\n  \\mu = -\\frac{\\theta_1}{2\\theta_2},\n  \\qquad\n  \\sigma^2 = -\\frac{1}{2\\theta_2},\n\\]\n\nwe see that\n\n\\[\n  \\mathbb{E}_\\theta[X] = \\mu,\n  \\qquad\n  \\mathrm{Var}_\\theta(X) = \\sigma^2.\n\\]\n\nThus, for the Gaussian exponential family, the gradient of $\\psi$ recovers the\nmean and second moment, and the usual variance $\\sigma^2$ appears as a simple\ncombination of the natural parameters.\n\n"

                "latexMainText": "\n\nWe now assume that $T$ is real valued and that for every $\\theta \\in \\Theta$,\n\n\\[\n  \\mathrm{Var}_\\theta\\left(T(X)\\right) > 0.\n\\]\n\nExercise : show that the condition on the variance amounts to saying that the function $T$ takes at least two different values, with non null probabilities. \n\nUnder this assumption,\n\n\\[\n  \\psi''(\\theta) = \\mathrm{Var}_\\theta\\left(T(X)\\right) > 0\n  \\qquad \\text{for all } \\theta \\in \\Theta.\n\\]\n\nTherefore:\n\\begin{itemize}\n  \\item $\\psi$ is a \\emph{strictly convex} function on $\\Theta$.\n  \\item Its derivative $\\psi' : \\Theta \\to \\mathbb{R}$ is \\emph{strictly increasing}.\n\\end{itemize}\n\nSince $\\Theta$ is an interval in $\\mathbb{R}$ and $\\psi'$ is continuous and strictly\nincreasing on $\\Theta$, the map\n\n\\[\n  \\theta \\;\\longmapsto\\; \\psi'(\\theta) = \\mathbb{E}_\\theta[T(X)]\n\\]\n\nis a bijection between $\\Theta$ and its image\n\n\\[\n  \\mathcal{E}\n  :=\n  \\psi'(\\Theta)\n  =\n  \\left\\{\\mathbb{E}_\\theta[T(X)] : \\theta \\in \\Theta \\right\\}.\n\\]\n\nThe set $\\mathcal{E}$ is an interval in $\\mathbb{R}$, called the\n\\emph{expectation parameter space}.\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Expectation parameter}}\\\\\n\n\\noindent \nWe define the \\emph{expectation parameter} by\n\n\\[\n  \\eta\n  =\n  \\mathbb{E}_\\theta[T(X)]\n  =\n  \\psi'(\\theta).\n\\]\n\nBy the discussion above, for each $\\eta \\in \\mathcal{E}$ there is a unique\n$\\theta \\in \\Theta$ such that $\\psi'(\\theta) = \\eta$. We denote this inverse map by\n\n\\[\n  \\theta(\\eta)\n  \\quad\\text{such that}\\quad\n  \\psi'\\left(\\theta(\\eta)\\right) = \\eta.\n\\]\n\nThus the same exponential family can be parametrized either by $\\theta$ (the\n\\emph{natural parameter}) or by $\\eta$ (the \\emph{expectation parameter}):\n\n\\[\n  P_\\eta(x)\n  :=\n  P_{\\theta(\\eta)}(x)\n  =\n  \\frac{1}{Z\\left(\\theta(\\eta)\\right)}h(x)\n  \\exp\\left(\\theta(\\eta)\\,T(x)\\right),\n  \\qquad x \\in \\mathcal X,\\; \\eta \\in \\mathcal{E}.\n\\]\n\nIn this parametrization we have, by construction,\n\n\\[\n  \\mathbb{E}_\\eta[T(X)] = \\eta.\n\\]\n\n\\medskip\n\n\\textbf{Remark:} it is relatively frequent that the derivative of $\\psi$ can be computed explicitely. In that case $\\eta$ is easily obtained from $\\theta$. However finding the $\\theta(\\eta)$ associated with $\\eta$ is sometimes more complicated. We need to be able to compute the inverse function $\\psi'^{-1}$: $\\quad \\theta(\\eta) = \\psi'^{-1}(\\eta)$.  \n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Vector case}}\\\\\n\nIn the $n$-dimensional case, $T : \\mathcal X\\to \\mathbb{R}^n$ and\n$\\theta \\in \\Theta \\subset \\mathbb{R}^n$, one defines\n\n\\[\n  \\psi(\\theta) = \\log Z(\\theta), \\qquad\n  \\nabla \\psi(\\theta) = \\mathbb{E}_\\theta[T(X)], \\qquad\n  \\nabla^2 \\psi(\\theta) = \\mathrm{Cov}_\\theta\\left(T(X)\\right).\n\\]\n\nIf the covariance matrix $\\mathrm{Cov}_\\theta(T(X))$ is positive definite for all\n$\\theta \\in \\Theta$, then $\\psi$ is strictly convex and the gradient map\n\n\\[\n  \\nabla \\psi : \\Theta \\to \\mathbb{R}^n\n\\]\n\nis a bijection between $\\Theta$ and its image\n$\\mathcal{E} = \\nabla \\psi(\\Theta)$, which is then the expectation parameter space.\nThe parameter $\\eta = \\mathbb{E}_\\theta[T(X)]$ is again called the expectation\nparameter.\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Example: expectation parameter for the exponential distribution}}\\\\\n\nFor the exponential distribution, we had\n\n\\[\n  \\mathcal X= [0,+\\infty[,\\qquad T(x) = x,\\qquad h(x) = 1,\n\\]\n\nnatural parameter\n\n\\[\n  \\theta \\in \\Theta = ]-\\infty,0[,\n\\]\n\nand log-partition function\n\n\\[\n  \\psi(\\theta) = -\\log(-\\theta), \\qquad \\theta \\in ]-\\infty,0[.\n\\]\n\nFrom the previous computations,\n\n\\[\n  \\eta = \\mathbb{E}_\\theta[T(X)] = \\psi'(\\theta) = -\\frac{1}{\\theta}.\n\\]\n\nSince $\\theta<0$, we have $\\eta>0$, so the expectation parameter space is\n\n\\[\n  \\mathcal{E} = ]0,+\\infty[.\n\\]\n\nThe map between the two parametrizations is therefore\n\n\\[\n  \\eta = -\\frac{1}{\\theta}\n  \\qquad\\Longleftrightarrow\\qquad\n  \\theta = -\\frac{1}{\\eta},\n\\]\n\nwith\n\n\\[\n  \\theta \\in \\Theta = ]-\\infty,0[,\n  \\qquad\n  \\eta \\in \\mathcal{E} = ]0,+\\infty[.\n\\]\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Example: expectation parameter for the Gaussian distributions}}\\\\\n\n\nFor the Gaussian exponential family, we had\n\n\\[\n  \\mathcal X= \\mathbb{R},\\qquad\n  T(x) = (x,x^2),\\qquad\n  h(x) = 1,\n\\]\n\nwith natural parameter\n\n\\[\n  \\theta = (\\theta_1,\\theta_2) \\in \\Theta\n  = \\{(\\theta_1,\\theta_2)\\in\\mathbb{R}^2 : \\theta_2 < 0\\}.\n\\]\n\nFrom the identification with $\\mathcal{N}(\\mu,\\sigma^2)$, we have\n\n\\[\n  \\mu = -\\frac{\\theta_1}{2\\theta_2},\n  \\qquad\n  \\sigma^2 = -\\frac{1}{2\\theta_2}.\n\\]\n\nWe also computed\n\n\\[\n  \\mathbb{E}_\\theta[X] = -\\frac{\\theta_1}{2\\theta_2} = \\mu,\n  \\qquad\n  \\mathbb{E}_\\theta[X^2] = \\frac{\\theta_1^2}{4\\theta_2^2} - \\frac{1}{2\\theta_2}\n  = \\mu^2 + \\sigma^2.\n\\]\n\nThe expectation parameter is the vector\n\n\\[\n  \\eta\n  =\n  \\mathbb{E}_\\theta[T(X)]\n  =\n  \\left(\\mathbb{E}_\\theta[X],\\,\\mathbb{E}_\\theta[X^2]\\right)\n  =\n  (\\eta_1,\\eta_2)\n  =\n  (\\mu,\\mu^2+\\sigma^2).\n\\]\n\nSince $\\sigma^2 > 0$, we have\n\n\\[\n  \\eta_2 - \\eta_1^2 = \\sigma^2 > 0,\n\\]\n\nso the expectation parameter space is\n\n\\[\n  \\mathcal{E}\n  =\n  \\left\\{ (\\eta_1,\\eta_2) \\in \\mathbb{R}^2 : \\eta_2 > \\eta_1^2 \\right\\}.\n\\]\n\nConversely, given $(\\eta_1,\\eta_2)$ with $\\eta_2 > \\eta_1^2$, we recover\n\n\\[\n  \\mu = \\eta_1,\n  \\qquad\n  \\sigma^2 = \\eta_2 - \\eta_1^2,\n\\]\n\nand thus\n\n\\[\n  \\theta_1\n  = \\frac{\\mu}{\\sigma^2}\n  = \\frac{\\eta_1}{\\eta_2 - \\eta_1^2},\n  \\qquad\n  \\theta_2\n  = -\\frac{1}{2\\sigma^2}\n  = -\\frac{1}{2(\\eta_2 - \\eta_1^2)}.\n\\]\n\nThis gives the inverse map $\\theta(\\eta)$ between the natural parameter and the\nexpectation parameter for the Gaussian exponential family.\n\n"

                "latexMainText": "\n\nStart by considering an exponential family with trivial carrier term $h(x)=1$. The following derivations are done in the discrete setting but sums can be turned into integral for the case of probability densities.  \n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Entropy in an exponential family}}\\\\\n\nWe keep the discrete setting where $\\mathcal X$ is finite, $T : \\mathcal X\\to \\mathbb{R}$. The entropy of $P_\\theta$ is given by\n\n\\begin{align*}\n  H(P_\\theta)\n  &= - \\sum_{x} p_\\theta(x)\\log p_\\theta(x) \\\\\n  &= - \\sum_{x} p_\\theta(x)\\,\\bigl[\\theta T(x) - \\log Z(\\theta)\\bigr] \\\\\n  &= - \\theta \\sum_{x} p_\\theta(x) T(x)\n     + \\log Z(\\theta) \\sum_{x} p_\\theta(x) \\\\\n  &= - \\theta\\,\\mathbb{E}_\\theta[T(X)] + \\log Z(\\theta).\n\\end{align*}\n\nRecall that $\\eta(\\theta) = \\mathbb{E}_\\theta[T(X)]$ (expectation parameter), hence\n\n\\[\n  H(P_\\theta) = - \\theta \\eta(\\theta) + \\log Z(\\theta).\n\\]\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Constraint set}}\\\\\n\nFix a real number $\\eta$. We denote by\n\n\\[\n  \\mathcal{C}_\\eta\n  =\n  \\left\\{\n    P \\text{ probability on }\\mathcal X\n    : \\mathbb{E}_P[T] = \\eta\n  \\right\\}\n\\]\n\nthe set of all probability measures on $\\mathcal X$ that give $T$ the same expectation\n$\\eta$. \n\nWe have seen that when $\\eta\\in \\mathcal E$, there is a corresponding natural parameter $\\theta(\\eta)$ with \n\n\\[\n  \\mathbb{E}_{\\theta(\\eta)}[T] = \\eta.\n\\]\n\nThus, for $\\eta \\in \\mathcal{E}$, the distribution $P_{\\theta(\\eta)}$ belongs to\n$\\mathcal{C}_\\eta$.\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Maximum entropy property}}\\\\\n\nLet $\\eta \\in \\mathcal{E}$. Then\n\n\\[\n  H(P) \\;\\le\\; H\\bigl(P_{\\theta(\\eta)}\\bigr)\n  \\qquad\\text{for all } P \\in \\mathcal{C}_\\eta,\n\\]\n\nwith equality if and only if $P = P_{\\theta(\\eta)}$.\nIn other words, among all probability distributions on $\\mathcal X$ having the same\nexpectation $\\eta$ for $T$, the exponential-family distribution\n$P_{\\theta(\\eta)}$ is the unique one that maximizes the entropy.\n\nA similar statement can be made for the differential entropy of exponential families of densities.\n\n\\textbf{Interpretation. }\nFixing $\\mathbb{E}_P[T] = \\eta$ imposes a constraint on the average value of\n$T$. Among all probabilities $P$ that satisfy this constraint, the\nexponential-family distribution $P_{\\theta(\\eta)}$ is the ``most spread out'' one in the sense of having the largest entropy.\n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Proof}}\\\\\n\nFor any probability $P$ on $\\mathcal X$ with mass function $p(x)$, the cross-entropy with $P_{\\theta(\\eta)}$ is\n\n\\begin{align*}\n  H(P, P_{\\theta(\\eta)})\n  &= -\\sum_{x\\in\\mathcal X} p(x)\\,\\log p_{\\theta(\\eta)}(x)\\\\\n  &= - \\sum_{x} p(x)\\,\\bigl[\\theta(\\eta) T(x) - \\log Z(\\theta(\\eta))\\bigr] \\\\\n  &= -\\theta(\\eta) \\sum_{x} p(x) T(x)\n     + \\log Z(\\theta(\\eta)) \\sum_{x} p(x)\\\\\n  &= -\\theta \\sum_{x} p(x) T(x)\n     + \\log Z(\\theta(\\eta))\\\\\n  &= -\\theta(\\eta) \\eta + \\log Z(\\theta(\\eta))\\\\\n  &= H(P_{\\theta(\\eta)})\n\\end{align*}\n\nBy the Gibbs inequality\n\n\\[\n  H(P)\\leq H(P, P_{\\theta(\\eta)}) = H(P_{\\theta(\\eta)}).\n\\]\n\nwith equality only if $P=P_{\\theta(\\eta)}$.\\\\\n\n\\textbf{Remark:} standard approach is to use Lagrange multipliers. This other approach has the interest of making the form of the exponential family appear from the entropy optimization problem. \n\n\\textcolor{blue}{\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\hrule\n\\vspace{0.2cm}\n\\textbf{Non trivial carrier term}}\\\\\n\nWhen the carrier $h$ is not constant, the entropy maximization result needs to be slightly modified.\\\\\n\nWhen $h(x) = 1$, we can write\n\n$$\nH(P) = - \\sum_x p(x)\\log(p(x)) = - \\sum_x p(x)\\log\\left(\\frac{p(x)}{h(x)}\\right)\n$$\n\nThis strongly resembles the Kullback-Leibler divergence between probability distributions. Even though formally speaking $h$ does not necessarily correspond to a probability distribution (its sum is infinite when $Omega$ is infinite) the notion of Kullback-Leibler divergence can still be defined for arbitrary second term. Hence when $h(x)=1$,\n\n$$\nH(P) = - D_{\\mathrm{KL}}(P\\,\\|\\,h),\n$$\n\nand the statement about entropy maximization can be seen as a minimization of the Kullback-Leibler divergence to the carrier function. This is the correct approach to express the optimization result for arbitrary carrier $h$: $P_{\\theta}$ is always the unique minimizer of\n$D_{\\mathrm{KL}}(P \\,\\|\\, h)$ on $\\mathcal{C}_\\eta$. The proof is left as an exercise. \n\n\n"

                "latexMainText": "\n\nIn general, the Kullback--Leibler divergence between two probability\ndistributions $P$ and $Q$ on the same space is defined by\n\n\\[\n  D_{\\mathrm{KL}}(P \\,\\|\\, Q)\n  =\n  \\sum_x p(x)\\,\\log\\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}\n\\]\n\nin the discrete case, or with integrals in the continuous case. For a general pair $(P,Q)$, there is no obvious simplification of this formula. However, for two members of the \\emph{same} exponential family, the expression\nbecomes much simpler.\n\nConsider a one-dimensional exponential family with carrier $h$ and statistic\n$T : \\mathcal X\\to \\mathbb{R}$. Let $\\theta,\\theta'$ be two parameters in $\\Theta$. Then\n\n\\[\n  \\log p_\\theta(x)\n  =\n  \\theta T(x) + \\log h(x) - \\psi(\\theta),\n  \\qquad\n  \\log p_{\\theta'}(x)\n  =\n  \\theta' T(x) + \\log h(x) - \\psi(\\theta').\n\\]\n\nSubtracting, the carrier term $\\log h(x)$ cancels:\n\n\\[\n\n  \\log\\frac{p_\\theta(x)}{p_{\\theta'}(x)}\n  =\n  (\\theta-\\theta')\\,T(x) - \\left(\\psi(\\theta)-\\psi(\\theta')\\right).\n\\]\n\nHence the Kullback--Leibler divergence between $P_\\theta$ and $P_{\\theta'}$ is\n\n\\begin{align*}\n  D_{\\mathrm{KL}}(P_\\theta \\,\\|\\, P_{\\theta'})\n  &= \\sum_x p_\\theta(x)\\,\\log\\frac{p_\\theta(x)}{p_{\\theta'}(x)}\\\\[0.1cm]\n  &= \\sum_x p_\\theta(x)\\,\\left[(\\theta-\\theta')\\,T(x)\n     - \\left(\\psi(\\theta)-\\psi(\\theta')\\right)\\right]\\\\[0.1cm]\n  &= (\\theta-\\theta')\\,\\mathbb{E}_\\theta[T(X)]\n     - \\left(\\psi(\\theta)-\\psi(\\theta')\\right).\\\\[0.1cm]\n\\end{align*}\n\nFinally,\n\n\\[\n  D_{\\mathrm{KL}}(P_\\theta \\,\\|\\, P_{\\theta'})\n  =\n  (\\theta-\\theta')\\,\\eta(\\theta)\n  - \\psi(\\theta) + \\psi(\\theta'),\n  \\qquad \\theta,\\theta' \\in \\Theta.\n\\]\n\nIn the $n$-dimensional casethe product becomes an inner product,\n\n\\[\nD_{\\mathrm{KL}}(P_\\theta \\,\\|\\, P_{\\theta'}) = \\langle \\theta-\\theta',\\,\\eta(\\theta)\\rangle\n     - \\psi(\\theta) + \\psi(\\theta').\n\\]\n\nIn other words, the Kullback-Leibler divergence between two members of the same\nexponential family can be written purely in terms of the natural parameter,\nthe expectation parameter and the log-partition function.\n\n\n\\textbf{Remark (to go further):} The fact that the Kullback-Leibler divergence simplifies on exponential families is an instance of a more general phenomenon: how the Bregman divergence associated with a convex function $F$ behaves when restricted to the set of minimizers of $F$ under linear constraints.\n\n"

Write as usual $\\eta=\\psi'(\\theta)$ and\n$\\theta(\\eta)$ for the inverse map on the expectation parameter space $\\mathcal E$.\nThe log-likelihood written as a function of $\\eta$ is\n\n\\[\n  \\log \\ell_n(\\eta;x_1,\\dots,x_n)\n  = \\theta(\\eta) \\sum_{i=1}^n T(x_i)\n    - n\\psi(\\theta(\\eta))\n    + \\sum_{i=1}^n \\log h(x_i).\n\\]\n\nSet $\\bar T_n = \\frac{1}{n}\\sum_{i=1}^n T(x_i)$.
