                "summary": "<div class=\"theorem\" id=\"Converse : characterization by the CRB\">\n<p><strong>Theorem 22</strong> (Converse : characterization by the CRB).\r\n</p>\n<p>If the estimator of the parameter of a family of probability\r\ndistributions is unbiased and attains the CRB, then the family must be\r\nan exponential family.</p>\n</div>",
                "hasSummary": true,
                "hasTitle": true,
                "title": "Converse : characterization by the CRB",
                "display_order": 103,
                "latexMainText": "\n\nConsider a family of probability distributions $P_{\\eta}$ over a set $\\mathcal X$\nparametrized by $\\eta$. For now we do not assume that $P_{\\eta}$ is an exponential family.\nWe assume however that we have an estimator $\\hat\\eta(X)$ of the parameter $\\eta$, which is\nunbiased for all $\\eta$, and which attains the Cramer-Rao bound. We will show that $P_{\\eta}$ is actually an epxonential family.\\\\\n\n\nIn the demonstration of the CRB for an unbiased estimator, we\nfound that\n\n\\[\nbias=1=\\mathbb{E}\\!\\left( V(\\eta,X)(\\hat{\\eta}(X)-\\eta) \\right)\n\\le\n\\sqrt{\\mathbb E\\!\\left(V(\\eta,X)^2\\right)}\\,\n\\sqrt{\\mathbb E\\!\\left((\\hat\\eta(X)-\\eta)^2\\right)} =\\sqrt{\\mathcal I(\\eta)} \\cdot\\sqrt{\\operatorname{Var}(\\hat{\\eta}(X))},\n\\]\n\nhence\n\n\\[\n\\mathrm{Var}_\\eta(\\hat\\eta(X)) \\ge \\frac{1}{\\mathbb E_\\eta\\!\\left(V(\\eta,X)^2\\right)}\n= \\frac{1}{\\mathcal I(\\eta)}.\n\\]\n\nSince the CRB comes from a Cauchy--Schwarz inequality, equality holds if and only if\nthere exists a scalar $c(\\eta)$ such that,\n\n\\[\n\\hat\\eta(X)-\\eta = c(\\eta)\\,V(\\eta,X).\n\\]\n\nMultiplying by $V(\\eta,X)$ and taking expectations gives\n\n\\[\n1=\\mathbb E_\\eta\\!\\left(V(\\eta,X)(\\hat\\eta(X)-\\eta)\\right)\n= c(\\eta)\\,\\mathbb E_\\eta\\!\\left(V(\\eta,X)^2\\right)\n= c(\\eta)\\,\\mathcal I(\\eta),\n\\]\n\nso\n\n\\[\nc(\\eta)=\\frac{1}{\\mathcal I(\\eta)}.\n\\]\n\nTherefore, in the equality case,\n\n\\[\nV(\\eta,x) = \\mathcal I(\\eta)\\,(\\hat\\eta(x)-\\eta).\n\\]\n\nNow write the score as a derivative of the log-likelihood:\n\n\\[\nV(\\eta,x)=\\frac{\\partial}{\\partial\\eta}\\log p_\\eta(x).\n\\]\n\nThe equality case becomes the differential equation\n\n\\[\n\\frac{\\partial}{\\partial\\eta}\\log p_\\eta(x)\n=\n\\mathcal I(\\eta)\\,(\\hat\\eta(x)-\\eta).\n\\]\n\nFor a fixed $x$, integrate with respect to $\\eta$:\n\n\\[\n\\log p_\\eta(x)\n=\n\\log p_{\\eta_0}(x)\n+\n\\left(\\int_{\\eta_0}^{\\eta}\\mathcal I(u)\\,du\\right)\\hat\\eta(x)\n-\n\\int_{\\eta_0}^{\\eta} u\\,\\mathcal I(u)\\,du.\n\\]\n\nDefine\n\n\\[\nh(x)=p_{\\eta_0}(x),\n\\qquad\nT(x)=\\hat\\eta(x),\n\\qquad\n\\theta(\\eta)=\\int_{\\eta_0}^{\\eta}\\mathcal I(u)\\,du,\n\\qquad\n\\tilde\\psi(\\eta)=\\int_{\\eta_0}^{\\eta} u\\,\\mathcal I(u)\\,du.\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\n\\log p_\\eta(x)=\\log h(x)+\\theta(\\eta)\\,T(x)-\\tilde\\psi(\\eta),\n\\]\n\nor equivalently\n\n\\[\np_\\eta(x)=h(x)\\exp\\!\\left(a(\\eta)\\,T(x)-\\tilde\\psi(\\eta)\\right).\n\\]\n\nThis is exactly the shape of a one-parameter exponential family where $\\tilde \\psi(\\eta) = \\psi(\\theta(\\eta))$. \n\n\n"

We call\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mi>\u03c3</mi><mo>:</mo><mi>\ud835\udcae</mi><mo>\u2192</mo><mi>\ud835\udcae</mi></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\sigma:\\mathcal{S}\\rightarrow \\mathcal{S}</annotation></semantics></math>\r\na permutation when it is a bijection. If we remember the order in\r\nwhich we take the elements, how many different configurations can we\r\nobtain? If we don\u2019t remember the order in which the different elements\r\nwere taken, how many different configurations can we obtain?</p>\r\n</div>\r\n<div id=\"rem:IntProb\" class=\"remark\">\r\n<p><strong>Remark 1</strong> (<strong>Introductory remark</strong>).\r\n</p>\r\n<p><br />\r\n<br />\r\n<strong>Probabilistic / Deterministic</strong><br />\r\n<em>uncertain</em>\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mspace width=\"1.0em\"></mspace><mspace width=\"1.0em\"></mspace></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\quad\\quad</annotation></semantics></math>\r\n<em>certain</em><br />\r\n<strong><math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mo>\u2192</mo><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nVocabulary of prediction.</strong></p>\r\n<p><strong>Attention</strong><br />\r\nIn and of itself, probability theory is not intrinsically tied to the\r\nnotion of prediction. Probability theory can be viewed as an advanced\r\ntheory of proportion calculations. These proportion calculations can\r\nthen be applied to prediction problems.</p>\r\n<p>Similarly, the concept of probability is often associated with the\r\nconcept of randomness. Randomness itself is linked to the notion of\r\nprediction and therefore does not, strictly speaking, belong to\r\nprobability theory. Probability theory is a tool that can be used in\r\nmodeling randomness.</p>\r\n<p>For instance, the question</p>\r\n<p><math display=\"block\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mtext mathvariant=\"normal\">\r\n&quot;what is the probability of this event?&quot; </mtext><mspace usually be interpreted as</p>\r\n<p><math display=\"block\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mtext mathvariant=\"normal\">\r\n&quot;what is the proportion of possible configurations in which this event occurs?&quot; </mtext><mspace width=\"0.333em\"></mspace></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\text{\r\n&quot;what is the proportion of possible />\r\n<p><strong>Introduction</strong></p>\r\n</div>\r\n<p><br />\r\nEarlier, events have been defined as subsets\r\n<math display=\"inline\" \\Omega</annotation></semantics></math>.\r\nWhen\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi mathvariant=\"normal\">\u03a9</mi><annotation \\Omega</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nis considered to be an event. These subsets lead to unconvienient\r\nresults, and we often which to exclude them. xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi>\u03c3</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\sigma</annotation></semantics></math>-algebra\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi>\ud835\udc9c</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\mathcal{A}</annotation></semantics></math>\r\non\r\n<math display=\"inline\" \\mathcal{A}</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nfor\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>\u2208</mo><mi>\u2115</mi></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">i\\in \\mathbb{N}</annotation></semantics></math>,\r\nthen\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><msub><mo>\u22c3</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>\u2208</mo><mi>\u2115</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>\u2208</mo><mi>\ud835\udc9c</mi></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\bigcup_{i\\in \\mathbb{N}} A_i \\in \\mathcal{A}</annotation></semantics></math>\r\n(<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mo>\u2192</mo><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math>\r\naxiom 3 of probabilities)</p></li>\r\n</ul>\r\n<div style=\"color: blue\">\r\n<hr />\r\n<p><strong>Examples</strong></p>\r\n</div>\r\n<p><br />\r\n</p>\r\n<ul>\r\n<li><p>When\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi mathvariant=\"normal\">\u03a9</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\Omega</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nis finite, the\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi>\u03c3</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\sigma</annotation></semantics></math>-algebra\r\nis usually\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mi>\ud835\udcab</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><mi mathvariant=\"normal\">\u03a9</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\mathcal{P}(\\Omega)</annotation></semantics></math>:\r\nevery subset of\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi mathvariant=\"normal\">\u03a9</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\Omega</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nis an event.</p></li>\r\n<li><p>when\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant=\"normal\">\u03a9</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>\u211d</mi></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\Omega= \\mathbb{R}</annotation></semantics></math>,\r\nthe\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi>\u03c3</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\sigma</annotation></semantics></math>-algebra\r\nis obtained by taking countable unions of intervals and their\r\ncomplements.</p></li>\r\n</ul>\r\n<div style=\"color: blue\">\r\n<hr />\r\n<p><strong>Stochastic process</strong></p>\r\n</div>\r\n<p><br />\r\nThough the concept of\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi>\u03c3</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\sigma</annotation></semantics></math>-algebra\r\nis first used to avoid the problems brought by some subsets of\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi>\u211d</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\mathbb{R}</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nand can be seen as a mere technicallity, it later becomes an important\r\ntool to formalize properties of stochastic processes. This will also be\r\nout of the scope of this course.</p>\r\n</div>\r\n<div id=\"rem:ProbAss\" class=\"remark\">\r\n<p><strong>Remark 3</strong> (<strong>Assignment of\r\nprobabilities</strong>). </p>\r\n<p><br />\r\nTo model real life situations, we assign probabilities to events that\r\nreflect what we know about the situation. The probabilities on the\r\nconfiguration space\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi mathvariant=\"normal\">\u03a9</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\Omega</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nare usually assigned according to one of the two following\r\nprinciples.</p>\r\n<ul>\r\n<li><p><strong>Indistinguishability</strong>. Assume that in a certain\r\nexperiment, the elements of\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi mathvariant=\"normal\">\u03a9</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\Omega</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nare perfectly indistinguishable. The probability of an event\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi>A</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">A</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nis then given by the number of configuration\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">k</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nin which it occurs\r\n(<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mi>\u03c9</mi><mo>\u2208</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\omega \\in A</annotation></semantics></math>)\r\ndivided by the total number of configuration\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">n</annotation></semantics></math>:\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mfrac><mi>k</mi><mi>n</mi></mfrac><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\frac{k}{n}</annotation></semantics></math>.\r\nIt is for instance the case when we draw a card from a card game without\r\nseeing what is on the card: they are all indistinguishable.</p></li>\r\n<li><p><strong>Probabilities as frequencies</strong>. Assume that an\r\nexperiment that produces output value in\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi mathvariant=\"normal\">\u03a9</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\Omega</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nhas been repeated\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">n</annotation></semantics></math>\r\ntimes. If\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">k</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nof the output values belongs to the event\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi>A</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">A</annotation></semantics></math>,\r\nthe probability assigned to\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi>A</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">A</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nis the number\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mfrac><mi>k</mi><mi>n</mi></mfrac><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\frac{k}{n}</annotation></semantics></math>.\r\nThis can be used to evaluate the probabilities of the outcomes of an\r\nasymmetrical die. We will come back to the link between probabilities\r\nand frequencies later in the course.</p></li>\r\n</ul>\r\n<p>We will come back in detail on the assignment of probabilities in the\r\nsection \"Statistical estimation\".</p>\r\n<p>Independently from how they are assigned, probability values should\r\nverify several rules.</p>\r\n</div>\r\n<div id=\"def:Prob\" class=\"definition\">\r\n<p><strong>Definition 3</strong> (<strong>Probability</strong>). </p>\r\n<p><br />\r\n</p>\r\n<div style=\"color: blue\">\r\n<hr />\r\n<p><strong>Definition</strong></p>\r\n</div>\r\n<p><br />\r\nA probability\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi>P</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">P</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nis a function which takes in input an <strong>event</strong> and returns\r\na positive real number. It must verify the following axioms:</p>\r\n<ul>\r\n<li><p>axiom 1:\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><mi mathvariant=\"normal\">\u03a9</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">P(\\Omega) = 1</annotation></semantics></math></p></li>\r\n<li><p>axiom 2:\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>\u2282</mo><mi mathvariant=\"normal\">\u03a9</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">)</mo><mo>\u2265</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">P(A\\subset \\Omega) \\geq 0</annotation></semantics></math></p></li>\r\n<li><p>axiom 3: if\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>\u2229</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>\u2205</mi></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">A\\cap B=\\emptyset</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nthen\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>\u222a</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">P(A\\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)</annotation></semantics></math>\r\n(also true for countable sums)</p></li>\r\n</ul>\r\n<p>Direct consequences:</p>\r\n<ul>\r\n<li><p>consequence\r\n1:<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><msup><mi>A</mi><mi>c</mi></msup><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>\u2212</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">P(A^c) = 1-P(A)</annotation></semantics></math></p></li>\r\n<li><p>consequence 2\r\n:<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><mi>\u2205</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">P(\\emptyset) = 0</annotation></semantics></math></p></li>\r\n<li><p>consequence\r\n3:<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>\u222a</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">)</mo><mo>\u2212</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>\u2229</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">P(A\\cup B) = P(A)+P(B)-P(A\\cap B)</annotation></semantics></math></p></li>\r\n</ul>\r\n<div style=\"color: blue\">\r\n<hr />\r\n<p><strong>Interpretation</strong></p>\r\n</div>\r\n<p><br />\r\nThe probability gives a notion of \u2019size\u2019 to events. Given that the size\r\nof\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi mathvariant=\"normal\">\u03a9</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\Omega</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nis\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mn>1</mn><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">1</annotation></semantics></math>,\r\nthe size of events can be interpreted as the proportion they occupy in\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi mathvariant=\"normal\">\u03a9</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\Omega</annotation></semantics></math>.\r\nHence, the\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi>P</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">P</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nof probability can also be read as the\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi>P</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">P</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nof <strong>proportion</strong>.<br />\r\n</p>\r\n<p>Assume that a die is a perfect cube. All faces are indistinguishable\r\nfrom each other, except for the written number. In this case, it is\r\nrelevant to assign probabilities according to the indistinguishability\r\nprinciple:</p>\r\n<p><math display=\"block\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">}</mo><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>6</mn></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">{</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">}</mo><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>6</mn></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">{</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">}</mo><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>6</mn></mfrac><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">P(\\{1\\}) = \\frac{1}{6}, P(\\{2\\}) = \\frac{1}{6},P(\\{3\\}) = \\frac{1}{6},</annotation></semantics></math>\r\n<math display=\"block\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">{</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">}</mo><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>6</mn></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">{</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">}</mo><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>6</mn></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">{</mo><mn>6</mn><mo encoding=\"application/x-tex\">P(\\{4\\}) = \\frac{1}{6},P(\\{5\\}) = \\frac{1}{6},P(\\{6\\}) = \\frac{1}{6}.</annotation></semantics></math></p>\r\n<p>The distribution is called uniform. It is now possible to compute the\r\nprobability of every event, using the axiom 3 (if\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>\u2229</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>\u2205</mi></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">A\\cap B=\\emptyset</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nthen\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>\u222a</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" encoding=\"application/x-tex\">P(A\\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)</annotation></semantics></math>):</p>\r\n<p><math display=\"block\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo stretchy=\"true\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">{</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>6</mn><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">}</mo><mo stretchy=\"true\" form=\"postfix\">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo stretchy=\"true\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">{</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">}</mo><mo>\u222a</mo><mo stretchy=\"false\" encoding=\"application/x-tex\">P\\left(\\{2,4,6\\}\\right) = P\\left(\\{2\\}\\cup\\{4\\}\\cup \\{6\\}\\right)=P(\\{2\\})+P(\\{4\\})+P(\\{6\\})=\\frac{1}{2}.</annotation></semantics></math></p>\r\n<p>Assume now that our die is a bit damaged. It is no longer perfectly\r\nsymmetrical. Hence, we can no longer use the principle of\r\nindistinguishability. In that case a relevant approach is to roll the\r\ndie many time and to assign probabilities according to the frequency of\r\napparition of the numbers.</p>\r\n<p><math display=\"block\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy=\"false\" \\frac{k_5}{N},P(\\{6\\}) = \\frac{k_6}{N}.</annotation></semantics></math></p>\r\n<p>Exactly as before, the probability of other events is calculated with\r\nthe rule \u2019if\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>\u2229</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>\u2205</mi></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">A\\cap B=\\emptyset</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nthen\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" encoding=\"application/x-tex\">P(A\\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)</annotation></semantics></math>\u2019.</p>\r\n</div>\r\n<div id=\"def:Densities and pmf\" class=\"definition\">\r\n<p><strong>Definition 4</strong> (<strong>Densities and pmf</strong>).\r\n</p>\r\n<p><br />\r\n<br />\r\nWhen\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi>P</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">P</annotation></semantics></math>\r\na probability distirbution on\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi id=\"subsec:RV\">Random Variables</h2>\r\n<div id=\"def:RV\" class=\"definition\">\r\n<p><strong>Definition 5</strong> (<strong>Random variables</strong>).\r\n</p>\r\n<p><br />\r\n</p>\r\n<div style=\"color: blue\">\r\n<hr />\r\n<p><strong>Introduction</strong></p>\r\n</div>\r\n<p><br />\r\nConsider a game where a player rolls a dice and gains a score depending\r\non the face of the dice. The face\r\n(<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">x</annotation></semantics></math>)\r\nand the gain\r\n(<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">y</annotation></semantics></math>)\r\nare related by the following equation:</p>\r\n<p><math display=\"block\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>\u2212</mo><mn>10</mn><mi>.</mi></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">y = x^2-10.</annotation></semantics></math></p>\r\n<p><math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">y</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nand\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">x</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nare variables of the equation. When we build a probabilistic model, we\r\nwant to know what are the possible values that the variables can take,\r\nand in which proportions.</p>\r\n<p>In this particular setting, everything is determined by the dice\u2019s\r\nface, and due to symmetry considerations, we assign each face an equal\r\nproportion: let</p>\r\n<p><math display=\"block\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant=\"normal\">\u03a9</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy=\"false\" \\frac{1}{6}.</annotation></semantics></math> The variables\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation \\Omega</annotation></semantics></math>.\r\nHence they can be seen as functions of\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>i</mi><mspace 10.</annotation></semantics></math></p>\r\n<p>The variables\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>\u2208</mo><mi>\u2124</mi></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">x, y \\in \\mathbb{Z}</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nhave been replaced by functions</p>\r\n<p><math display=\"block\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>:</mo><mi answer to the question \"what is the probability to win a certain\r\namount\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">P(\\{ \\omega \\in \\Omega \\text{ such that } Y(\\omega)=y \\}).</annotation></semantics></math></p>\r\n<p><strong>Remark.</strong><br />\r\nIt is common to read \"the value of the random variable depends on the\r\nresult of the experiment\". This formulation can be slightly misleading.\r\nIndeed, it is then tempting to believe that a random variable is a\r\nfunction which associates an observed value to each new repetition of an\r\nexperiment. This would suggest to chose\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant=\"normal\">\u03a9</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><msup><mi>\u211d</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>\u00d7</mo><msup><mi>\u211d</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><msup><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">)</mo><mi>N</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\Omega = (\\mathbb R^3\\times \\mathbb R^3)^N</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nwhere\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">N</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nis the number of particules. Wind speed, temperature, air pressure or\r\nfluctuations are functions of the type\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant=\"normal\">\u03a9</mi><mo>\u2192</mo><mi>\u211d</mi></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\Omega \\rightarrow \\mathbb{R}</annotation></semantics></math>,\r\nhence they are random variables. Doing that would enable us to always\r\nuse the same configuration space\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi mathvariant=\"normal\">\u03a9</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\Omega</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nregardless of the details of the modelisation.</p>\r\n<p>In practice, evaluating and manipulating a probability\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi>P</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">P</annotation></semantics></math>\r\non the positions and velocities of each particles is unrealistic. class=\"definition\">\r\n<p><strong>Definition 14</strong> (<strong>Independent random\r\nvariables</strong>). </p>\r\n<p><br />\r\n<br />\r\n</p>\r\n<div style=\"color: blue\">\r\n<hr />\r\n<p><strong>Motivation</strong></p>\r\n</div>\r\n<p><br />\r\nThe notion of independence of two random variables\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi>X</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">X</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nand\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi>Y</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">Y</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nis based on the notion of independence of events.<br />\r\n</p>\r\n<p>Consider two consecutive dice rolls. Call\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi>X</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">X</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nand\r\n<math information on one of them does not affect the\r\nother.</p>\r\n<div style=\"color: blue\">\r\n<hr />\r\n<p><strong>Definition</strong></p>\r\n</div>\r\n<p><br />\r\nTwo random variables\r\n<math Y^{-1}(B) \\text{ are independent events in } \\Omega.</annotation></semantics></math></p>\r\n<div style=\"color: blue\">\r\n<hr />\r\n<p><strong>Remarks</strong></p>\r\n</div>\r\n<p><br />\r\n</p>\r\n<ul>\r\n<li><p>Recall that it means that when\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" Let\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>:</mo><mi mathvariant=\"normal\">\u03a9</mi><mo>\u2192</mo><mi>\u211d</mi></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">X:\\Omega \\rightarrow \\mathbb{R}</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nand\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mi>Y</mi><mo>:</mo><mi mathvariant=\"normal\">\u03a9</mi><mo>\u2192</mo><mi>\u211d</mi></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">Y:\\Omega \\rightarrow \\mathbb{R}</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nbe\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mn>2</mn><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">2</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nrandom variables. \\mapsto X(\\omega)Y(\\omega)</annotation></semantics></math>.<br />\r\n</p>\r\n<p>Why is it an inner product ?</p>\r\n<ul>\r\n<li><p>It is easy to check that the set of random variables\r\n<math </p>\r\n<p><br />\r\n<br />\r\nGiven a random variable\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi>X</mi><annotation It shows\r\nthat regardless of the distribution, the probability of deviating\r\nsignificantly from the mean is controlled by the variance. />\r\n</p>\r\n<div style=\"color: blue\">\r\n<hr />\r\n<p><strong>Definition</strong></p>\r\n</div>\r\n<p><br />\r\nIn general, the adjective \u2019empirical\u2019 is understood as \u2019coming xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover><mi>X</mi><mo xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><msub><mover><mi>X</mi><mo accent=\"true\">\u203e</mo></mover><mi>n</mi></msub><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\bar X_n</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nis called the \u2019empirical mean\u2019.<br />\r\n</p>\r\n<p>By linearity, the expectation of\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><msub><mover><mi>X</mi><mo accent=\"true\">\u203e</mo></mover><mi>n</mi></msub><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\bar X_n</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nis given by\r\n<math display=\"block\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mi>\ud835\udd3c</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><msub><mover><mi>X</mi><mo accent=\"true\">\u203e</mo></mover><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>\ud835\udd3c</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>.</mi><mi>.</mi><mi>.</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>\ud835\udd3c</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">)</mo></mrow><mi>n</mi></mfrac><mi>.</mi></mrow><annotation with expectation</strong></p>\r\n</div>\r\n<p><br />\r\nThe notion of empirical mean has connections but is different from the\r\nnotion of expectation, which is a mean over configurations from\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi mathvariant=\"normal\">\u03a9</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\Omega</annotation></semantics></math>.\r\nRemember that when\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi mathvariant=\"normal\">\u03a9</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\Omega</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nhas a uniform probability over a finite numbers of element,\r\n<math display=\"block\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mi>\ud835\udd3c</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><munderover><mo>\u2211</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">|</mo><mi stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">|</mo><mi mathvariant=\"normal\">\u03a9</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">|</mo></mrow></mfrac><mi>.</mi></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\mathbb{E}(X) = \\frac{\\sum_{i=1}^{|\\Omega|}X(\\omega_i)}{|\\Omega|}.</annotation></semantics></math></p>\r\n<p>Hence,</p>\r\n<ul>\r\n<li><p>the empirical mean is its self a random variable, computed as a\r\nsum over different random variables.</p></li>\r\n<li><p>the expectation is a number, computed for a single random\r\nvariable, as a sum over configurations\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mi>\u03c9</mi><mo>\u2208</mo><mi mathvariant=\"normal\">\u03a9</mi></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\omega\\in \\Omega</annotation></semantics></math>.</p></li>\r\n</ul>\r\n</div>\r\n<div id=\"th:WLLN\" class=\"theorem\">\r\n<p><strong>Theorem 7</strong> (<strong>(Weak) Law of large\r\nnumbers</strong>). </p>\r\n<p><br />\r\n<br />\r\n</p>\r\n<div style=\"color: blue\">\r\n<hr />\r\n<p><strong>Statement of the theorem</strong></p>\r\n</div>\r\n<p><br />\r\nWe are now ready state an important result of form=\"postfix\">)</mo><munderover><mo>\u2192</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>\u2192</mo><mi>\u221e</mi></mrow><mrow></mrow></munderover><mn>0</mn><mi>.</mi></mrow><annotation 0.</annotation></semantics></math></p>\r\n<p>In simple words: when\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mi>\ud835\udd3c</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><mover><mi>X</mi><mo accent=\"true\">\u203e</mo></mover><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>\ud835\udd3c</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy=\"false\" that\r\n<math display=\"block\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mi>v</mi><mrow><mo stretchy=\"true\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><msub><mover><mi>X</mi><mo tells us that the probability\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">|</mo><mo>&gt;</mo><mi>\u03f5</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">P(|\\bar X_n-\\mu |&gt;\\epsilon)</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nshould be smaller and smaller:</p>\r\n<p><math display=\"block\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo 0.</annotation></semantics></math></p>\r\n</div>\r\n<div id=\"th:CLT\" class=\"theorem\">\r\n<p><strong>Theorem 8</strong> (Central Limit Theorem). </p>\r\n<p>The (weak) law of large numbers shows that the empirical mean\r\nconcentrates around the true mean as we increase the number of random\r\nvariables. The Central Limit Theorem (CLT) is a stronger result which\r\ndescribes more precisely how the empirical mean is distributed around\r\nthe true mean. We will not prove the theorem.<br />\r\n</p>\r\n<p>Assume that\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>\u2026</mi></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">X_1,X_2,\\ldots</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nare i.i.d.\u00a0random variables with</p>\r\n<p><math display=\"block\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mi>\ud835\udd3c</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>\u03bc</mi><mspace width=\"1.0em\"></mspace><mtext mathvariant=\"normal\">and</mtext><mspace width=\"1.0em\"></mspace><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>\u03c3</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>.</mi></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\mathbb{E}(X_i)=\\mu \\quad \\text{and} \\quad v(X_i)=\\sigma^2.</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nWe have seen already that</p>\r\n<p><math display=\"block\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mi>\ud835\udd3c</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><msub><mover><mi>X</mi><mo accent=\"true\">\u203e</mo></mover><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>\u03bc</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace width=\"1.0em\"></mspace><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><msup><mi>\u03c3</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>n</mi></mfrac><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\mathbb{E}(\\bar{X}_n)=\\mu, \\quad v(\\bar{X}_n)=\\frac{\\sigma^2}{n},</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nwhere\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><msub><mover><mi>X</mi><mo accent=\"true\">\u203e</mo></mover><mi>n</mi></msub><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\bar{X}_{n}</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nis the empirical mean. The WLLN tells us that the probability of\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><msub><mover><mi>X</mi><mo accent=\"true\">\u203e</mo></mover><mi>n</mi></msub><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\bar{X}_{n}</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nbeing \"far\" from\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi>\u03bc</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\mu</annotation></semantics></math>\r\ngoes to zeros. In some sens, the law of\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><msub><mover><mi>X</mi><mo accent=\"true\">\u203e</mo></mover><mi>n</mi></msub><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\bar{X}_{n}</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nconverges to a Dirac in\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi>\u03bc</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\mu</annotation></semantics></math>.\r\nIn order to characterize more precisely how this convergence happens, we\r\n\"zoom in\" around\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi>\u03bc</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\mu</annotation></semantics></math>.\r\nTo do so, we shift the random variable to move the mean to\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mn>0</mn><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">0</annotation></semantics></math>,\r\nand we multiply it by a scaling factor in order to make it of variance\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mn>1</mn><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">1</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>\r\n<p><math display=\"block\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msqrt><mi>n</mi></msqrt><mspace width=\"0.167em\"></mspace><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><msub><mover><mi>X</mi><mo accent=\"true\">\u203e</mo></mover><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>\u2212</mo><mi>\u03bc</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">)</mo></mrow><mi>\u03c3</mi></mfrac><mi>.</mi></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">Z_n=\\frac{\\sqrt{n}\\,(\\bar{X}_n-\\mu)}{\\sigma}.</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nIt is easy to check that\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mi>\ud835\udd3c</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\mathbb{E}(Z_n)=0</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nand that\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy=\"false\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>\u2192</mo><mi>\u221e</mi></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">n\\to\\infty</annotation></semantics></math>,\r\nthe distribution of\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">Z_n</annotation></semantics></math>\r\napproaches a Gaussian distribution of mean\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mn>0</mn><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">0</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nand variance\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mn>1</mn><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">1</annotation></semantics></math>.\r\nIn other words, for any interval\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">[</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">[a,b]</annotation></semantics></math>,</p>\r\n<p><math display=\"block\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><munder><mi mathvariant=\"normal\">lim</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>\u2192</mo><mi>\u221e</mi></mrow></munder><msub><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></msub><mo minsize=\"300%\" maxsize=\"300%\" stretchy=\"true\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">[</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">]</mo><mo minsize=\"300%\" maxsize=\"300%\" stretchy=\"true\" form=\"postfix\">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mo>\u222b</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi></msubsup><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>\u03c0</mi></mrow></msqrt></mfrac><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>\u2212</mi><mfrac><msup><mi>t</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></msup><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>.</mi></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\lim_{n\\to\\infty}P_{Z_n}\\Bigg( [a,b] \\Bigg)\r\n=\\int_{a}^{b} \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2\\pi}} e^{-\\frac{t^2}{2}}dt.</annotation></semantics></math></p>\r\n<div style=\"color: blue\">\r\n<hr />\r\n<p><strong>Gaussian noise</strong></p>\r\n</div>\r\n<p><br />\r\nThe physical processes generating noises can often be modeled by a sum\r\nof independent tiny contributions. The CLT is a way to explain why noise\r\nvalues often follow a Gaussian distribution.</p>\r\n</div>\r\n<h1 id=\"sec:Statistical estimation\">Statistical estimation</h1>\r\n<div id=\"rem:Disclaimer\" class=\"remark\">\r\n<p><strong>Remark 6</strong> (<strong>Disclaimer</strong>). </p>\r\n<p>In section <a href=\"#sec:Proba\" data-reference-type=\"ref\"\r\ndata-reference=\"sec:Proba\">[sec:Proba]</a>, particular care has been\r\ntaken with the rigor of the notation. From now on, we will not always be\r\nas rigorous and will sometimes commit abuses of notation.</p>\r\n</div>\r\n<h2 id=\"subsec:Estimators\">Estimators</h2>\r\n<div id=\"def:Parametric statistical models\" class=\"definition\">\r\n<p><strong>Definition 23</strong> (<strong>Parametric statistical\r\nmodels</strong>). </p>\r\n<p>Consider a set\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">S</annotation></semantics></math>,\r\nand a certain set\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi>\u2133</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\mathcal{M}</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nof probability distributions on\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">S</annotation></semantics></math>.\r\nWhen elements of\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi>\u2133</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\mathcal{M}</annotation></semantics></math>\r\ncan be parametrized with a finite number of real values, it is called a\r\n<strong>parametric statistical model</strong>.</p>\r\n<p>Ex:\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>\u211d</mi></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">S = \\mathbb{R}</annotation></semantics></math>,\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mi>\u2133</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy=\"true\" form=\"prefix\">{</mo><mtext mathvariant=\"normal\">Gaussian distributions</mtext><mo stretchy=\"true\" form=\"postfix\">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\mathcal{M} = \\left\\{ \\text{Gaussian distributions} \\right\\}</annotation></semantics></math>.\r\nSince Gaussian distributions can be parametrized by\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><mi>\u03bc</mi><mo>=</mo><mtext mathvariant=\"normal\">mean</mtext><mo>,</mo><mspace \\text{mean},\\; \\sigma = \\text{std})</annotation></semantics></math>,\r\nthey form a parametric statistical model.</p>\r\n</div>\r\n<div id=\"def:Estimators\" class=\"definition\">\r\n<p><strong>Definition 24</strong> (<strong>Estimators</strong>). </p>\r\n<p><span style=\"color: blue\"><strong>Context</strong></span><br />\r\nAssume that we are interested in modeling the output of an experiment by\r\na certain probability distribution in\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi>\u2133</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\mathcal{M}</annotation></semantics></math>.\r\nThe task of choosing this distribution from a set of observations\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>\u2026</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">x_1, \\dots, x_n</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nis an \u201cestimation problem\u201d. This course is only focused on \u201cparametric\u201d\r\nestimation, that is to say estimation problems in a parametric\r\nstatistical model\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi>\u2133</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\mathcal{M}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>\r\n<p><strong>Ex:</strong> Given observations\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>\u2026</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>\u2208</mo><mi>\u211d</mi></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">x_1, \\dots, x_n \\in \\mathbb{R}</annotation></semantics></math>,\r\nwhich element of\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mi>\u2133</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy=\"true\" form=\"prefix\">{</mo><mtext mathvariant=\"normal\">Gaussian distributions</mtext><mo stretchy=\"true\" form=\"postfix\">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\mathcal{M} = \\left\\{ \\text{Gaussian distributions} \\right\\}</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nwill we choose to model the experiment?</p>\r\n<div style=\"color: blue\">\r\n<hr />\r\n<p><strong>Definition</strong></p>\r\n</div>\r\n<p><br />\r\nAn estimator is a function that takes a collection of observations and\r\ngives a certain probability distribution in the statistical model\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi>\u2133</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\mathcal{M}</annotation></semantics></math>.\r\nIf the observations are in\r\n<math function\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>:</mo><msup><mi>\u211d</mi><mi>n</mi></msup><mo>\u2192</mo><mi>\u2133</mi></mrow><annotation xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi>\u2133</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\mathcal M</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nis parametrized by\r\n<math />\r\n<p><strong>Exemple</strong></p>\r\n</div>\r\n<p><br />\r\nLet\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mi>\u2133</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo \\right\\}</annotation></semantics></math>.\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi>\u2133</mi><annotation x_i^2</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nis also a function\r\n<math display=\"inline\" \\mathbb{R}</annotation></semantics></math>,\r\nso it is also an estimator. It is just a bad estimator.<br />\r\n</p>\r\n<div style=\"color: blue\">\r\n<hr />\r\n<p><strong>2 remarks</strong></p>\r\n</div>\r\n<p><br />\r\n</p>\r\n<ul>\r\n<li><p>Sometimes we are not interested in estimating a probability\r\ndistribution but just a parameter of that distribution. When</p>\r\n<p><math display=\"block\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mi>\u2133</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy=\"true\" form=\"prefix\">{</mo><mtext xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>:</mo><msup><mi>\u211d</mi><mi>n</mi></msup><mo>\u2192</mo><mi>\u211d</mi><mo>,</mo><mspace \\mathbb{R}^n.</annotation></semantics></math></p></li>\r\n</ul>\r\n</div>\r\n<div id=\"def:Likelihood function\" class=\"definition\">\r\n<p><strong>Definition 25</strong> (<strong>Likelihood\r\nfunction</strong>). </p>\r\n<p>Assume that we have a collection\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>\u2026</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>\u2208</mo><mo stretchy=\"false\" \\{0,1\\}</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nwas obtained by repeating an experiment in identical conditions. In a\r\nprobabilistic model, a random variable\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">X_i</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nis associated to each repetition of the experiment.</p>\r\n<p>If we assume that the experiment is not affected by the previous\r\noutcome, the\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">X_i</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nshould be independent. If the experiment is repeated in identical\r\nconditions, then the\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">X_i</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nfrom the model should have the same law.</p>\r\n<p>Hence the\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">X_i</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nare i.i.d. random variables.</p>\r\n<p>In the rest of the course, we always consider an i.i.d. hypothesis on\r\nobservations. Though it is a common hypothesis, it is not always true in\r\npractice and results should be adapted in consequence.</p>\r\n<p>In an estimation problem, we wish to determine the law\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi>P</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">P</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nof these random variables. The joint law is then obtain by taking\r\nproducts of probabilities,</p>\r\n<p><math display=\"block\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant=\"normal\">\u03a0</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">P(X_1=x_1,\\dots,X_n=x_n) = \\Pi_i P(X_i=x_i)</annotation></semantics></math></p>\r\n<p>When we restrict the estimation problem to a statistical model\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mi>\u2133</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">{</mo><msub><mi>\u2119</mi><mi>\u03b8</mi></msub><mo parameter\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi>\u03b8</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\theta</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nand gives the probability of the observation is called the\r\n<strong>likelihood function</strong>\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi>L</mi><annotation xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mi>\u03b8</mi><mo>\u21a6</mo><mi>L</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>\u2026</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant=\"normal\">\u03a0</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\theta \\mapsto L(\\theta; x_1, \\dots, x_n) = P(X_1=x_1,\\dots,X_n=x_n) = \\Pi_i P(X_i=x_i)</annotation></semantics></math></p>\r\n<p>The symbol ; is an informal way of indicating that the function\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi>L</mi><annotation xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi>\u03b8</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\theta</annotation></semantics></math>.\r\nFor each\r\n<math display=\"inline\" <em>log-likelihood</em>,</p>\r\n<p><math display=\"block\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mi>\u2113</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" stretchy=\"true\" form=\"postfix\">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><munderover><mo>\u2211</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><mrow><mi mathvariant=\"normal\">log</mi><mo>&#8289;</mo></mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>\u03b8</mi></msub><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy=\"false\" P_\\theta(x_i)</annotation></semantics></math></p>\r\n</div>\r\n<div id=\"disc:What makes an estimator good or bad?\" class=\"discussion\">\r\n<p><strong>Discussion 1</strong> (<strong>What makes an estimator good\r\nor bad?</strong>). </p>\r\n<p>This question is non-trivial.</p>\r\n<p>Assume that the repetition of an experiment produced the observations\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>\u2026</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">)</mo><mo>\u2208</mo><msup><mi>S</mi><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">(x_1, \\dots, x_n)\\in S^n</annotation></semantics></math>.\r\nWe want to build a probabilistic model of the experiment. \\hat{\\theta}-\\theta_{\\mathrm{true}}}\r\n  \\bigr)^{2}\r\n\\Bigr)\r\n&amp;=\r\n\\left( \\mathbb{E}_{\\theta_{\\mathrm{true}}}(\\hat{\\theta}) - \\theta_{\\mathrm{true}} \\right)^2\r\n+ \\mathbb{E}_{\\theta_{\\mathrm{true}}}\\!\\left( \\left( \\hat{\\theta} - \\mathbb{E}_{\\theta_{\\mathrm{true}}}(\\hat{\\theta}) \\right)^2 \\right).\r\n\\end{aligned}</annotation></semantics></math></p>\r\n<p>Or,\r\n<math display=\"block\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mtext mathvariant=\"normal\">MSE</mtext><mo>=</mo><msup><mtext mathvariant=\"normal\">bias</mtext><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mtext mathvariant=\"normal\">variance</mtext></mrow><annotation have bias\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">= 0</annotation></semantics></math>.\r\nThis means that\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mover><mi>\u03b8</mi><mo accent=\"true\">\u0302</mo></mover><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\hat{\\theta}</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nis \u201cevenly distributed\u201d around\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><msub><mi>\u03b8</mi><mtext mathvariant=\"normal\">true</mtext></msub><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\theta_{\\text{true}}</annotation></semantics></math>.\r\nIn that case,\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mtext mathvariant=\"normal\">MSE</mtext><mo>=</mo><mtext mathvariant=\"normal\">variance</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\text{MSE} = \\text{variance}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>\r\n</div>\r\n<div id=\"def:Unbiased estimators\" class=\"definition\">\r\n<p><strong>Definition 31</strong> (<strong>Unbiased\r\nestimators</strong>). </p>\r\n<p>An estimator is called unbiased when,\r\n<math display=\"block\" mathvariant=\"normal\">true</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mi>.</mi></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\forall \\theta_{\\text{true}}, \\quad \\mathbb{E}_{\\theta_{\\text{true}}}(\\hat{\\theta}) - \\theta_{\\text{true}} = 0.</annotation></semantics></math></p>\r\n<div style=\"color: blue\">\r\n<hr variance</mtext><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\mathcal{M} = \\{ \\text{Gaussians with fixed variance} \\nu</annotation></semantics></math></p>\r\n<p>Hence\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mover><mi>\u03bd</mi><mo xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mover><mi>\u03bd</mi><mo accent=\"true\">\u0302</mo></mover><mo stretchy=\"false\" \\right) \\right)^2</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nis biased.</p>\r\n</div>\r\n<h2 id=\"subsec:The Cramer-Rao bound\">The Cramer-Rao bound</h2>\r\n<div id=\"disc:Variations between probability distributions\"\r\nclass=\"discussion\">\r\n<p><strong>Discussion 3</strong> (<strong>Variations between probability\r\ndistributions</strong>). </p>\r\n<p>Consider a statistical model\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi>\u2133</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\mathcal{M}</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nparametrized by\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi>\u03b8</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\theta</annotation></semantics></math>.\r\nHow difficult is it to build a \u201cgood\u201d estimator?<br />\r\nGeneral idea: if the probability distributions in\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi>\u2133</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\mathcal{M}</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nare very different from each other, they are easy to distinguish. If the\r\ndistribution are almost identical, it will be difficult to build a good\r\nestimator. If we quantify how different the probability distributions\r\nare in\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi>\u2133</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\mathcal{M}</annotation></semantics></math>,\r\nwe can also hope to quantify how good can an estimator can be. To do so,\r\nwe will first start by describing a way to quantify variations between\r\nprobability distributions. This will later lead us to the Cramer-Rao\r\nbound (CRB), which informs us on how good an estimator can be. Though\r\nthe CRB is a fundamental brick of the theory of statistical estimation,\r\nthere exists many other ways of linking distances between probability\r\ndistirbutions and quality of estimators, which we will not address in\r\nthis course.<br />\r\n</p>\r\n<p>Assume that there are\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Q</mi><mo>\u2208</mo><mi>\u2133</mi></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">P, Q \\in \\mathcal{M}</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nwhich are very similar. \\right)\r\n  = \\operatorname{Var} \\left( \\frac{\\partial}{\\partial \\theta} \\ln \\ell(\\theta; X_1) \r\n  + \\frac{\\partial}{\\partial \\theta} \\ln \\ell(\\theta; X_2) \\right),</annotation></semantics></math></p>\r\n<p>and if\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation independent,</p>\r\n<p><math display=\"block\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mtable><mtr><mtd columnalign=\"right\" style=\"text-align: \\ell(\\theta; X_1, X_2) \\right)^2 \\right) &amp;=&amp; \\operatorname{Var} \\left( \\frac{\\partial}{\\partial \\theta} \\ln \\ell(\\theta; X_1) \\right) \r\n  + \\operatorname{Var} \\left( \\frac{\\partial}{\\partial \\theta} \\ln \\ell(\\theta; X_2) \\right)\\\\\r\n&amp;=&amp; 2 \\cdot \\operatorname{Var} \\left( \\frac{\\partial}{\\partial \\theta} \\ln \\ell(\\theta; X_1) \\right).\r\n\\end{align*}</annotation></semantics></math></p>\r\n<p>For\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">n</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nobservations, it gives\r\n<math display=\"block\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>\u2110</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><mi>\u03b8</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>\u22c5</mo><mi>\u2110</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><mi>\u03b8</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" information grows proportionnally to the number of\r\nobservations.</p>\r\n</div>\r\n<div id=\"th:The Cramer-Rao bound\" class=\"theorem\">\r\n<p><strong>Theorem 9</strong> (<strong>The Cramer-Rao bound</strong>).\r\n</p>\r\n<p>Fix a parameter\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><msub><mi>\u03b8</mi><mtext mathvariant=\"normal\">true</mtext></msub><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\theta_{\\text{true}}</annotation></semantics></math>.\r\nThis sets a probability distribution\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><msub><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>\u03b8</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>e</mi></mrow></msub></msub><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">P_{\\theta_{true}}</annotation></semantics></math>,\r\nor simply\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><msub><mi>P</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>e</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">P_{true}</annotation></semantics></math>,\r\non\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">S</annotation></semantics></math>.\r\nUnder the independence assumption, this distribution gives a\r\ndistribution on\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><msup><mi>S</mi><mi>n</mi></msup><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">S^n</annotation></semantics></math>.\r\nRecall that an estimator\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mover><mi>\u03b8</mi><mo accent=\"true\">\u0302</mo></mover><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\hat \\theta</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nis a function\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>S</mi><mi>n</mi></msup><mo>\u2192</mo><mi mathvariant=\"normal\">\u0398</mi></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">S^n\\rightarrow \\Theta</annotation></semantics></math>.\r\nThe more the law of\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mover><mi>\u03b8</mi><mo accent=\"true\">\u0302</mo></mover><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\hat \\theta</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nis concentrated around\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><msub><mi>\u03b8</mi><mtext mathvariant=\"normal\">true</mtext></msub><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\theta_{\\text{true}}</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nthe better. When\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant=\"normal\">\u0398</mi><mo>\u2282</mo><mi>\u211d</mi></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\Theta \\subset \\mathbb{R}</annotation></semantics></math>,\r\nthis can be quantified by the mean squared error. If the estimator\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mover><mi>\u03b8</mi><mo accent=\"true\">\u0302</mo></mover><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\hat{\\theta}</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nis assumed unbiased, the MSE is simply the variance.<br />\r\n</p>\r\n<p>For any unbiased estimator\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mover><mi>\u03b8</mi><mo accent=\"true\">\u0302</mo></mover><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\hat{\\theta}</annotation></semantics></math>,\r\nthe <strong>Cram\u00e9r\u2013Rao bound</strong> is\r\n<math display=\"block\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant=\"normal\">Var</mi><mo>&#8289;</mo></mrow><mtext mathvariant=\"normal\">true</mtext></msub><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><mover><mi>\u03b8</mi><mo accent=\"true\">\u0302</mo></mover><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">)</mo><mo>\u2265</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>\u2110</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><msub><mi>\u03b8</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>e</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">)</mo></mrow></mfrac><mi>.</mi></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\operatorname{Var}_{\\text{true}}(\\hat{\\theta}) \\geq \r\n\\frac{1}{\\mathcal{I}(\\theta_{true})}.</annotation></semantics></math></p>\r\n<p>This is the relation announced in the begining of discussion <a\r\nhref=\"#disc:Variations between probability distributions\"\r\ndata-reference-type=\"ref\"\r\ndata-reference=\"disc:Variations between probability distributions\">3</a>.</p>\r\n<div style=\"color: blue\">\r\n<hr />\r\n<p><strong>Remarks</strong></p>\r\n</div>\r\n<p><br />\r\n</p>\r\n<ul>\r\n<li><p>The bound depends on\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><msub><mi>\u03b8</mi><mtext mathvariant=\"normal\">true</mtext></msub><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\theta_{\\text{true}}</annotation></semantics></math>,\r\nsome parameters might be easier to estimate than others.</p></li>\r\n<li><p>The bound only looks at the neighborhood of\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>\u03b8</mi></msub><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">P_\\theta</annotation></semantics></math>.\r\nEven if neighboring distributions are significantly different from\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>\u03b8</mi></msub><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">P_\\theta</annotation></semantics></math>,\r\nthere might be a\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><msup><mi>\u03b8</mi><mo>\u2032</mo></msup><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\theta&#39;</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nfar from\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi>\u03b8</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\theta</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nwith\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><msup><mi>\u03b8</mi><mo>\u2032</mo></msup></msub><mo>\u2243</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>\u03b8</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">P_{\\theta&#39;} \\simeq P_\\theta</annotation></semantics></math>.\r\nIf\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>\u03b8</mi><mtext mathvariant=\"normal\">true</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>\u03b8</mi></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\theta_{\\text{true}} = \\theta</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nor\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><msup><mi>\u03b8</mi><mo>\u2032</mo></msup><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\theta&#39;</annotation></semantics></math>,\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant=\"normal\">Var</mi><mo>&#8289;</mo></mrow><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><mover><mi>\u03b8</mi><mo accent=\"true\">\u0302</mo></mover><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\operatorname{Var}(\\hat{\\theta})</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nwill be large even though it is not reflected in the bound. This shows\r\nthat there are cases for which there are no estimators which achieve the\r\nminimal variance given by the bound.</p></li>\r\n<li><p>When the estimator\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mover><mi>\u03b8</mi><mo accent=\"true\">\u0302</mo></mover><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\hat{\\theta}</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nhas a bias\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><msub><mi>\u03b8</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>e</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>\ud835\udd3c</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>e</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><mover><mi>\u03b8</mi><mo accent=\"true\">\u0302</mo></mover><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">)</mo><mo>\u2212</mo><msub><mi>\u03b8</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>e</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">b(\\theta_{true}) = \\mathbb{E}_{true}(\\hat{\\theta}) - \\theta_{true}</annotation></semantics></math>,\r\nthe bound becomes\r\n<math display=\"block\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant=\"normal\">Var</mi><mo>&#8289;</mo></mrow><mtext mathvariant=\"normal\">true</mtext></msub><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><mover><mi>\u03b8</mi><mo accent=\"true\">\u0302</mo></mover><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">)</mo><mo>\u2265</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>b</mi><mo>\u2032</mo></msup><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><msub><mi>\u03b8</mi><mtext mathvariant=\"normal\">true</mtext></msub><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">)</mo><msup><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">)</mo><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mrow><mi>\u2110</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><msub><mi>\u03b8</mi><mtext mathvariant=\"normal\">true</mtext></msub><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">)</mo></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\operatorname{Var}_{\\text{true}}(\\hat{\\theta}) \r\n  \\geq \\frac{(1 + b&#39;(\\theta_{\\text{true}}))^2}\r\n         {\\mathcal{I}(\\theta_{\\text{true}})}</annotation></semantics></math></p></li>\r\n<li><p>Consider a constant estimator\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mover><mi>\u03b8</mi><mo accent=\"true\">\u0302</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>\u03b8</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>\u2208</mo><mi mathvariant=\"normal\">\u0398</mi></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\hat \\theta = \\theta_0 \\in \\Theta</annotation></semantics></math>.\r\nWhen\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>\u03b8</mi><mtext mathvariant=\"normal\">true</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>\u03b8</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\theta_{\\text{true}}=\\theta_0</annotation></semantics></math>,\r\nthe estimator always gives the correct value, which mean that its\r\nvariance is\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mn>0</mn><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">0</annotation></semantics></math>,\r\napparently contradicting the CRB. Note that such an estimator is biased:\r\n<math display=\"block\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><msub><mi>\u03b8</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>e</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>\ud835\udd3c</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>e</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><mover><mi>\u03b8</mi><mo accent=\"true\">\u0302</mo></mover><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">)</mo><mo>\u2212</mo><msub><mi>\u03b8</mi><mtext mathvariant=\"normal\">true</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>\u03b8</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>\u2212</mo><msub><mi>\u03b8</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>e</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mspace width=\"1.0em\"></mspace><msup><mi>b</mi><mo>\u2032</mo></msup><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><msub><mi>\u03b8</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>e</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>\u2212</mi><mn>1</mn><mi>.</mi></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">b(\\theta_{true})=\\mathbb{E}_{true}(\\hat \\theta) - \\theta_{\\text{true}}=\\theta_0-\\theta_{true}, \\quad b&#39;(\\theta_{true})=-1.</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nApplying the correct formula for biased estimators only tells that the\r\nvariance is positive. So, the CRB still holds, though not it is not very\r\nusefull.</p></li>\r\n</ul>\r\n<div style=\"color: blue\">\r\n<hr />\r\n<p><strong>Proof of the CRB (clean this!!)</strong></p>\r\n</div>\r\n<p><br />\r\nAssume that\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mi>X</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">X</annotation></semantics></math>\r\nfollows\r\n<math display=\"inline\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><msub><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>\u03b8</mi><mtext mathvariant=\"normal\">true</mtext></msub></msub><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">P_{\\theta_{\\text{true}}}</annotation></semantics></math>.\r\nIn the discrete case, we have\r\n<math display=\"block\" xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML\"><semantics><mrow><mi>\ud835\udd3c</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><mi>V</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><msub><mi>\u03b8</mi><mtext mathvariant=\"normal\">true</mtext></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">)</mo><mover><mi>\u03b8</mi><mo accent=\"true\">\u0302</mo></mover><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">)</mo><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">)</mo><mo>=</mo><munder><mo>\u2211</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>\u2208</mo><mi>S</mi></mrow></munder><mi>V</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><msub><mi>\u03b8</mi><mtext mathvariant=\"normal\">true</mtext></msub><mo>;</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">)</mo><mover><mi>\u03b8</mi><mo accent=\"true\">\u0302</mo></mover><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"postfix\">)</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>X</mi></msub><mo stretchy=\"false\" form=\"prefix\">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\"
